#6224. 7 Things Pilots Say That Make The Boeing 737 A Unique Jet To Fly

MC MEDIASTUDIO | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Ask a pilot who has flown both Airbus and Boeing narrowbodies to describe the Boeing 737, and the conversation will probably turn to something other than speed, range, or passenger capacity. It might be the feel of the controls, or the way the aircraft responds to a pilot's hands. Boeing has repeatedly updated the aircraft since the late 1960s, as its own history of the family shows. But despite all those changes, the 737 has retained some characteristics that have become rather unusual in modern commercial aviation.

These differences are particularly noticeable to pilots who have experience with both Boeing and Airbus aircraft. Some appreciate the physical feedback and the involvement it demands, while others point to additional workload and features that newer designs have automated. So what actually makes the 737 such a distinctive aircraft to fly? We have picked seven characteristics that pilots often discuss on aviation forums and that have featured in our previous reporting. The countdown moves from the broader philosophy behind the aircraft to the mechanical feature that arguably explains everything else. The last one is particularly important, because it is the reason several of the others still exist.

To understand why the 737 feels different, it helps to look at the philosophy behind its design. Boeing has traditionally maintained a more direct relationship between the pilot and several aircraft systems, allowing crews to see, hear, and physically feel things that newer aircraft increasingly handle through automation. This does not mean the 737 lacks advanced systems. The Boeing 737 MAX, in particular, has a thoroughly modern flight deck. However, some of the fundamental design choices made decades ago remain visible in the way pilots interact with the aircraft.

The difference becomes particularly apparent when airlines move crews between Boeing and Airbus fleets. Simple Flying examined how Qantas pilots transitioning from the 737 to the Airbus A321XLR leave behind traditional control columns and a different approach to flight control for fly-by-wire sidesticks and flight envelope protection. The aircraft are built around fundamentally different control philosophies, which is why moving between them requires a full type rating, and not simply learning a different arrangement of cockpit buttons. For pilots, the adjustment involves changing familiar habits and learning to interpret the aircraft's responses in a different way.

This broader philosophy is difficult to describe through a single component. It is an attitude towards aircraft design that runs through much of the 737's cockpit. And one of those design choices is visible even before the aircraft leaves the gate.

Walk around a parked 737 and look underneath the wings. Unlike most modern commercial aircraft, the Boeing narrowbody does not have conventional doors covering its main landing gear wheels when they retract. Instead, the wheels remain partially exposed, with their hubs and rubber seals forming the visible outer surface of the landing gear installation. It is one of those details that makes the aircraft instantly recognizable to aviation enthusiasts, although most passengers probably never give it a second thought.

There is a practical reason for the arrangement. The 737's main landing gear design reflects an emphasis on simplicity and reduced mechanical complexity. The aircraft was originally intended to operate from smaller airports, where ground handling and maintenance requirements mattered considerably. Its relatively low stance also made it easier for baggage handlers and mechanics to reach cargo holds and engine components without requiring additional lifting equipment. Boltflight's engineering analysis explores the reasoning behind the exposed wheels, while Simple Flying has also examined how this particular characteristic has survived successive generations of the aircraft.

There is also an engineering price to pay for keeping the aircraft so close to the ground. A 2019 HeraldNet report highlighted how the 737's low profile became a constraint when engineers attempted to modernize the aircraft. Raising the airframe or substantially changing the landing gear arrangement would have involved much more than a cosmetic redesign.

Still, this characteristic does not explain why pilots can have such strong opinions about actually flying one. For that, we need to move into the cockpit, where a seemingly small difference can make itself felt on every flight.

Explore the striking Airbus A320 vs. Boeing 737 cockpit differences, from sidesticks to noise, and learn how pilots see these iconic flight decks.

One of the less obvious differences between the 737 and many newer airliners concerns something pilots use throughout practically every flight: pitch trim. The system helps maintain the aircraft's desired attitude without requiring the pilots to apply continuous pressure to the control column. On many modern aircraft, automatic trim adjustments are integrated into the flight control system. The 737 MAX, however, retains a more traditional approach, leaving pilots with a greater degree of manual involvement in managing trim.

It might sound like a relatively minor distinction, but the difference becomes noticeable during a busy operating day. Trim settings need to change as the aircraft accelerates, climbs, descends, and changes configuration. The autopilot can also make adjustments, but pilots still have to understand what the aircraft is doing and manage the trim accordingly. The workload is not necessarily dramatic, yet it is another task that remains part of the 737 flying experience.

Not every pilot considers this a disadvantage. In fact, opinions on the subject are quite divided. Some appreciate having more direct control over the aircraft and feel that manual trimming is simply part of flying a conventional airliner. Others would happily let the automation take care of more of the work. One former 737 Classic pilot, writing on PPRuNe, described the frustration of disconnecting the autopilot during an approach only to find that the aircraft was not properly trimmed. It is hardly the ideal moment to discover that another adjustment is needed, particularly when the crew is already managing a busy approach.

This illustrates how the same characteristic can be appreciated by one pilot and disliked by another. The 737 makes it difficult to forget that a human being is still managing the machine. And sometimes, the aircraft makes that involvement particularly obvious by moving something that pilots can actually see.

Imagine sitting in the cockpit with your hands resting near the thrust levers when, without anyone touching them, both levers begin moving forward. There is no malfunction and no mysterious force at work. It is simply the 737's autothrottle doing its job. Unlike systems that adjust engine power without physically moving the cockpit controls, the Boeing system drives the thrust levers forward and backward as the required thrust changes.

For pilots, this creates a very tangible connection between the automation and the aircraft's engines. The crew can see the thrust levers move and, if their hands are resting on them, physically feel the adjustments. It is a small detail, but one that gives the flight deck a rather different character from aircraft where the automation operates largely out of sight. The system is still doing much of the work, but it is not hiding its actions from the people responsible for the flight.

This familiarity also extends across generations of the aircraft. Simple Flying's look at the 737 MAX cockpit explains how pilots moving from the Next-Generation 737 to the MAX encounter a familiar yoke, throttle quadrant, and general cockpit arrangement despite the introduction of newer displays and systems. The moving thrust levers are part of that continuity. A pilot transitioning between generations does not have to relearn the basic relationship between the thrust controls and the automation.

The system offers something pilots can appreciate immediately. There is no need to look through a technical manual to understand what is happening: the thrust levers move, and the crew knows that the autothrottle is making an adjustment. But there is another cockpit component that takes this physical feedback considerably further. It is positioned right beside the pilots' knees, and when it starts moving, nobody in the cockpit needs a display to know about it.

Look down beside a 737 pilot's knees, and you will find two large stabilizer trim wheels. They are among the most recognizable features of the aircraft's cockpit. Whenever the stabilizer trim system makes an adjustment, the wheels rotate, often producing a distinctive mechanical whirring or rattling sound. During certain phases of flight, particularly when the aircraft is climbing or changing configuration, that sound becomes part of the cockpit's background noise.

The wheels provide a visible indication of what the trim system is doing, but their usefulness does not stop there. Pilots can physically grab them and operate the stabilizer trim manually, including when overriding electric trim or the autopilot. This is an unusual arrangement in modern commercial aircraft, where flight control systems have progressively moved away from large, exposed mechanical controls. Simple Flying has described the wheels as a feature that quietly disappeared from newer aircraft, making them one of the more distinctive parts of the 737 cockpit.

Their importance is also apparent to aviation enthusiasts who build home flight simulators. Guides to constructing a home 737 cockpit devote considerable attention to reproducing the trim wheels and their position beside the pilots. The wheels are an integral part of the way the aircraft is operated, giving crews a direct mechanical indication of stabilizer movement.

Few cockpit details make the 737's traditional approach to flight controls quite so apparent. The wheels are visible, audible, and physically accessible, even when the aircraft is operating under autopilot. Yet their importance becomes even clearer when something goes wrong. The mechanical connection has a very important job when the aircraft loses the hydraulic assistance that normally makes its controls easy to operate.

Explore the striking Airbus A320 vs. Boeing 737 cockpit differences, from sidesticks to noise, and learn how pilots see these iconic flight decks.

A failure of both main hydraulic systems is not something any pilot wants to experience. Hydraulic power is essential to the normal operation of an airliner's flight controls, and losing it would create an extremely serious situation. The 737, however, has a feature that gives it an additional layer of protection: manual reversion. Even after losing hydraulic assistance, pilots retain a mechanical connection through cables that allows them to operate certain flight controls, including the ailerons and elevators.

This is one of the more unusual characteristics of the aircraft when compared with many other twin-engine commercial jets. Simple Flying has noted how the 737's flight control arrangement retains mechanical connections that provide a means of control when hydraulic assistance is unavailable. The system is not designed to make the aircraft feel normal after such a failure. Rather, it provides a way for the crew to retain control and attempt to bring the aircraft to a safe landing.

Pilots discussing the subject on PPRuNe have offered a useful comparison: flying the aircraft in manual reversion is like driving a car without power steering. The mechanical connection remains, but moving the controls requires considerably more physical effort. The aircraft can still be controlled, but the workload and physical demands are substantially different.

There is also an interesting discussion about how often crews should practice this kind of operation. One PPRuNe thread makes the case for regular manual reversion training, highlighting how important it is for pilots to understand what the aircraft will feel like when hydraulic assistance is lost. It is one thing to know that a backup system exists; it is quite another to experience the force required to operate the controls.

Manual reversion demonstrates just how much of the 737's original mechanical architecture remains relevant. It is a backup that pilots hope never to need, but one that can make a critical difference when normal systems are no longer available. And it leads directly to the most important characteristic on this list: the physical connection between the pilots and the aircraft.

The defining characteristic of the 737 is arguably the simplest one to identify: it is flown using a traditional control wheel, or yoke, connected to the aircraft's flight control surfaces through a mechanical system. This is a fundamental difference from Airbus fly-by-wire aircraft, where pilots use sidesticks, and their inputs are transmitted electronically to the flight control computers. On the 737, the yoke is connected through cables and pulleys to the ailerons and elevators, maintaining a physical connection between the pilot's movements and the aircraft's controls. Simple Flying examined some of the most striking differences between the Airbus A320 and Boeing 737 cockpits, including this traditional control arrangement.

That does not mean pilots are moving the control surfaces entirely through their own physical strength. The 737 uses two main hydraulic systems, A and B, to provide the assistance needed to operate the controls during normal flight. Either system can provide hydraulic power to the flight controls, giving the aircraft redundancy in the event of a single-system failure. Simple Flying's detailed tour of the 737 MAX flight controls explains how this arrangement works in the latest generation of the aircraft. The mechanical linkage remains an important part of the system, while hydraulic assistance makes the controls manageable throughout the flight.

This is the number one feature because it provides the foundation for almost everything else on the list. The mechanical connections explain why manual reversion remains possible. The hydraulic systems explain how the aircraft combines that traditional arrangement with the assistance needed for normal commercial operations. The trim wheels and their physical movement are another expression of the same design philosophy, as is the cockpit's emphasis on letting pilots see and feel what the aircraft is doing.

The 737 has evolved enormously since its first generation entered service. Its engines, avionics, cockpit displays, and performance have all changed, and the MAX is a considerably more sophisticated aircraft than the original Boeing 737-100. Yet the basic relationship between the pilot and the flight controls remains recognizable. That is ultimately what makes the aircraft so distinctive to fly. Even with modern automation doing much of the work, the 737 still gives its pilots a cockpit in which the machinery has a very visible, and sometimes very audible, presence.

#6223. Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur Opens With 268 Suites And Record Pricing

The Waldorf Astoria brand has been on an impressive growth trajectory in recent times, and has opened several new flagship properties. This Hilton luxury brand has just opened its latest hotel, in Kuala Lumpur. It looks beautiful, but I can’t help but wonder if it will succeed. Let me explain…

The Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur has opened as of late October 2026. The residential-style, all-suite property features 268 accommodations, ranging in size from 80 square meters (861 square feet) to 745 square meters (8,019 square feet).

The property is set within Kuala Lumpur’s “Golden Triangle” district, and as you’d expect, it’s intended to be an urban retreat with both extensive dining and wellness facilities.

Dining options are headlined by Jean-Georges Vongerichten’s signature market-to-table concepts at JG KL, abc kitchens KL, and The Bar by JG. Then there’s also The Istana (where breakfast is served), Yaari (serving Indian cuisine), and Peacock Alley (the signature Waldorf Astoria bar concept).

The Waldorf Astoria Spa is 2,275 square meters (24,488 square feet), and features La Prairie treatments. Then there’s a fitness center, along with an outdoor pool.

Based on the renderings that have been shared so far, the property looks beautiful, in my opinion.

Kuala Lumpur is one of my favorite hotel markets in the world, in terms of how reasonably priced luxury hotels are, at least by international standards (of course I understand that doesn’t factor in local buying power). The city’s current top hotels, like the Four Seasons and Park Hyatt, can be had for around $300 per night.

With that in mind, what are rates like at the Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur? Well, the hotel is trying to set a new pricing record in the city, and not just by a small margin. I see the absolute lowest rate currently being $479 per night, though seasonally rates are $600+. That’s before taxes and fees, for a base suite.

If you’re booking a cash rate, I’d recommend doing so through the Hilton for Luxury program, which offers extra perks when booking through select travel advisors, including breakfast, a hotel credit, an upgrade subject to availability, and more.

For those redeeming Hilton Honors points, the rate seems to be 100,000 points per night, assuming a standard suite is available. At my valuation of 0.5 cents per Hilton point, that’s like “paying” $500 per night to stay here, inclusive of taxes and fees.

When you consider that standard suites are over 860 square feet, that price probably doesn’t seem unreasonable. You’re getting more than twice the space you’d ordinarily get at the city’s top luxury hotels, so it’s not illogical that the pricing would be higher.

If this hotel had 60 accommodations, I’d say there’s probably a market for that, by just chasing the very top end of consumers who value space. But 268 accommodations?! That’s an absolutely massive number of suites to fill at record prices. I mean, this hotel will have more keys than the Park Hyatt Kuala Lumpur.

I just can’t imagine the hotel will be able to run any sort of decent occupancy with that pricing, and so many suites to fill. Either I’m wrong, or the hotel will have to lower prices, or will consistently run low occupancy.

The other thing is that if you’re not specifically looking for a suite, it’s really hard to compete with the Park Hyatt Kuala Lumpur, which is also new, and a really stellar property. It also creates intrigue among people, given that it’s one of the world’s highest up hotels.

The Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur is now open. The 268-suite property is setting new records in the city, both for entry level room size, and also for pricing. The property looks beautiful, and the dining options also look top notch. However, filling 268 rooms at rates that are 50%+ higher than any existing option will be a challenge.

What do you make of the Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur? Do you think they’ll be able to get these rates while running decent occupancy?

#6221. United Airlines’ JFK Return Is Imminent: What’s The Strategy, Though?

We know that United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby thinks that one of the carrier’s biggest mistakes in the past was pulling out of New York Kennedy Airport (JFK). He’s committed to changing that, and the airline still seems to think that it’s on track to return to the airport in 2027.

A lot has changed since this was initially a big topic of conversation, including United seemingly no longer being interested in any sort of merger with JetBlue. So with United potentially within a year of returning to JFK, I’d like to talk a bit more about what that could look like, as I’m still not sure I fully understand the strategy.

United obviously has a huge hub at Newark Liberty Airport (EWR), and different airline executives have different takes as to the overlap in demand between Newark and Kennedy.

Through late 2015, United had a relatively small presence at JFK, with a majority of the service consisting of premium transcontinental flights to Los Angeles (LAX) and San Francisco (SFO), with a product that was branded as p.s. The airline operated these flights with specially configured, three cabin Boeing 757-200s.

However, in late 2015, the airline made the decision to end service at JFK, and instead consolidate flights at EWR. The airline was reportedly losing money on these flights, and just couldn’t compete with American and Delta, which both had major hubs there.

Shortly after that decision was made, Kirby joined United, before eventually being appointed CEO. For as long as he has been at United, Kirby has felt that leaving JFK was one of the carrier’s biggest strategic blunders. In 2021, United briefly returned to JFK, operating transcon routes with Boeing 767-300ERs. However, the airline pulled out by 2022, as it couldn’t get permanent slots, and couldn’t scale service in a way that made sense.

Ever since, United has been determined to return to JFK. We know that United wants up to 20 daily slot pairs at the airport, to offer very frequent coast-to-coast service. So, where do things stand? As flagged by JonNYC, United Chief Commercial Officer Andrew Nocella recently went on record to confirm that United is on track to return to JFK in 2027, which is just around the corner.

So, how will United secure the slots needed for service?

United management is generally on top of things when it comes to strategy, and I can make sense of most things. However, I still struggle to fully rationalize the plans for returning to JFK. That’s not to say it doesn’t make sense, or that I’m right, but here’s how I think through this:

On the surface, entering a market as a fourth place player, with limited opportunity to grow, little connectivity on the JFK side, and limited ability to have a great ground experience, seems like it could create a challenge.

United Airlines executives still insist the airline will return to JFK in 2027. This seems to involve getting some number of slots from JetBlue (as part of their partnership), and then possibly acquiring slots from some other carriers. It’s still not entirely clear how this will play out, though last we heard, the goal is to get 20 slot pairs, and aggressively fly to LAX and SFO.

I know Kirby thinks it was a big mistake to leave JFK, though I remain a bit confused by how the airline offering high frequency service from JFK to the West Coast, when the markets are already served by three large carriers, will be lucrative.

How do you see United’s JFK strategy playing out?

If you have a Capital One credit card, you may be able to earn extra rewards on purchases through Capital One Offers.

Similar to Amex Offers and Chase Offers, the program gives eligible cardholders access to shopping deals that can help them save on purchases they were already planning to make.

Here's how Capital One Offers works, how to use it and what to know before shopping.

Capital One Offers is a shopping rewards platform that gives eligible Capital One customers access to special deals at participating merchants. Offers span categories such as clothing, electronics, home goods and travel.

The platform is available to eligible U.S. consumer Capital One credit card holders, including those with cards in the Venture, Savor and Quicksilver families. (Business credit cards are not eligible.)

You can access available offers through your online account or the Capital One mobile app. However, eligibility varies by account, so you'll need to sign in to see which offers are available to you.

Unlike the standard rewards you earn on everyday purchases, Capital One Offers requires you to select an eligible deal and follow its redemption instructions.

For example, if you find an offer for 5% back at a retailer, you could earn that reward on top of the points or miles you'd normally earn with your credit card, as long as your purchase meets the offer's terms.

Capital One Offers is different from Capital One Shopping. Capital One Offers provides deals through eligible Capital One accounts, while Capital One Shopping is a separate shopping tool that helps users find coupon codes, compare prices and track price drops.

Related: Everything you need to know about credit card merchant offers

The deals you'll find through Capital One Offers depend on what's available when you sign in. You might see discounts on clothing, electronics or hotel bookings, with participating merchants and reward rates varying.

Some offers apply to most purchases from a retailer, while others are limited to certain products or categories. Keep in mind that rewards may also exclude taxes, shipping and other fees.

You can find Capital One Offers through the issuer's website or mobile app:

From there, you can browse deals or search for a specific merchant.

How you redeem an offer depends on whether you're shopping online or in a physical store.

Keep in mind that for online offers, the link you use matters, as Capital One relies on tracking information to associate your purchase with the offer.

Be sure to confirm which locations, payment methods and purchases qualify. An online offer won't necessarily apply to an in-store transaction, or vice versa.

Related: How to maximize online shopping portals for your purchases

Capital One says rewards typically arrive in about 45 days, although some can take up to three billing cycles. Certain offers may take longer.

For hotel offers, payouts are issued after you complete your stay, and the reservation must be completed within one year of booking.

Related: The best credit cards for online shopping

There are a few things worth keeping in mind before taking advantage of an offer.

I've gotten into the habit of checking Capital One Offers whenever I'm shopping online with my Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card. Sometimes there's a deal worth using, but other times I'll find a better offer through another shopping portal.

That's why it's worth comparing your options before making a purchase. For example, an offer for 5% back through Capital One, for example, might not be as valuable as a higher reward rate elsewhere.

Just keep in mind that you generally can't stack Capital One Offers with other shopping portals or promotional codes. Using another portal or certain coupons could invalidate your reward, so you'll want to decide which offer to use before checking out.

For travel purchases, I'd also recommend comparing the total price and booking conditions rather than focusing solely on the advertised reward.

Each offer has its own terms, including potential spending requirements, expiration dates and usage limits. Some deals may exclude gift cards, certain products or other purchases, while others may be limited to a single transaction.

Look at the terms before shopping, particularly if you're making a large purchase or planning to use an offer more than once.

You can check the status of your Capital One Offers rewards by opening the menu on the right side of the Capital One Offers page and selecting "Shopping Trips." From there, you'll see a tracker showing the status of your purchases and rewards.

It's also worth saving your offer details and order confirmations, especially for purchases with longer payout timelines.

If your reward hasn't arrived when expected, double-check that you met the offer requirements before contacting Capital One.

Related: Capital One miles: How to earn, redeem and transfer rewards

Capital One Offers can be an easy way to earn extra rewards on purchases you're already planning to make.

Before shopping, check your account for available deals, compare your options and follow the offer's instructions to make sure your purchase qualifies.

Just remember that offers and eligibility can vary, so a deal available to one Capital One customer may not be available to another.

Related: Tips and tricks to get maximum value from your Capital One miles

#6219. Ryanair Weighs Fare Hikes, Pay Freeze As Fuel Prices Soar

Irish discount carrier Ryanair is bracing for a difficult 2027 as jet fuel prices rise and European oil hedges expire.

In its most recent earnings report, the airline said it is considering temporarily freezing pay for workers, lowering crew ratios, and ramping up use of artificial intelligence. The company did not specify how long it would look to freeze wages, or how it would adjust staffing.

Ryanair has over 27,000 employees across its group.

Speaking to CNBC on Monday, Ryanair CEO Michael O’Leary said ticket prices will rise across Europe as lower-price oil hedges run out.

“The market customers have been insulated for the last 12 months,” O’Leary said. “But those hedges are rolling off. There’s still no resolution in the Middle East. Jet oil today is $170 a barrel. I mean, this is a very significant cost cliff we’re all facing next year. I believe you’re going to see air fares rise next year across Europe by 10 percent, maybe even 20 percent.”

In its earnings report, Ryanair said that while short-haul air fares will increase “materially,” it will not be enough to offset the expected €2 billion increase in fuel costs, necessitating the additional cost-saving measures.

Fuel prices have prompted several major European airlines and airline groups to cut capacity this fall and winter, and to retire some older, less efficient aircraft. Price volatility also pushed Lufthansa to accelerate the shutdown of Lufthansa CityLine, and made the U.K.’s EasyJet amenable to a roughly $7.7 billion takeover by Apollo Global Management.

The price shock has generally been worse in Europe and Asia than in North America, as those regions are more dependent on Gulf oil and lack domestic refining capacity.

#6218. My Atmos Rewards Summit Card Application Approval Experience

The $395 annual fee Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card is the premium credit card of Atmos Rewards, which is the combined loyalty program of Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines.

I’d argue that this is one of the best airline credit cards we’ve seen in a long time, and there are many reasons to pick up this card, from the ability to earn 3x points on foreign purchases, to the Global Companion Awards offered by the card, to the waived partner award booking fees, to the free points sharing, to the Alaska Lounge passes.

Perhaps the most obvious reason to get the Atmos Rewards Summit Card is that it’s offering a limited time welcome bonus, which in and of itself is a reason to apply. Specifically, you can receive 100,000 bonus points and a 25,000-point Global Companion Award with this offer. To qualify, spend $6,000 or more on purchases within the first 90 days of opening your account.

This is in line with the best-ever publicly available welcome offer we’ve seen on the Atmos Rewards Summit Card, and this is exactly the offer with which I applied for the card last year. In this post, I’d like to talk a bit about the rules when it comes to getting approved for the card, and my experience when I applied last year.

Link: Learn more about the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card

The Atmos Rewards Summit Card is issued by Bank of America. The good news is that eligibility for this card is unrelated to having any other card from Bank of America, Atmos Rewards, Alaska, or Hawaiian. So you’re eligible for this card (including the welcome bonus) if you have any other card in the portfolio.

For example, if you look at the terms of the Atmos Rewards Summit Card application, you’ll see the following:

This one-time promotion is limited to customers opening a new account in response to this offer and will not apply to requests to convert existing accounts.

That’s great, because it means that anyone who doesn’t yet have this card should be eligible for the bonus. Beyond that, what general restrictions does Bank of America have when it comes to approving people for cards? Here are a couple of common Bank of America restrictions that are often discussed, though let me emphasize that enforcement seems really inconsistent:

Both of these rules are specific to personal cards, and not business cards. Beyond that, neither of those rules seem to be totally consistently enforced, and in particular, that latter policy doesn’t seem consistent at all. For example, I opened more than three new cards in the 12 months before applying, and still ended up being approved.

Bank of America can sometimes be quirky in terms of approvals. I find that with Bank of America, I often get instant approvals with massive credit lines, and then every once in a while, I get random, inexplicable denials. So make of that what you will. If you’re interested in picking up more than one Atmos Rewards card in a day, it’s worth pointing out that you can potentially be approved for two in one day.

What’s the application process like when applying for the Atmos Rewards Summit Card? The online application process is really straightforward, and consists of just one page.

It just asks for personal details — name, date of birth, social security number, address, phone number, income, etc. You’ll also be asked for your Atmos Rewards number, so you’ll want to include that, so that your points are credited to the right account.

The process is even simpler if you already have a Bank of America account, as you’ll be asked to log-in with your account, and then you only have to provide updated income information.

For example, I applied for the card when it launched last year, and was instantly approved, with a pretty big credit line, no less!

Now that I’ve had the Atmos Rewards Summit Card for quite some time, what’s my strategy? I think the first thing to acknowledge is that the welcome bonus on this card is significant. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Atmos Rewards points to be worth 1.5 cents each, so the current 100,000 points plus a 25,000-point Global Companion Award are worth around $1,875 to me. There’s no reason not to give this card a try, and see how it works out, as that’s among the best card welcome bonuses out there.

What about beyond that, though? At a minimum, this is a card that I’ll keep on an ongoing basis, as long as the benefits don’t materially change, even if I don’t spend much on it. The annual 25,000-point Global Companion Award plus waived partner award booking fees more than justify the annual fee for me, given how many awards I book through the Atmos Rewards program, particularly for travel on American (you also get great travel protection with this card, which is useful).

But for the time being, the Atmos Rewards Summit Card is actually a major part of my credit card strategy, and I think there’s an argument to be made for being loyal to Atmos Rewards instead of American AAdvantage:

As I’ve already covered, I’ve actually made the switch from American AAdvantage to Atmos Rewards, and have already earned Platinum status, and am considering going for Titanium. While not specific to the credit card, the fact that award flights count toward elite status is really a selling point of the program.

The Atmos Rewards Summit Card is Bank of America’s premium credit card in the Alaska & Hawaiian Atmos Rewards ecosystem. It’s an incredibly compelling card — it’s worth signing up for given the huge welcome bonus, it’s worth keeping for the ongoing perks, and for many people, it’ll be worth spending money on.

Bank of America can be quirky with approving people for cards, but the good news is that many people should be eligible for this product, given that it’s quite new, and eligibility is unrelated to having other Atmos Rewards, Alaska, or Hawaiian cards. I applied for the card back when it launched, and was instantly approved. I’ve had a good experience so far with this card, and don’t see myself canceling it any time soon.

I’d highly recommend giving this card a try and applying with the current bonus, given the value it offers.

#6216. 60% Of Southwest Airlines Flyers Are Now Paying To Upgrade & It Reveals What LCC Loyalty Was Really About

Southwest Airlines has recently embarked on a series of new product, practice, and policy changes in an effort to boost profitability. The reactions were overall mixed, with some new changes being a net positive, while others were more controversial.

As a whole, the changes have mainly been controversial when the carrier began charging for products/services that were previously free, and Southwest Airlines as a whole has become less differentiated from the competition. However, while many passengers have not responded positively to Southwest's new practices, the changes appear to have worked.

Profits have been up ever since the changes were implemented, and Southwest has been successful in getting customers to purchase add-ons. While it's charging for items that were previously free, the carrier has only aligned itself with the legacy carriers and is distancing itself from the low-cost carriers that it was historically associated with. In a way, Southwest is more differentiated now compared to before.

The planes still wear the same livery and the branding hasn't changed, but flying with Southwest is entirely different today than it was five years ago. Previously, Southwest offered four fare classes, all of which included two complimentary checked bags, and passengers could not select seats online.

Instead, passengers were grouped into three different lettered sections and assigned a number, indicating their boarding position. Once on board the aircraft, passengers could select any available seat. Today, Southwest has updated and rebranded its fare classes, while the old open seating policy is gone. Instead, passengers are either assigned a seat at check-in or can pay extra money to select their own seat.

Checked bags now cost money, and passengers are now sorted into one of eight boarding groups rather than being assigned a position. What's more, Southwest now sells extra-legroom seats for an upcharge, whereas seats on Southwest flights before were intended to be largely equal. The main issue that customers have with the changes is the added fees.

Previously, passengers could select any seat at no charge, so long as they arrived at the airport early enough, but Southwest now charges more for extra-legroom seats as well. While there were no dedicated extra-legroom seats in the past, exit and front-row seats were available at no charge, unlike today. In addition, the carrier's decision to begin charging for checked luggage was met with heavy backlash.

Southwest has reportedly seen roughly 60% of its passengers pay for seat add-ons, compared to about 20% before the changes. Given that the airline now offers significantly more, higher-priced options (such as seat selection and extra-legroom seats) to customers, this reflects a major leap in revenue for the carrier.

Curiously, Southwest was originally founded with an intent to offer every passenger an equal onboard experience, but the company's customers today are overwhelmingly paying to upgrade their experience. Ultimately, the airline industry in the United States has moved towards segmentation, with airlines offering increasingly tailored experiences with varying levels of flexibility and onboard comfort.

For Southwest, the changes are simply moving with the times. However, this was riskier for Southwest because the carrier had historically earned strong loyalty due to its brand positioning, which was in part due to the unique attributes and benefits of flying with Southwest. This included features like open seating and free checked bags. Without these, what separates Southwest from the rest?

However, the significant increase in passengers buying seating add-ons indicates that customers have largely remained loyal to the carrier. If anything, Southwest's customers are responding positively to the increased optionality on seating. For the most part, the seats themselves are the same as before, but customers have additional choices if they want more legroom and can securely select their desired seat if they're willing to pay for it.

Southwest tweaks its policy after a rough rollout.

Southwest's recent financial growth and the success of initiatives like extra legroom seating show that passengers weren't loyal to the 'equal experience for all onboard' concept. It was a unique philosophy in Southwest's early days, but all-economy seating is more closely associated with true budget airlines today, whereas full-service carriers almost universally offer multiple seating and cabin options.

In the US, even low-cost and ultra-low-cost airlines are now offering premium seating options. Southwest was originally run as a low-cost carrier, but as the airline grew and grew, it began to straddle the line. It charges prices close to those of full-service airlines, while offering standard economy seats (now with an extra legroom option).

Today, Southwest can best be described as a hybrid carrier, blending elements of budget airlines and full-service carriers. The term is also commonly applied to Alaska Airlines and JetBlue in the US, although Alaska Airlines in particular has been aligning itself closer to the legacy full-service carriers in recent years.

With recent changes to its practices and products, Southwest has aligned itself almost completely with the legacy carriers, apart from its lack of a true premium product and long-haul network. Otherwise, Southwest differentiates itself through its extremely competitive schedules, robust domestic network, and friendly service from crew members. Based on its current financial performance, this seems to be what drives loyalty towards Southwest.

Southwest was profitable for nearly 50 years until the COVID-19 pandemic, but its comparatively weak recovery made it a target for activist investment firm Elliott Investment Management. Elliott argued that company leadership has failed to evolve to changing market conditions, and many of the changes made to Southwest's business model were made under the influence of Elliott.

The primary purpose of these initiatives was to increase profits and to further align Southwest with the US legacy carriers. While some passengers mourned the end of open seating, Elliott's own research showed that the policy turned away many customers. Although passengers now pay for seat selections, this is the case with essentially every airline today.

Similarly, losing the complimentary checked bags was detrimental to consumers, but Southwest merely followed the industry trend. Throughout all of its recent revisions to its policies and practices, Southwest only aimed to become more orthodox rather than move downmarket. It's now clear more than ever that, apart from small niche groups, people were historically loyal to Southwest because of the network, schedule, and service rather than these quirks.

Unlike features like open seating or free checked bags, the carrier's network and schedule are material advantages, and the airline has been optimizing its routes, focusing on operating bases where it holds a dominant market position. Meanwhile, the carrier's customer-facing employees are known for being friendly and attentive, a result of the company's relatively good labor relations.

Southwest Airlines once pulled off the impossible, using an ambitious strategy to save the company.

Southwest Airlines now offers extra legroom seats across its entire Boeing 737 fleet, but it does not offer domestic first class. The US legacy carriers have long offered this cabin, while Frontier and JetBlue are working on their own first class cabins. Southwest, meanwhile, has not officially announced its own first class, but it's believed that the carrier is seriously considering it.

Given the high margins associated with premium cabins and how they drive loyalty program engagement, a Southwest first class is almost certainly a matter of when, not if. Loyalty programs have become the biggest factor behind airline profitability in the US, with carriers now focusing on driving engagement via initiatives such as route expansions and premium capacity growth.

Southwest Rapid Rewards Credit Cards (Chase)

Southwest's possible first class would help, and the airline is also reportedly planning two additional major initiatives to boost Rapid Rewards engagement. Specifically, it's planning a new premium credit card with Chase to slot above its current portfolio, while also working on a new lounge network that will likely be for Rapid Rewards members who will hold this credit card. Southwest has signed partnerships with multiple foreign carriers and is reported to be exploring long-haul routes.

For instance, Iceland can be served using its existing 737 MAX 8 fleet, and Southwest partners with Icelandair. However, while CEO Bob Jordan has suggested that widebodies could be looked at in the future, this would introduce a new world of cost and complexity. As such, expect that Southwest will stick with the 737, and any potential expansion will be to destinations that can be served by the 737 MAX 8 for the near future.

London routinely ranks among the world’s most-visited cities. It is home to incredible museums, a fabulous theater scene, great restaurants, luxurious hotels and its main airport, Heathrow (LHR), is a hub for multiple airlines, making it a great stopping-over point on a larger trip.

That said, the British capital is well worth visiting on its own for anything from a few days to a few weeks, depending on how much of an Anglophile you are.

Despite the strong U.S. dollar, London is still an expensive destination, so if price points have been putting you off lately, here are some easy strategies to stretch your London trip budget even further using miles and points.

And if you have some strategies of your own to use airline miles, hotel points and credit card rewards to maximize a trip to London, please share those in the comments below!

Where you should stay in London depends on the purpose of your visit. If you are in town for business, you might want to stay near the City of London, while folks who want a quieter neighborhood might like Kensington or Notting Hill. Knightsbridge is best for those who want upscale shopping, while Mayfair has fantastic restaurants and boutiques.

London can get dreary and gray during the winter months and crowded during the summer, so your best bets are fall from September-November and spring from March-May when the temperatures tend to be mild and days will include a mix of sun and rain.

The number of miles you need to fly to London depends on which airline you take and which miles you redeem, as well as the time of year since some mileage programs require more miles during peak travel times. That said, you can find flights on some airlines, like Virgin Atlantic, by redeeming as few as 6,000 miles each way.

American Airlines, Delta Air Lines and United Airlines all fly to London from various U.S. airports. You’ll also find plenty of flights from over a dozen U.S. cities from the U.K.’s two main carriers, British Airways and Virgin Atlantic.

The cost of a trip to London depends on when you visit, how long your trip is and where you want to stay. The city has options for travelers ranging from budget flights and accommodations to luxury hotels that can cost well over $500 a night. Luckily, many hotels are accessible using credit card rewards and hotel points.

Now that the FAQs are out of the way, here's what else you need to know to start planning your trip to London.

Virgin Atlantic flies to London Heathrow from 11 U.S. cities and using Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points can be a real bargain. Just beware of taxes and fees that can be several hundred dollars, even for economy tickets.

I like using the airline’s Reward Seat Checker tool to price out tickets between city pairs over a month at a time. You can often find economy tickets between the East Coast and London for as few as 6,000 miles each way. Yes, you read that correctly — you can cross the Atlantic for just 6,000 miles. Even better, premium economy starts at just 10,500 miles and Upper Class can require as few as 29,000 miles (though it’s often much higher).

Unfortunately, you’ll be on the hook for anywhere from $450-$1,700 in taxes and fees round-trip depending on your class of service. That’s a lot, but perhaps not so bad considering even some economy flights are costing upwards of $1,400 at the moment, saving a few hundred dollars by redeeming a few thousand miles can be well worth it.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is a 1:1 transfer partner of:

What’s more, some of these partners, including Amex and Bilt, offer limited-time transfer bonuses, so you can score even more of a deal on award tickets.

Related: The best ways to travel to London with points and miles

British Airways is one of the most generous airlines in the world when it comes to releasing award seats in its four classes of long-haul service: economy, premium economy, business class and first class.

The downside is the hefty fuel surcharges and taxes on the airline's flights to and from its London Heathrow hub. There are, however, some ways to mitigate those.

The key is to redeem points and miles from the right programs. The extra charges will still be relatively high, but you can end up saving hundreds of dollars per ticket — each way! To illustrate this most clearly, let's focus on British Airways business class.

While American Airlines AAdvantage would only require 57,500 miles each way in business class for British Airways flights between the U.S. and London, the taxes and fees can cost between $750-$1,000 each way. The same is true if you were to redeem 45,000-70,000 Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards points each way – with taxes and fees that can top $1,100.

Instead, you might want to consider redeeming Cathay Pacific Asia Miles. Flights from the East Coast start at 63,000 miles plus $200-$450 in each direction, while those from the West Coast incur the same taxes and fees, but require 93,000 miles.

For its part, British Airways Club would require 88,000-99,000 Avios in each direction depending on which city in the U.S. you’re flying from, plus taxes and fees closer to $400-$500. Yes, that is still a chunk of change, and it’s a lot more Avios or Asia Miles, but it can be well worth it to save close to a thousand dollars per person.

British Airways Club is a transfer partner of:

Cathay Pacific Asia Miles is a transfer partner of:

That means that although you’re spending more miles for a ticket than redeeming through AAdvantage or Atmos, you have a lot more transfer partner options to top up your British Airways or Cathay Pacific accounts.

Related: Great award availability but beware the taxes: British Airways business class review

Another way to save on taxes and fees on award tickets as well as sparing yourself a few miles is to redeem United MileagePlus miles for a ticket on United. Not only does United charge far lower taxes and fees than British Airways and Virgin Atlantic, but if you are either a United MileagePlus elite or carry a United cobranded card, you might be eligible for preferential redemption rates on award tickets booked through MileagePlus.

You’ll pay just $5.60 flying from the U.S. to London, in any class of service, and around $200-$400 on the return, depending on which cabin you’re in.

Plus, you can save on the mileage portion of your ticket if you’re an elite or a credit cardholder. Take these flights from London to Chicago O’Hare International Airport (ORD), for instance. Regular MileagePlus members would have to redeem 40,000 miles for coach, 50,000 for premium economy and 80,000 for United Polaris business class. But if you have access to preferential rates, you’ll save at least 10% of the miles and need just 36,000 for coach, 45,000 for premium economy and 72,000 for business class.

If you don’t currently carry a United credit card, consider the United℠ Explorer Card (see ) or the United Quest℠ Card (see ).

United is also a 1:1 transfer partner of Chase Ultimate Rewards if you carry one of the following cards:

Finally, don’t forget that United has a special partnership with Marriott. Normally, when you transfer 60,000 Marriott Bonvoy points to one of its airline partners, you end up with 20,000 airline miles plus a 5,000-mile bonus for 25,000 miles total.

With United, however, you get a 10,000-mile bonus, so 60,000 Marriott Bonvoy points convert to 30,000 United miles. That’s probably a special-circumstance use for most folks, but still something to consider if you’re swimming in Marriott points.

Related: The best times to apply for Chase’s United cards based on offer history

As you might expect, London is lousy with points hotels, and more are on the way. I’m most excited about the Waldorf Astoria London – Admiralty Arch and the St. Regis London, both of which should open in early 2027.

I’d suggest picking the area you want to stay in and then doing a search with your preferred hotel programs around there. In the meantime, here are some of my top picks with each program.

The swanky NoMad London opened in 2021 and immediately gained a following thanks to its maximalist decor and popular bars and restaurants, not to mention its central Covent Garden location. It’s now part of Hilton, so you can redeem points for stays. Nights start at $550 or 100,000 Hilton Honors points.

I also love the colorful BoTree Hotel, which is part of Hilton’s Curio Collection. It opened in a quiet pocket of Mayfair in 2023 and has bright but sophisticated rooms and is home to an outpost of the see-and-be-seen Italian eatery Lavo. Rates start at $400 or 108,000 Hilton Honors points per night.

I love Mayfair, so my top Hyatt pick for the city is Hyatt Regency London – The Churchill, which sits right on stately Portman Square and is turning 50 years old next year. The room decor is not exactly overawing, but the public spaces are grand indeed and the service is impeccable. Nights start at $440 or 25,000-55,000 World of Hyatt points per night.

TPG staffers also love the Great Scotland Yard Hotel, which is part of Hyatt’s Unbound Collection. Rooms are on the small side, but you can’t beat the history since it’s in a heritage-listed building that was once the Metropolitan Police headquarters. Rates start at $380 or 20,000-40,000 World of Hyatt points per night.

For something a bit hipper as well as budget-friendlier, try the Standard. It’s in a very busy area right near Kings Cross, but chic, 70s-inspired room decor and several buzzy bars and restaurants will make your time here feel like an upscale city experience. Rates start at $305 or 20,000-40,000 points per night.

Related: Which credit cards should you use for Hyatt stays?

Even among quirky Kimptons, the Kimpton Fitzroy is a standout thanks to the magnificent 1900 landmark building that houses it and its central Bloomsbury location. Make time for afternoon tea in Palm Court, which is a veritable London institution. Rates start at $319 or 66,000 IHG One Rewards points per night.

The InterContinental London Park Lane has an utterly convenient location at Hyde Park Corner and features spacious rooms, specialty drinks inspired by the royal family at Arch Bar and an expansive spa and fitness center. Rates start at $433 or 83,000 points per night.

Related: Which credit card should you use for IHG stays?

It might occupy a heritage-listed building from 1910, but the London Edition feels utterly of the moment (even though it opened over 13 years ago). Rooms have Edition’s signature look of white textiles, wood paneling and minimalist bathrooms. It’s worth spending an evening admiring the sculpted ceiling at Berners Tavern while enjoying dishes from chef Jason Atherton’s menu. Rates start at $485 or 70,400 Marriott Bonvoy points per night.

Formerly a Renaissance hotel, St. Pancras has since joined Marriott’s Autograph Collection and is a favorite among train enthusiasts thanks to its location in a landmark neo-Gothic edifice attached to the train station of the same name. Rooms feel opulent in a Victorian way, and its Moorish-inspired spa is a treat. Rates start at $280 or 52,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night.

While hotel points come in handy for saving bundles of money on otherwise expensive stays, if you are looking to splurge while in London, there are still ways to save on luxury hotels.

Travelers with either the American Express Platinum Card® or The Business Platinum Card® from American Express should check American Express Fine Hotels + Resorts, which sometimes has third- or fourth-night free packages at some of the city’s finest hotels. These bookings also come with perks like free daily breakfast for two, a $100 on-property credit, availability-based upgrades and guaranteed 4 p.m. late checkout.

There are plenty to choose from, but my personal favorite London hotels that participate in Amex FHR include:

Remember, if you have the American Express Platinum Card or The Business Platinum Card from American Express you are also eligible for up to $300 in statement credits biannually for up to a total of $600 per year on prepaid Fine Hotels + Resorts, The Hotel Collection or Airbnb Luxe bookings (of two nights or more for THC and Airbnb) through American Express Travel® or the Amex Travel App™. Starting Jan. 1, 2027, those FHR bookings will require two nights or more to be eligible for this credit.

You might also consider booking a luxury hotel through the Capital One Premier Collection if you have the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card or the Capital One Venture X Business for valuable benefits like free daily breakfast for two, up to $100 in on-property experience credits and room upgrades (if available).

Likewise, if you have the Chase Sapphire Reserve or the Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business you can book a hotel that is part of The Edit by Chase Travel℠. Cardholders are eligible for two statement credits of up to $250 each (for a total of $500) this calendar year to put toward stays of two nights or more booked through The Edit. During your stay, you are also eligible for availability-based upgrades, complimentary daily breakfast and a $100 on-property credit.

Related: Chase Sapphire Reserve’s The Edit credit: What to know

Although British food was long a punchline, the city has become one of the world’s premier dining destinations in the past two decades or so. These days, you can find everything from Sri Lankan hoppers and Scandinavian smoked fish to French haute cuisine and sustainable farm-to-table fare.

Prices are high, though, so it’s best to maximize rewards on your spending and any statement credits your credit cards might afford you.

Another favorite tip of mine: You can often find discounts of up to 50% at some restaurants by booking reservations via The Fork. Then, just show your reservation details at check in, enjoy your meal, and the savings will be automatically applied to your bill.

Related: The best credit cards for dining

Taxis and Ubers are easy to come by in London, though rides can be expensive. So if you do go this route, so to speak, make sure to use a card that earns bonus points on ride-hailing services.

It’s also easy to hop on the city’s Tube lines and buses, both of which are easy to navigate and affordable, by simply tapping on with your credit card. If you decide to do so, keep a card that earns bonus points on public transportation at the top of your wallet.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card (see ) earns 2 points per dollar on local transit and commuting, for example, and the Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card earns 2 points per dollar on local transit purchases.

You might be able to use the Chase Sapphire Reserve’s $300 in annual travel statement credits toward transit purchases as well as taxis and Ubers since these charges often code as “travel.”

Related: The best credit cards for commuting expenses

No matter whether you spell it “theater” or “theatre,” no trip to London would be complete without seeing a production in one of the West End’s magnificent venues. Ticket prices tend to be more reasonable than in the U.S. but can still put a dent in your budget. Luckily, you can take advantage of the Chase Sapphire Reserve Stubhub credit to offset some of that cost.

Chase Sapphire Reserve cardholders receive up to $300 per year to use on purchases made through StubHub or its sister site, Viagogo. The credit is split into two biannual credits of up to $150 (activation required; through Dec. 31, 2027).

Among the productions currently available through Stubhub in London are “Paddington: The Musical” (just beware it’s mostly sold out except for last-minute tickets) and “Oh, Mary!”.

A few years ago, Capital One partnered with The Cultivist, a service that grants members free, priority access to dozens of museums around the world. Eligible Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card holders can register for half-price membership that costs $220 per year instead of $440. This auto-renews at the discounted rate for the second year and then is full price after that.

While $220 is a lot, if you visit museums frequently, you can end up saving far more than that on tickets since The Cultivist Enthusiast-level membership available with the Venture X includes priority admission for the cardholder plus a guest. In London, the participating museums include:

Finally, some credit cards levy foreign exchange fees on purchases you make outside the U.S. They tend to add 1-3% to your purchase price, which can add up quickly. Instead, use a credit card that waives foreign transaction fees, of which there are many to choose from.

If you travel abroad frequently, you might also want to consider the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card. In addition to waiving foreign transaction fees, the card actually earns 3 points per dollar on foreign transactions, in any category. It’s almost too good to be true, and that makes it one of the best credit cards for trips abroad.

Related: The best credit cards with no foreign transaction fees

#6212. Bilt Rent Day Promotion November 2026: Up To $150 Off Hotel, Up To 100% Gift Card Bonus

Bilt is the platform known for providing rewards for housing payments. Earlier this year we saw massive changes at Bilt, including an overhaul of the credit card portfolio, plus new ways that housing rewards are offered.

There are many innovative things about Bilt, including that there’s a Bilt Rent Day promotion on the first day of each month. With it now being a new month, I’d like to post a reminder of the November 2026 Bilt Rent Day offer, as it includes both a gift card redemption bonus and a hotel booking promo code. While there’s no transfer bonus to a travel program, I imagine this will still interest some.

There are a couple of aspects to the Bilt Rent Day promotion, including the ability to earn bonus points (which is the same every month), plus at least one additional promotion.

Note that Bilt Rent Day promotions are generally valid from 12:00AM ET until 11:59PM PT, so technically you have around 27 hours to take advantage of them.

Bilt has a portfolio of credit cards, including the no annual fee Bilt Blue Card (learn more), $95 annual fee Bilt Obsidian Card (learn more), and $495 annual fee Bilt Palladium Card (learn more) (Rates & Fees). Personally, I think the Bilt Palladium Card is by far the most lucrative.

On the first day of each month, you earn double those rewards on these cards, and earn up to 1,000 bonus points each month. It could be worth strategically making some purchases on the first day of each month to maximize this as much as possible.

For example, with double points, the Bilt Palladium Card offers 4x points on everyday spending on the first day of the month, so that’s pretty awesome (up to a cap of $500 worth of spending, since that would earn you 1,000 bonus points).

On November 1, 2026 only, Bilt is offering a bonus when members redeem points for gift cards. The bonus you’re eligible for depends on your Bilt elite status, as follows:

This same bonus is available for all 125+ gift cards that Bilt Points can be redeemed for. There’s no option to use Bilt Cash to increase your bonus here.

For what it’s worth, ordinarily Bilt points can be redeemed for 0.7 cents each toward gift card purchases. That means a Blue member would be getting 0.875 cents per point of value, while a Platinum member would be getting 1.4 cents per point of value. For me that’s a hard pass, though I suppose for some Platinum members, it could be an interesting way to “cash out” points, if that’s what you’re looking to do.

For the November 2026 Bilt Rent Day promotion, we’re actually seeing an additional offer as well. Bilt members can unlock up to $150 off a hotel stay booked in the Bilt Travel Portal during Rent Week, so it’s available for bookings between 9AM ET on October 28 and 3AM ET on November 2, 2026.

The catch here is that different members are eligible for different offers, so members have to log into their Bilt account, and they will see a targeted chart delineating different savings of up to $150 for hotel bookings. Here are the key details:

On the first day of each month, Bilt offers a Rent Day promotion. In addition to earning up to double points for purchases, for November 2026, there are two offers members can take advantage of.

One offer is for up to a 100% bonus on gift card redemptions, which can get you at most 1.4 cents per point of value. That’s not terribly exciting, in my opinion, but maybe others will appreciate it. The other offer is for up to $150 off a hotel stay booked through the Bilt Travel Portal. There are different offers there that members will be eligible for, so you’ll want to check in the Bilt app to see what you’re targeted for.

Are you taking advantage of the Bilt Rent Day promotion for November 2026?

#6210. Transfer Chase Points To IHG With 80% Bonus: Why It’s Not Worth It

Chase Ultimate Rewards has just launched a new transfer bonus to IHG One Rewards. The bonus is for 80%, which on the surface sounds huge. However, even with such a big bonus, I’d still argue this almost certainly isn’t worth it…

Chase Ultimate Rewards is offering a bonus when you transfer points to IHG One Rewards. Between 12AM ET on November 1, 2026, and 11:59PM ET on December 3, 2026, members can receive an 80% bonus when moving points.

Points ordinarily transfer at a 1,000:1,000 ratio, so with this 80% bonus offer, points transfer at a 1,000:1,800 ratio. You can take advantage of this an unlimited number of times. Transfers from Chase Ultimate Rewards to IHG One Rewards are typically instant.

For context, we typically see a transfer bonus from Chase to IHG two or three times per year, and so far the bonuses have been in the range of 50% to 100%. So this 80% bonus is roughly average as far as these bonuses go, and isn’t quite as good as the 100% bonus we saw earlier this year.

An 80% transfer bonus sounds like it could be valuable, since that’s a big percentage bonus. That being said, I still wouldn’t consider this to be a good deal under a vast majority of circumstances.

Why? Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider IHG One Rewards points to be worth 0.5 cents each, while I value Chase Ultimate Rewards points at ~1.7 cents each. Even when you’re getting 1.8 IHG One Rewards points per Ultimate Rewards point, you’re still only getting under one cent of value per Ultimate Rewards point.

I certainly hope that most people are able to redeem their Chase Ultimate Rewards points for well over a penny each, since that’s a really low cash out value.

Even if you value IHG One Rewards points more than I do, the reality is that IHG frequently sells points for 0.5 cents each, so I would instead buy points at that rate. It would be silly to redeem Ultimate Rewards points when you’re only getting one cent of value vs. paying cash.

Chase Ultimate Rewards is offering a new transfer bonus, as you can get an 80% bonus when you move points to IHG One Rewards. While I’m always happy to see a transfer bonus, I’m afraid that this simply isn’t worth it under a vast majority of circumstances.

Transfers to most of Chase’s partners are generally at a 1:1 ratio. While the simplicity of that is nice, the reality is that points have significantly different values, and this creates a few partners that I would never recommend transferring Chase points to.

Anyone have a different take, and see a reason to transfer Chase points to IHG?

#6209. "Short-Sighted": Delta CEO Vows To Fight Heathrow’s Move To Split It From Virgin Atlantic

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian has publicly criticized Heathrow Airport's decision to move the airline to Terminal 4 in 2028, calling the decision "short-sighted" and "bad for airline consumers." The criticism comes after a once-in-a-decade review at Europe's busiest international airport resulted in five airlines being ordered to move terminals in 2028, including Delta.

This change has been met with upset after both Delta and Virgin Atlantic, in which the American carrier holds a 49% share, argued that it will move the US carrier away from its UK partner and put the airline at a disadvantage to its competitors. Bastian has vowed to "pursue all available remedies" to reverse the decision.

As part of Heathrow Airport Limited's review, Delta will be required to relocate to the airport's Terminal 4. This comes after more than a decade in which Delta and Virgin have cohabitated in Terminal 3. This one-terminal approach for the two airlines has enabled convenient connections, premium shared amenities, and a collaboration to provide travelers access to the airlines' two extensive long-haul networks.

Having the two airlines co-located in Terminal 3 has provided a valuable competitive alternative to other legacy carriers operating transatlantic flights. When separated, this will undermine the years of investment that the two airlines have spent in the last decade, and it is suggested that the decision has disregarded the customer benefits that are offered by the co-location. In a lengthy statement released on Monday, Bastian said:

"Heathrow Airport Limited’s decision to relocate Delta’s operation to Terminal 4, away from our partner Virgin Atlantic, is short-sighted, deeply disappointing and bad for airline consumers . . . Separating our operation undermines years of investment and disregards the tightly integrated customer benefits that we offer in our co-located terminal."

As detailed in Bastian's statement, both Delta and Virgin are planning to fight this decision, and Delta is urging Heathrow Airport Limited to reconsider the decision. Virgin is considering its legal options, and SkyTeam, of which both airlines are partners, has argued that the move would put its members at a disadvantage to other airlines sharing terminals.

For Delta, the move matters as they are arguing that the relocation to Terminal 4 would split the airline from its joint venture partner after more than a decade. This would result in connecting passengers between the two airlines being forced to connect across the airfield by bus transport.

Heathrow Airport Limited has said that the once-a-decade review would free up available capacity at the airport, while easing congestion at one of the most slot-controlled airports in the world.

Heathrow's decision to separate Delta and Virgin Atlantic sparks competition concerns and potential legal challenges.

For US carriers, Delta is tied second with United Airlines by total destinations served at Heathrow, with both airlines serving seven year-round US gateways. They trail behind American Airlines, who operate year-round to nine US airports, and add a sole seasonal service.

Virgin Atlantic operates year-round to ten destinations in the US, with a seasonal service added during the Northern Hemisphere summer season to Seattle. The full Heathrow network for both airlines is below:

Atlanta (ATL), Boston (BOS), Detroit (DTW), Minneapolis/Saint Paul (MSP), New York-JFK (JFK), Salt Lake City (SLC), Seattle/Tacoma (SEA)

Atlanta (ATL), Boston (BOS), Las Vegas (LAS), Los Angeles (LAX), Miami (MIA), New York-JFK (JFK), Orlando (MCO), San Francisco (SFO), Tampa (TPA), Washington-Dulles (IAD), Seattle/Tacoma (SEA) – seasonal

Antigua (ANU), Barbados (BGI), Bengaluru (BLR), Cancún (CUN), Cape Town (CPT) – seasonal, Delhi (DEL), Dubai (DXB), Grenada (GND), Johannesburg (JNB), Lagos (LOS), Malé (MLE) – seasonal, Montego Bay (MBJ), Mumbai (BOM), Seoul (ICN), St. Vincent (SVD), Toronto (YYZ), Phuket (HKT) – seasonal

In Heathrow Terminal 3 currently, Delta and Virgin share a number of facilities and infrastructure, including the Virgin Atlantic Clubhouse, providing an iconic lounge for eligible business class passengers and top-tier frequent flyers. Travelers also have access to the Virgin Revivals Lounge, which provides lounge facilities for arriving passengers.

Shared ground labor, check-in, and transfer coordination also see the two airlines working collaboratively for the benefit of passengers and airline operations.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6208. Transfer Chase Points To British Airways, Iberia, Aer Lingus, With 30% Bonus

Chase Ultimate Rewards has just launched its latest airline transfer bonus. Actually, it’s a trio of transfer bonuses, as it’s valid for British Airways Club, Iberia Club, and Aer Lingus AerClub. This is a popular bonus when available, so I think some members will find this to be worthwhile.

Chase Ultimate Rewards is offering a bonus when you transfer points to British Airways Club, Iberia Club, or Aer Lingus AerClub. Between 12AM ET on November 1, 2026, and 11:59PM ET on December 1, 2026, members can receive a 30% bonus when moving points.

A transfer bonus like this seems to be offered an average of once to twice per year, and it’s typically in the range of 20-30%. So the 30% bonus is as good as it gets, and this is the biggest percentage bonus that we’ve seen so far in 2026.

Keep in mind that this bonus covers three different Avios currencies, and on top of that, you can freely transfer Avios between the various “flavors.” When you go to make a transfer, you should immediately see the 30% bonus reflected. Transfers from Ultimate Rewards to these partners are typically instant.

Keep in mind the various Avios currencies also partner with other major transferable points currencies, and we do sometimes see transfer bonuses with other programs as well.

I think there’s value to be had in taking advantage of a 30% bonus on points transfers from Ultimate Rewards to Avios. That’s not because of any one particular redemption opportunity, but rather because of the collective value of the Avios ecosystem.

Back in the day, the best uses of British Airways Avios were for short haul travel on partner airlines, including on Alaska and American. Unfortunately those redemption opportunities have been devalued horribly.

However, lots of great new options using Avios have emerged. For example, I love how Qatar Airways Privilege Club is now an Avios airline, as this opens up some great opportunities:

Anyway, there’s a ton of potential value here, so see my guides to maximizing Avios with British Airways Club, Iberia Club, Aer Lingus Aer Club, Qatar Airways Privilege Club, and Finnair Plus.

For the next several weeks, you can get a 30% bonus when you convert your Chase Ultimate Rewards points into Avios with British Airways Club, Iberia Club, and Aer Lingus AerClub.

Avios is one of the most useful points currencies out there, especially given across how many airlines you can redeem these rewards. I think for many people, this could be worth a speculative transfer.

Do you plan on taking advantage of this transfer bonus from Chase Ultimate Rewards to British Airways, Iberia, and Aer Lingus?
