#6206. Transfer Capital One Miles To Air France-KLM Flying Blue With 20% Bonus: Worth It?

Capital One has just introduced its latest points transfer promotion, whereby members can receive a 20% bonus when moving rewards to Air France-KLM Flying Blue. This has the potential to be an excellent deal.

Capital One is offering a bonus when you transfer points to Air France-KLM Flying Blue. Between 12AM ET on November 1, 2026, and 11:59PM ET on November 30, 2026, members can receive a 20% bonus when moving points.

The transfer ratio is usually 1:1, so through this promotion you can transfer miles at a 1,000:1,200 ratio. The 20% bonus should post at the same time as the standard rewards. There’s no registration required, and no limit to how many bonus points you can earn. Transfers from Capital One to Flying Blue are generally instant.

We see bonuses from various transferable points currencies to Flying Blue every so often, in the range of 20-30%. So if you’re in the market for earning some Flying Blue miles, this is a good opportunity.

Air France-KLM Flying Blue is a valuable SkyTeam frequent flyer program. The program has attractive award pricing on Air France and KLM, offering many of the best ways to cross the Atlantic. Admittedly saver award availability can be tough to come by, though if you have Flying Blue Platinum status, you get access to more award space, which is an awesome perk.

On top of that, Air France and KLM make more award seats available to members of the Flying Blue program than to members of partner programs. So even when Flying Blue’s pricing isn’t the best, there are situations where it could make sense to book through Flying Blue (though with all of the Delta SkyMiles devaluations we’ve seen, typically you will find the best pricing through Flying Blue).

I should mention that in September 2026 we saw a Flying Blue devaluation, whereby awards now followed a tiered pricing structure. This means that the cheapest awards are now “Light” fares, and if you want the same inclusions as before, you need to buy up to a “Standard” fare, which costs more miles.

There’s always value in having a stash of Flying Blue miles if you think you’ll be traveling transatlantic in the coming months. I redeem through Flying Blue every year (usually multiple times per year), and consistently get value. I find it to be one of the most useful frequent flyer programs for redeeming points.

The only other consideration here is that all major transferable points currencies partner with Air France-KLM Flying Blue, and we see transfer bonuses with some frequency. So I’d be strategic with which program you transfer points from, especially based on how you’d otherwise redeem them.

Through November 30, 2026, you can receive a 20% bonus when you transfer miles from Capital One to Air France-KLM Flying Blue. This bonus is being offered on Capital One’s end, so you should see the bonus right away, and can take advantage of this as often as you’d like.

This has the potential to be a good deal for redemptions on Air France-KLM as well as SkyTeam and other airline partners. If I didn’t already have a stash of Flying Blue miles, I’d take advantage of this.

Do you plan on converting Capital One miles into Flying Blue miles with this bonus?

#6204. Air France-KLM Flying Blue Promo Rewards: Save 25% On Select Awards

The Air France-KLM Flying Blue program has its monthly Promo Rewards promotion, whereby members can save 25% on select award tickets over a limited travel period. The program has just published its new Promo Rewards list for November 2026, offering discounted short haul and long haul awards for travel over the coming months.

There are quite a few destinations bookable with this promotion, including several in the Americas, with options in business class, premium economy, and economy. This has the potential to be a great deal.

I’m a big fan of the Air France-KLM Flying Blue program, especially for long haul premium cabin redemptions. Not only does Flying Blue largely have attractive award pricing for business class travel, but the program also has access to more Air France and KLM award space than other programs.

The Promo Rewards offer is published every month by the Flying Blue program, and offers 25% discounts off select awards for travel on Air France and KLM. The Flying Blue program has dynamic award pricing, and this promotion specifically applies for the lowest, saver level award costs.

Flying Blue has published its November 2026 Promo Rewards, valid for bookings between November 1 and November 30, 2026. Most of these Promo Rewards have long travel windows, and can be used for flights all the way through April 30, 2027.

As a reminder, Flying Blue has standardized saver award pricing, so ordinarily you’ll pay the following amounts for one-way transatlantic awards between Europe and most of North America, when booking a “Light” fare:

Let me emphasize that with the recent Flying Blue devaluation, the entry level pricing is now for a “Light” fare rather than a Standard fare, so it comes with fewer inclusions. For example, a long haul business class “Light” fare doesn’t offer any flexibility, and also doesn’t offer lounge access.

However, if you have Flying Blue Platinum status, then you still receive most of the perks of a “Standard” fare automatically. So as an example, a Promo Rewards ticket that costs 45,000 miles in business class for a “Light” fare would now cost 56,250 miles for a “Standard” fare.

Here are the awards that are available with the Promo Rewards list this month for travel between Europe and North America, along with the pricing:

On top of that, the Flying Blue Extra program was recently launched (the cost starts at €379 per year), which is essentially a paid membership program that offers extra perks. One of the perks of Flying Blue Extra is access to additional Promo Rewards, so eligible members receive access to the following extra Promo Rewards availability to North America this time around:

There are of course also Promo Rewards opportunities outside of North America, including some business class options to South America, so check out the full list.

All of the lowest priced awards in the above markets through April 30, 2027, should be bookable with the Promo Rewards pricing (though not necessarily the extra award availability that Flying Blue Platinum members receive). You can use all of these awards for travel to and from destinations across Europe, so you can travel beyond Amsterdam and Paris.

If you’re having trouble finding availability, remember to use Flying Blue’s secret award calendar. Also keep in mind that children ages two to 12 receive 25% off Flying Blue award tickets, including Promo Rewards.

One of the things that’s awesome about the Flying Blue program is how easy it is to rack up miles:

The Air France-KLM Flying Blue program offers a Promo Rewards promotion, whereby members can book discounted award tickets in select markets. This can be a great deal, especially when you consider how easy Flying Blue miles are to come by, and also how much award space is sometimes available through Flying Blue.

With the latest Promo Rewards, you can save 25% to several destinations in the Americas, with options in economy, premium economy, and business class. This has the potential to be quite a good deal, so if you have any travel you’re interested in booking, this would be a great time to do so.

#6203. Aman At Sea: Amangati “Superyacht” Sets Sail Spring 2027, From $6K+ Per Night

Aman at Sea voyages are best booked through travel advisors, who can get you the best price possible, while adding extra perks. Ford and his team are happy to help with any requests, and can be reached at [email protected].

In 2027, we’re going to see the launch of a new ultra-luxury cruise line, as hotel group Aman is getting into the cruising industry, with the Aman at Sea concept, and its Amangati “superyacht,” as it’s called.

I’d like to provide an update about this concept, as sailings are now bookable well into 2028, so we have a sense of both the summer sailings in Europe and winter sailings in the Caribbean. If you think the recent entrants into the market are expensive, wait until you learn the details of this one.

It’s interesting to see the increasing trend of luxury hotel groups launching cruise lines, or perhaps more accurately, licensing out their names to partner on new cruising concepts. For example, in 2022 we saw the launch of Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection, and in 2026, we’ve seen the launch of Four Seasons Yachts and Orient Express Sailing Yachts.

Amangati (“peaceful motion” in Sanskrit) is expected to set sail in the spring of 2027, as Aman’s first superyacht. Yes, this marks the Aman brand getting into the luxury cruising industry, on a ship that’s being described as a “floating sanctuary.”

The 600-foot ship will be around 23,000 gross tons, and will have a hybrid propulsion system, using battery power to reduce emissions and improve efficiency. It’s currently being built in Italy’s T. Mariotti shipyard, and it will be delivered to Neptune Co., which is a joint venture between hotel group Aman and Cruise Saudi.

The ship is expected to feature a total of 47 suites, each with a balcony and floor-to-ceiling windows. The suites will be among the largest at sea.

When it comes to amenities, the ship will have four restaurants, a jazz club, a 52-foot pool, a beach club and marina, a spa with a Japanese garden, two helipads, and much more. Sinot Yacht Architecture & Design is behind the design, and the intent is to take cues from traditional ryokan architecture.

For those not familiar, Cruise Saudi is owned by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, and is intended to promote the cruise and tourism industry in Saudi Arabia. However, it doesn’t appear that the plan is actually for the ship to cruise in Saudi Arabia, at least for the foreseeable future. So it seems to primarily be part of the country’s larger investment in the cruising industry.

Here’s how Aman CEO Vlad Doronin describes the idea behind the ship:

Aman has published the inaugural voyages for Amangati, for sailings between May 7, 2027, and March 31, 2028. Unsurprisingly, the ship will spend summers in Europe and winters in the Caribbean, with transatlantic sailings in November and March.

In both summer in Europe and winter in the Caribbean, sailings will be five to eight nights each, and they’re roughly what you’d expect in terms of itineraries. You can either book directly through Aman at Sea, or through a travel advisor.

An eligible travel advisor will be able to add a minimum of a $500 shipboard credit, while paying the standard rate. You can generally expect pricing parity between all booking sources, so you won’t find discounted sailing prices anywhere. Ford and his team are happy to help with these requests, and can be reached at [email protected].

Before we talk about the pricing for Aman at Sea, what’s included with journeys? It’s an interesting topic, because historically ultra luxury cruises have been all-inclusive. However, Four Seasons Yachts is countering that trend, by not including lunch, dinner, or alcoholic drinks.

With that in mind, Aman at Sea will include the following with the cost of sailings:

As you can see, Aman is sort of taking a middle ground approach here. Alcohol aside from beer isn’t included, and neither is dining at the specialty restaurants.

How much are Aman at Sea rates? Pricing is per suite rather than per guest. As it currently stands, I see five-night journeys starting at $32,500, while I see seven-night journeys priced as high as $54,600. So we’re looking at somewhere around $6,000-8,000 per night for an entry level suite. You’ll generally find that Caribbean sailings are a little cheaper than European sailings.

Admittedly these suites are massive by ship standards, but that’s definitely on the very high end of the market, and easily 50%+ more than Four Seasons Yachts is charging (though with some more inclusions).

Prior to 2026, I hadn’t taken a cruise since I was a kid. However, this year I’ve given all three of the luxury cruise lines associated with hotels a try, and I’ve shared my thoughts on Four Seasons Yachts, Orient Express Sailing Yachts, and Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection. I’ve even done a direct comparison of the three concepts, based on my firsthand experience.

Let me of course acknowledge that these cruise lines are all at the very top end of the market, so I’m not claiming or suggesting that they’re the best value options out there. Instead, I’ve taken such an interest in them because I find the crossover between hotels and cruise lines to be so interesting, and also find it noteworthy how these are all cruise lines targeted at people who historically haven’t considered cruising.

With that in mind, here’s how I’d broadly sum up the experiences offered by the three existing players:

In general, I’d expect Aman at Sea will probably be closest to Orient-Express Sailing Yachts in terms of exclusivity, while probably being more like Four Seasons Yachts in terms of design (since it’s not a sailboat). I will say, given the price point, I do find the lack of inclusions to be a bit frustrating. Then again, the standard suites will be absolutely massive.

The concept of luxury cruising is nothing new. However, there’s no denying that the industry is evolving a bit:

Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection is the only one of the concepts that has now been in service for some time, and based on what we know, the financial performance has left a bit to be desired. And that was before the cruise line expanded to three ships, and it’s before three competitors entered the industry.

Ultimately the success of these ventures comes down to whether they can convince people that cruising is “cool.” I don’t think these cruise lines will be cannibalizing brands like Silversea, but instead, I think they’re going after those who would otherwise vacation on land.

The other thing worth keeping in mind is that at some point, these cruise lines are competing with the concept of just chartering a yacht, which is a concept that will have more appeal for many people.

Obviously $6K+ per night is a massive amount to spend on a cruise. But the reality is that people easily pay that kind of money for peak season rooms in place like Saint-Tropez. Can these hotel-branded cruise lines convince people who want to “see and be seen” that it’s as cool to be on a ship as it is to be in the South of France? It seems like a tall order, but I guess time will tell.

Ironically, I think the volume of new entrants into the market is actually quite helpful in building demand, since cruises are finally being talked about more among non-cruisers. While they’re all competing for the same types of guests, I know a fair number of people have tried one of these cruise lines, then rebooked on another cruise line, etc.

Aman will be getting into the luxury cruising space in the spring of 2027, with the launch of its 600-foot Amangati superyacht. The ship looks incredible, and it seems like we’re seeing the luxury hotel groups all one-up each other.

The pricing is at the very top end of the market, which doesn’t come as much of a surprise. Will there be enough people willing to pay $6K+ per night for Aman’s cruising concept to keep these ships full, especially without most alcohol included? Only time will tell.

What do you make of Aman getting into the luxury cruise industry?

Glad that you identified correctly that the brands are licensing their names. Agree with the comment about unique ports and places. These cruises seem to go to the usual places.

I think it's time to call "yacht top". I can't see how there's a big enough market for this experience at the price point the high end brands are all trying to compete at. It was a great first mover idea but just so easily replicated with zero real differentiation between the products. The Orient Express has an amazing looking yacht, so Aman really has no room for error if they want to convince people to pay more for theirs. I'm with you, Ben, in that this whole situation is fascinating to me in a way that I can't really explain. Will be entertaining to see who succeeds and who fails.

The true answer varies from point to point and person to person. It also depends on your travel goals and how much you maximize a particular loyalty currency. Still, some rewards are worth more than others, and our goal is to give you a sense of how they stack up.

#6201. How Much Do Boeing 747-8 Pilots Make In 2026?

The Boeing 747-8 is one of the largest commercial aircraft in operation. With its distinctive humpbacked fuselage, four powerful engines, and substantial payload capacity, the aircraft requires highly trained flight crews. However, the salaries these pilots receive depend more on their airline, seniority, and position than on the aircraft itself.

In 2026, Boeing 747-8 pilots can earn anywhere from six-figure annual salaries to well over $400,000, particularly at major cargo operators such as UPS Airlines. However, there is no single industry-wide salary for a 747-8 pilot, as first officers, experienced captains, and newly hired pilots work under different pay structures, with contractual guarantees and additional benefits influencing their overall compensation.

Boeing 747-8 pilot salaries vary considerably depending on the airline, years of service, and whether a pilot serves as a captain or first officer. At the upper end of the pay scale, experienced captains at major cargo airlines can earn more than $400,000 annually, while first officers typically receive lower salaries that can still reach six figures after gaining experience.

UPS Airlines offers some of the highest compensation for pilots operating the Boeing 747-8F, the freighter version of the aircraft. Under its pilot pay agreement, the top captain hourly rate reached $401 in September 2025, while the highest first officer rate reached $284. These figures provide a useful benchmark for understanding the earning potential available to experienced pilots in 2026.

Atlas Air, another major Boeing 747-8F operator, follows a different pay structure that takes account of the aircraft, pilot position, and years of service. Its 747-8F captain hourly rate starts at $247 in the first year and increases to $259 in the second year, eventually reaching $332 by the twelfth year. Consequently, the difference between an experienced captain's earnings and those of a newer pilot can be substantial.

Although salary estimates sometimes place the average US Boeing 747-8 pilot's earnings at approximately $135,000 annually in 2026, such figures need careful interpretation. Broad estimates can include junior first officers, contract pilots, and pilots working for lower-paying operators, meaning they may not accurately represent the compensation available to experienced crews at large cargo airlines.

UPS Airlines operates the Boeing 747-8F as part of its extensive cargo network, and its pilots benefit from a compensation structure negotiated with the Independent Pilots Association. The agreement includes a two-year contract extension, with the published top hourly rates providing a strong indication of what experienced pilots can earn when they reach the highest levels of seniority.

At the top of the pay scale, a UPS Boeing 747-8F captain earns $401 per hour, while a first officer earns $284 per hour, based on rates established in September 2025. Estimates put a top-rate captain's earnings at approximately $34,000 per month, equivalent to around $408,000 annually. However, actual earnings can vary according to the pilot's schedule, additional duties, and applicable contractual payments.

One important detail is that UPS Airlines does not pay its pilots according to the Boeing 747-8 alone. Its widebody pilots operate under a common pay scale covering aircraft such as the Boeing 767 and McDonnell Douglas MD-11, meaning that a captain's hourly rate is determined primarily by seniority and position rather than by the particular aircraft flown. The latest data from ch-aviation shows that UPS Airlines' fleet is currently made up of the aircraft detailed in the table above.

Newly hired UPS Airlines pilots begin considerably lower on the compensation ladder, with a probationary rate of approximately $56 to $60 per hour regardless of whether they serve as first officers or captains. This illustrates why the highest published salary should not be treated as representative of every pilot employed by the airline, particularly those who are still building seniority and experience.

Atlas Air operates the world's largest fleet of Boeing 747 freighters and is another major employer for pilots seeking to fly the aircraft. Its compensation system is negotiated through a collective agreement with Teamsters Local 2750, with hourly rates varying according to the pilot's seat, aircraft assignment, and years of service.

For Boeing 747-8 captains, the hourly rate begins at $247 in the first year, increases to $259 in the second year, and reaches $332 by the twelfth year. These rates provide a clear picture of how experience influences earnings, although the captain's annual compensation also depends on the amount of credit earned under the applicable contract and any additional payments.

Atlas Air first officers generally earn between $120,000 and $230,000 annually, while captain salaries range from approximately $250,000 to more than $450,000, according to estimates. These broad ranges reflect differences in seniority, flying schedules, and total compensation, rather than a guaranteed salary for every pilot operating a Boeing 747-8.

Atlas Air pilots have sometimes described their compensation agreement as a contract cycle behind those of major airlines that secured substantial raises after the pandemic. Nevertheless, the airline remains an important option for experienced widebody pilots, particularly those interested in international cargo operations and the opportunities that come with building seniority at a large freighter operator.

Seniority is one of the most important factors determining how much a Boeing 747-8 pilot earns in 2026. As pilots progress through an airline's pay scale, their hourly rates generally increase, allowing experienced first officers and captains to earn considerably more than colleagues who have only recently joined the company. A useful rule of thumb is to multiply the applicable hourly rate by 1,000 to estimate annual earnings.

For example, a pilot earning $284 per hour would generate approximately $284,000 using this calculation, while a captain earning $401 per hour would reach approximately $401,000. This is only a rough estimate, however, because actual pay depends on credited hours and contractual provisions.

At UPS, pilots receive a contractual guarantee of approximately 81 hours per 28-day pay period, alongside potential per diem allowances, extra compensation for certain duties, and retirement contributions. These benefits can make the overall employment package more valuable than the hourly rate alone suggests, although the exact amount depends on individual circumstances and the terms of the applicable agreement.

Mid-career Boeing 747 first officers can often earn between $180,000 and $250,000 annually, while captains at major cargo and international airlines can exceed $350,000 once additional compensation is included. Consequently, comparing salaries requires more than simply examining the published hourly rate, since guaranteed credit, seniority progression, and retirement benefits also influence the final financial outcome.

The distinction between a first officer and a captain is another major factor behind the variation in Boeing 747-8 pilot salaries. Both pilots must meet demanding training and qualification requirements, but the captain has overall authority for the flight and carries additional responsibility for operational decisions, crew coordination, and the safe conduct of the aircraft.

First officers typically occupy the lower end of the pay scale, particularly during their early years with an airline. At UPS Airlines, for example, the highest published first officer rate is $284 per hour, compared with $401 for a captain, illustrating how a pilot's position can affect earnings even when both crew members operate the same Boeing 747-8F.

Promotion to captain generally depends on experience, qualifications, available vacancies, and seniority within the airline. A pilot may accumulate substantial flight experience before securing a command position, and the timing of that promotion can significantly influence lifetime earnings. The aircraft itself does not automatically guarantee a higher salary, as the employer's pay structure remains the decisive factor. Newly hired pilots must also account for the financial realities of entering a cargo airline. Initial compensation can be considerably lower than the salaries advertised for senior captains, and probationary pay arrangements may apply before a pilot progresses through the relevant contract. Therefore, published maximum salaries describe the potential at the top of the career ladder rather than the starting point for every new employee.

The compensation available to Boeing 747-8 pilots in 2026 reflects the continued importance of experienced flight crews to large-scale cargo operations. Airlines require qualified pilots who can manage complex international flights, operate sophisticated aircraft systems, and maintain professional standards across demanding schedules, making experienced captains particularly valuable within the industry. UPS Airlines provides one of the clearest examples of the earning potential available at the top of the market, with its $401 hourly captain rate translating into an estimated annual figure of approximately $408,000 for a senior Boeing 747-8F captain. Atlas Air also offers substantial earning opportunities, although its pay progression and contract structure differ from those at UPS Airlines.

When assessing Boeing 747-8 pilot compensation and comparing it to other aircraft, the airline, the pilot's position, years of service, guaranteed flight credit, and additional benefits must all be considered together. In 2026, experienced captains at major cargo operators can earn more than $400,000 annually, while first officers and junior pilots receive lower compensation as they progress through their careers.

#6199. United’s CEO Loves New American Airlines Boarding Gates—Here’s Why They Make Flying Worse

He saw it as something worth copying. When American announced the equipment, I thought it would make flying worse.

Kirby says he’s flown American, Delta and Southwest at least three times each over the past year, looking for things they do better than United. He lives in Dallas, and is regularly spotted on American but Southwest is based at Dallas Love Field as well.

American supplied this rendering when it announced the gates in April:

The glass barriers open after the system validates a boarding pass. American says the equipment can control the pace at which passengers enter the jet bridge, reduce manual work (cost savings on gate agents), and let employees spend more time helping customers (or just pocket the labor savings). The airline has since opened its new DFW Terminal C pier with the technology at all nine gates.

Airports are increasingly moving to e-gates, where facial recognition is used to confirm identity. So far this has mostly been used for international departures. The government wants more than a person looking at you and confirming it against the photo in your passport.

At many international departure gates, a camera is mounted at the gate or held by a government customs officer or airline staff member, to take a live photo of each passenger during boarding.

That image is sent to the Customs and Border Protection cloud-based Traveler Verification Service, which compares each person’s mugshot to a gallery built from your passport or visa photo and compares it to the flight manifest. The government has already checked the flight manifest and decided who can travel and who can’t. Now they want to match people against the manifest. If there’s a match, you’re allowed to depart the country. If there’s no match, you get a manual document check.

The biggest boarding bottlenecks aren’t actually the act of scanning a barcode. In fact, without human assistance each passenger may take longer to scan and wait for the gate to open.

Too many carry-ons, limited overhead bin space, gate-checking bags, families bunching up during preboarding and standby processing at the gate seem to be bigger issues. These gates do not solve any of that – just queue management and access control. The worst part of the experience is actually what Kirby says is his standard for judging this:

“I think of air travel for customers through the lens of traveling with small children,” Kirby said. “I have seven kids. I know what it’s like. I’ve tried to make it easy for people to travel with young children because if we do that, it’s going to be great for everybody.”

#6198. Southwest Performance Business Card Review: Is The $299 Annual Fee Worth It?

The Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card is the most premium card in the Chase and Southwest co-brand card portfolio. This card currently has a $299 annual fee and comes with many helpful perks when you fly Southwest, including a free checked bag, complimentary upgrades to Preferred seating when available, and an anniversary bonus of 9,000 points every year.

If you frequently travel with Southwest and qualify for a small business credit card, this card is worth a closer look. That’s especially true now, because not only is it offering a welcome bonus of 80,000 bonus points, but now is also your last chance to earn a Southwest credit card welcome bonus that counts toward the Companion Pass. I’ll get into all of that and more below, as this is my in-depth Southwest Performance Business Card review.

Link: Learn more about the Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card

Before I cover the Southwest Performance Business Card perks in detail, here’s a high-level view of this business credit card’s key details:

I also put together my pros and cons for the Southwest Performance Business Card:

When applying for a credit card, major considerations include the welcome bonus, the eligibility rules, and the fees, so let’s start by taking a look at those details for the Southwest Performance Business Card.

The Southwest Performance Business Card currently has a welcome bonus where you can earn 80,000 bonus points after spending $5,000 within the first three months.

Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider the points to be worth 1.2 cents each. That means I consider the 80,000 points to be worth $960, which is a solid bonus for a card like this (though admittedly we’ve seen slightly better limited time offers in the past).

When it comes to Southwest credit card eligibility rules, you’re potentially eligible for the Southwest Performance Business Card (including the welcome bonus) if you don’t currently have this card, and if you haven’t received a new cardmember bonus on this card in the past 24 months. You can have any of the Southwest personal cards, and/or the Southwest Premier Business Card, and they won’t impact eligibility for this card.

Beyond that, be aware of the general restrictions on applying for Chase cards. This includes the Chase 5/24 rule, whereby you generally won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more cards in the last 24 months. That said, business credit cards aren’t always included on your credit report, so they often don’t count toward 5/24.

The Southwest Performance Business Card has a $299 annual fee, making it the highest annual fee Southwest Airlines credit card. However, it also comes with plenty of perks that can justify it, as I’ll explain below.

There is no cost to add authorized users on the card, so you can add authorized users to your card, and be rewarded for their spending.

The Southwest Performance Business Card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s a good card to use for purchases abroad.

One of the main reasons you’ll want to consider picking up a card is because of its return on spending, so you’re sure it aligns with what you’re looking for. In the case of the Southwest Performance Business Card, it has a limited number of bonus categories, and spending can also help you toward earning elite status with Rapid Rewards. So let’s cover those details.

The Southwest Performance Business Card offers some potentially useful bonus categories, as follows:

These are some pretty solid bonus categories, though in general, I would only use this card for everyday spending if trying to earn Southwest Airlines status. Based on my valuation of 1.2 cents per point, this is like earning a 4.8% return on the 4x points categories, 2.4% return on the 2x points categories, and a 1.2% return on the 1x points categories.

The Southwest Performance Business Card lets you earn unlimited Tier Qualifying Points (TQPs) toward elite status. Specifically, you can earn 2,500 TQPs toward A-List status for every $5,000 spent on the card.

Southwest A-List status offers perks like priority boarding, a 25% points bonus, same-day standby, priority check-in and security lane access, and a dedicated phone number.

A-List status ordinarily requires earning 35,000 TQPs in a calendar year, so spending on a Southwest Performance Business Card could help you earn that. Whether or not that’s worth it depends on how much you’d otherwise fly with Southwest.

Do note that Southwest recently announced some big changes to its loyalty program, including new status level names and the introduction of a third tier called Platinum. Starting in 2027, A-List status will become Silver status, and earning it will require 35,000 TQPs or 25 qualifying flights.

According to the Southwest Performance Business Card’s terms & conditions, cardholders can earn TQPs on card spending at the current rate of 2,500 TQPs per $5,000 spent through December 31, 2026. After that date, A-List status will become Silver status, and every co-branded Southwest credit card will earn 1 TQP per dollar spent, so $35,000 in spending would get you to Silver.

One of the best values in travel is the Southwest Airlines Companion Pass. For those of you not familiar with Southwest’s Companion Pass, it allows someone else to travel with you for the entire year anywhere Southwest flies.

You still have to pay the taxes on their ticket, but the Companion Pass is valid on both award and revenue tickets. You can change your designated companion three times in a year, so you can potentially even use this for different people.

Historically, you’ve been able to get the Companion Pass by earning 135,000 Rapid Rewards points in a calendar year — and Southwest credit card welcome bonuses counted toward this, along with referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending on the card, and more. Starting January 1, 2027, this will no longer be the case.

Southwest is updating its elite status program to have three tiers, the highest of which is called Platinum and gets you unlimited Companion Pass trips. At that time, credit card welcome bonuses and all the other points earning mentioned above will no longer count toward qualifying for the Companion Pass (or any level of status).

To earn Platinum, and therefore the Companion Pass, you’ll instead need to earn 140,000 TQPs or take 100 qualifying flights. This change isn’t specific to the Southwest Performance Business Card, as it applies to welcome bonuses across all Southwest credit cards. But the good news is that welcome bonuses earned before the end of 2026 do count toward Companion Pass qualification, so now is your last chance to take advantage before this opportunity is closed.

I have an entire post on how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but I’ll briefly cover how redemptions work and how to get the most value out of your points here.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, which means that the value you’ll get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. That said, there are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, with Basic awards usually offering the highest redemption value.

In my experience, the best-value Southwest point redemptions are usually for international routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. Southwest also flies to Hawaii, which can be a good use of points, but I’ve found that the redemption value is often a bit lower on these in-demand routes. And of course, if you have the Companion Pass your points become twice as valuable because a friend can travel for free minus taxes and fees.

There are no change or cancellation fees on Southwest award bookings, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d want to cancel and rebook rather than change your existing itinerary.

While the Southwest Performance Business Card has a great bonus, the main reason you want to get this card is because of the perks that it offers. For those who fly Southwest with any frequency, the perks should more than cover the annual fee. In fact, for those who are frequent Southwest flyers, this card is almost too good to be true.

Just for having the Southwest Performance Business Card, you’ll receive 9,000 Rapid Rewards points on your account anniversary every year. As I said above, Southwest points can be redeemed for ~1.2 cents each toward airfare, so that’s the equivalent of ~$108 toward airfare annually.

The Southwest Performance Business Card offers a free first checked bag for you and up to eight additional passengers on your same reservation. If you usually check bags on Southwest — especially if you don’t have Southwest status, which gets you a free first checked bag — this benefit alone can quickly help you recoup the annual fee.

For non-elite Southwest travelers, a checked bag costs $45 one-way. If you maxed this benefit out with eight other travelers on a round-trip itinerary with checked bags, you’d be looking at over $800 in value.

When you book a Southwest flight as a Performance Business cardholder, you can select a Preferred or Standard seat at the time of booking, if they’re available. This benefit also extends to eight travelers on your same reservation.

The cost for a Preferred seat can vary from $28 to nearly $50 depending on the flight, so this benefit can also save you some real money.

The Southwest Performance Business Card also offers unlimited upgrades to extra legroom seats for cardholders and up to eight travelers on the same reservation. These upgrades are space available and will start within 48 hours of departure. This is another nice elite-style benefit that can noticeably improve your travel experience on Southwest.

Southwest Performance Business cardholders can board with Group 5, or earlier if they have status or a fare that entitles them to a higher boarding group. Once again, this perk extends to eight additional travelers on the same reservation.

The Southwest Performance Business offers 25% savings on inflight purchases of Wi-Fi and drinks. To take advantage of this, simply pay with your card. You’ll automatically receive a statement credit on eligible inflight purchases.

For having the Southwest Performance Card you receive a credit towards TSA PreCheck, Global Entry, or NEXUS. You can take advantage of this benefit once every four years. (up to $120 as of 10/1/24)

If you are going to use this perk, I’d highly recommend registering for Global Entry over TSA PreCheck. For those of you not familiar, TSA PreCheck gets you expedited US security screening, while Global Entry gets you expedited US immigration clearance.

Why register for Global Entry and not PreCheck? Because Global Entry also comes with TSA PreCheck, while the inverse isn’t true (signing up for TSA PreCheck doesn’t get you Global Entry).

If you have a small business and fly Southwest with any frequency, then the Southwest Performance Business Card is a no brainer. To start, the card has an excellent welcome bonus that could get you a lot of travel, and could even help you earn Companion Pass — at least until the end of 2026, which is coming up very fast.

On an ongoing basis, the card is worth it as well. It has a $299 annual fee but offers 9,000 points per year (which I value at ~$108) and more. This card should pay for itself for anyone who flies Southwest often.

In addition to the Southwest Performance Business Card, Southwest also has the Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Premier Business Credit Card (learn more). How does that card compare? Here’s a quick look:

If you fly Southwest only a handful of times a year, you might prefer this card and its lower annual fee to the more premium Southwest Performance Business.

In addition to comparing the Southwest Performance Business with other Southwest business credit cards, I want to take a minute to recommend another points strategy if you occasionally book award flights on Southwest.

Chase Ultimate Rewards is a transfer partner with Southwest Rapid Rewards, and points transfer at a 1:1 ratio. This means that you could earn points at a faster rate through Ultimate Rewards than through Rapid Rewards, and your points will be more flexible (since you can also transfer them to other airlines and hotel programs).

So, should you earn Rapid Rewards points directly with a Southwest Airlines credit card, or with a Chase Ultimate Rewards credit card?

For context, some of the best cards for earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points include the following:

The Ink Business Preferred Card could be an especially strong pick, considering you’re reading a review of a business credit card — and it has a significantly lower annual fee than the Southwest Performance Business Card.

On top of that, the following four no annual fee cards earn points that can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points at a 1:1 ratio in conjunction with one of the above cards:

The Southwest Performance Business Card is an exceptional option for those who frequently fly Southwest and want the best-possible experience with the airline.

In addition to the solid bonus, the card also offers 9,000 anniversary bonus points, space available Preferred and extra legroom seats, and more. The value of that should add up quickly if you fly Southwest frequently. This is especially true now that Southwest charges fees for checked bags and charges for assigned seats.

If you want to learn more about the Southwest Performance Business Card, follow this link.

#6196. Are Marriott Bonvoy Airline Mileage Transfers Worth It? They Could Be, But…

Among hotel loyalty programs, one thing that makes Marriott Bonvoy unique is the ability to (fairly) efficiently convert hotel points into airline miles. While most major hotel loyalty programs allow some sort of opportunity to convert hotel points into airline miles, it typically represents a very bad value.

In this post, I’d like to take a look at the opportunity to convert Marriott points into airline miles. Which airline programs can you move your Marriott points to, what’s the transfer ratio, and is it worth it?

It’s possible to convert Bonvoy points into airline miles, with your choice of nearly 40 different frequent flyer programs. Let’s take a look at which partners Marriott Bonvoy has, what the transfer ratios are, etc.

Marriott points generally convert into airline miles at a 3:1 ratio, and with most partners you get 5,000 bonus miles for every 60,000 Marriott points you transfer.

In other words, 60,000 Bonvoy points will convert into 25,000 airline miles (including the 5,000 bonus miles). You can take advantage of that bonus of 5,000 miles multiple times, meaning that you can convert Bonvoy points into airline miles at a ratio of up to 2.4:1.

Note that you can transfer a minimum of 3,000 Bonvoy points and a maximum of 240,000 Bonvoy points per day. So if you want to transfer more than 240,000 Bonvoy points, you’ll want to do so over multiple days.

Below is a chart with the airline frequent flyer programs you can transfer your Marriott points to, along with the standard transfer ratio, plus the ability to earn a bonus when transferring a minimum of 60,000 points.

While I covered these details above, let me specifically note the exceptions that apply here:

With the major transferable points currencies, converting points into airline miles is typically an instant process. So it’s worth being aware that Marriott points don’t convert into airline miles instantly. Rather, transfers generally take anywhere from a day to a couple of weeks, with transfers for most partners taking anywhere from two to five days.

I’d consider this to be a major weak point of this opportunity. I generally recommend converting points into airline miles in situations where you have a specific use in mind, and that could be a situation where you find award space on a particular flight.

Obviously that’s not exactly useful here, since it could take a couple of weeks for the transfer to happen, and odds are that whatever award availability you were looking at will be gone at that point.

The process of converting Marriott points into airline miles is really straightforward. Just go to the partner transfer page, click the “Transfer Points” button, and then you’ll be asked to enter the information for the account you want to move your points to. There you’ll be able to select how many points you want to transfer, and note that the amounts shown won’t reflect a bonus, if eligible.

It’s important to be sure that the names of the accounts match, as you can only transfer your Marriott points to an airline frequent flyer account that’s also in your name. Also keep in mind that once the miles are in your frequent flyer account, they’ll be subject to the standard airline mileage expiration policies of the program.

While I think converting Marriott points into airline miles could represent a good value, it’s not how I choose to redeem my Bonvoy points.

To briefly crunch some numbers, based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Bonvoy points to be worth 0.7 cents each. At a 2.4:1 transfer ratio (60,000 points per 25,000 miles), that’s like “paying” 1.68 cents per airline mile, which is a pretty decent cost.

Why do I choose not to convert Marriott points into airline miles?

I absolutely don’t think anyone is off base for choosing to convert Marriott points into airline miles. For that matter, this could be a good option if you’re in a crunch, and just need to top off an account for a high value redemption. However, it’s not how I choose to redeem my points, and I don’t think the value is there for most.

It’s more of a last resort redemption option, if you’re truly unable to get value elsewhere. In fairness, that might just be the direction the program is headed. While Bonvoy points have been significantly devalued over the years for hotel redemptions, the mileage conversion options have remained mostly consistent.

While the ability to convert Marriott points into airline miles has been around for a long time, we’re increasingly seeing two-way transfers, where you can convert airline miles into Marriott points.

The idea behind this is great — maybe someone has a lot of airline miles, but really wants to redeem for a hotel stay. Is this a good deal, though? Unfortunately the answer is almost always “no.”

Currently the below programs let you convert airline miles to Marriott Bonvoy, with both the transfer ratios and any exceptions listed.

While I suppose more flexibility is always a good thing, these transfers are almost never worth it. As a reminder, I value Bonvoy points at 0.7 cents each, and you’re getting at most one Bonvoy point per airline mile.

If you have the same valuation I do, at a 1:1 transfer ratio you’re getting up to 0.7 cents per mile, while at a 2:1 transfer ratio, you’re getting up to 0.35 cents per mile. That’s not a rate at which I’d be happy cashing in miles.

It’s possible to convert Marriott points into airline miles with over three dozen programs. While this is the best hotel points to airline miles transfer ratio that you’ll find with any program, it’s still not how I’d choose to redeem my Bonvoy points.

Yes, I appreciate the “insurance” that this redemption option provides, since it essentially creates a floor value for Bonvoy points. However, Bonvoy points are hard to efficiently earn through anything other than hotel stays, so I prefer to save them for hotel stays. I’d rather convert credit card points currencies into airline miles.

Where do you stand on the value of Marriott Bonvoy airline mileage transfers? Have you ever redeemed Bonvoy points this way?

Here in Germany, we don't have that many transferrable point currencies, and also the transfer partners are very limited. I used my Bonvoy points back in the days to transfer them to Korean Air and "rewarded" myself to a First Class award ticket from FRA to ICN for my 50th birthday. Well spent!

ND’s point is the key one IMO. With Bonvoy award pricing all over the place, a lot of redemptions now come in well under 0.7 cents, so the miles route isn’t the last resort it used to be. United at 60K for 30K with that extra bonus is the standout. Randy’s instant datapoint is a nice surprise vs the usual 2 to 5 days. FWIW the flip side of keeping points for hotels is checking what cash would cost first. Google Hotels gives a quick baseline. The same Marriott can price diff depending on which country you search from as inventory and rates vary by market. A free tool like Arbitrica checks it from roughly 195 countries and finds the lowest price in the world. If that cash rate is low, moving the points to miles starts to look smart

Generally I agree with this article. The points can be used with Marriott for better value but if you need to just top off for an airline redemption it may be worth doing. Buying Marriott points could be of good value when there is a 50% or 75% bonus offer.

If one looks at Bonvoy point redemption for award stays these days, unfortunately the average appears well below $.007 USD, maybe somewhere between $.004-$.006. Bonvoy-> Airline Transfers are increasingly becoming a more competitive redemption option. Not all FFPs are created equal, just like not all previously referenced Bonvoy transfer partners are equal. There are some good opportunities. Actually, Bonvoy points transferring to the airline FFP of my choice(s) are now my preferred way to use my Bonvoy points.

In terms of converting Marriott points to United miles, neither Marriott nor United should be seen as a “savings bank” for loyalty credits. I move some Marriott points to United miles (enough to get the special bonus) when (1) my supply of United miles is running “low” and I need same for flight(s) in the not too distant future and (2) one of the special bonuses is currently in effect. In general, over the last 30 years I've been accumulating airline miles (remember TWA?) and hotel points (remember SPG?), I've never seen the value of these miles and points increase over time! Devaluations and additional charges (such as so-called “destination fees” or “resort fees”) as well as no real redemption chart for Marriott points hardly make those Marriott points any type of stable currency. For that matter, airline miles are not really any better. 😀 As an aside, the best airline loyalty redemption value I ever got was in 1985 when I redeemed 90,000 miles on TWA for a open-jaw, round trip for two, first class, from SFO to CAI, returning TLV to SFO.

#6195. American Airlines Spent Years Making Its Cabins Worse—Now It’s Racing To Win Passengers Back From United And Delta

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby says one of his biggest competitive advantages won’t last. Other airlines will catch up with Starlink internet. He says he’s investing anyway, because two or three years is enough time to get passengers to try United, discover other things they like, and move their loyalty and credit card spending. That answers the argument Doug Parker made at American Airlines in 2017 for not investing in product: better products just get copied so can’t offer an enduring advantage. Delta spent nearly two decades showing how investment in the operation, product and employees could work together. United has improved more than any other U.S. airline over the past decade. American has made an impressive amount of progress since its premium pivot roughly 21 months ago. But it’s trying to win back customers while losing money, carrying heavy debt, and with fuel costs up. They’re in a race against time to show results before Wall Street gets impatient. I attended American’s September 2017 media and investor day. The airline’s theory was that competitors would match a better product, leaving corporate culture and employees to differentiate the airline. Take care of employees, who would take care of customers, who would take care of shareholders. (Of course American alienated all three groups.) They didn’t explain how that was going to happen. There were nicer employee facilities coming, help using their health and wellness benefits, and they spent a disproportionate amount of time on company-sponsored weight loss programs. I left without understanding the mission employees were supposed to rally around, or how American would install its workforce with a desire and knowledge to deliver exceptional service. Meanwhile, American was preparing to fly its new domestic interior with less legroom, less padded seats and no seatback screens. At that same media day, they didn’t even think they needed native booking in their mobile app. Sending customers to a mobile website was good enough. A year later, Parker told employees: we work really hard to match our service to our competitors, and they do the same to us. He described watching what competitors put onboard, including meals, to ensure American was comparable. He was surprised by the idea that customers might choose United or Delta because of a different inflight product. In contrast, Richard Anderson became Delta CEO in 2007. Along with Glen Hauenstein and Gil West, he built an airline around keeping its promises to passengers and driving hard bargains with its counterparties. Anderson later explained how much of the advantage came from line maintenance. An older airplane could be reliable if mechanics could work on it where it spent the night, fix recurring problems and have it ready in the morning. Delta also worked toward eliminating involuntary denied boarding. A customer who bought a ticket, arrived on time and followed every instruction shouldn’t be told they weren’t going to travel because the airline had sold too many seats. Finding enough volunteers protected the relationship with that customer. They leaned into seatback screens. Their non-union crews were somewhat friendlier than at competitors. Then Delta made itself relevant in the markets where customers had the most money to spend. The 2011 LaGuardia slot swap with US Airways was one of the great airline asset trades. Parker’s airline gave Delta 132 daily LaGuardia slot pairs in exchange for 42 pairs at Washington National and $66.5 million. Required divestitures reduced Delta’s net gain (they eventually got the slots back that were transferred to WestJet) but it gave them the platform to build the New York business. Delta fleeced Parker. US Airways strengthened Washington, but when it merged with American it had to give up slots there anyway. The combined airline couldn’t keep all of both carriers’ holdings. American – once headquartered in New York – would never be able to position itself in New York the way that Delta had. Delta invested in facilities at LaGuardia, JFK and Los Angeles. That all positioned Delta to overtake American in cobrand credit card spend. I’ve been critical of how much Delta has coasted on that reputation. Its operational advantage isn’t what it was (they’re still a bit more reliable than peers but when things go south they struggle to recover, and no longer go months without a mainline cancel). Their 767s out of New York are arguably the actual worst product across the Atlantic and among those who compete for premium transcon business. And Delta’s success despite weak mileage value shouldn’t have taught competitors to devalue their own programs. Delta offered a better experience – that’s eroding – and had strong positioning in some of the best spend markets, and lack of competition in their other key markets (Atlanta, Upper Midwest, Salt Lake). Kirby took a long time to arrive at his current view. He was president of American when it cut meal service in 2014. Planning for the domestic interior without screens began while he was still there, even though the first aircraft with that interior entered service after he left. He initially carried the same approach to United. They cut full domestic first class meals on flights under four hours outside the dinner window, before customer complaints forced a reversal. They eliminated Polaris wine flights and cocktail carts, then reduced business class staffing by one flight attendant and moved to pre-plated entrees. Some of United’s early product investment was probably overboard – greenlighting most everything when Oscar Munoz came back from medical leave. The later United NEXT commitment to screens, bigger bins and a better domestic cabin, combined with sustained investment in its mobile app, represented a different approach under later Kirby. Most passengers sit in coach. Improving their experience gets them to pay more and builds a reputation that qualifies the airline for their future purchases in business. Even business class passengers internationally are often coach passengers domestically, and bad experiences in domestic form the bulk of a passenger’s opinion when it coms time to buy long haul business. The app is part of the coach product just as well as the premium cabin one. Passengers can manage changes, get help improving their seat assignment and receive clearer explanations when something goes wrong. It gives them more control over their trip. They use it repeatedly, and it’s reason they may hesitate to move their flying elsewhere even after another airline matches the cabin. By 2025, Kirby was explaining a different test for food spending. He told Brian Sumers: Every year we’re going to consciously spend more for customers in a bet that we’ll just win more brand-loyal customers. He couldn’t prove exactly how much additional ticket revenue better food would generate. He was willing to make the investment anyway. The old approach could identify the savings from moving a meal window by 15 minutes, while the revenue lost through a series of small disappointments was much harder to see. United’s network rebuilding started earlier. Kirby restored domestic connectivity that had been cut back under Jeff Smisek, and explicitly explained in October 2017 that better connections would help sell credit cards. If United’s schedule didn’t work for someone, that person wasn’t going to take the card. American went the other way in New York, Chicago and Los Angeles. Retreating made the airline less useful in the country’s most valuable spending markets. Offering a less desirable product alienated customers from spending on the American card. And an airline’s route accounting can miss this. A Chicago customer’s work trips may be what persuade them to get an airline’s card, even if they eventually redeem the miles for Hawaii. Credit the Hawaii flight with all the benefit, cut Chicago because it looks weak, and you lose the spending that generated the miles in the first place. In contrast, aviation watchdog JonNYC shares excerpts attributed to Chief Commercial Officer Andrew Nocella laying out where the airline sees itself: United reached 50% of revenue from Chicago-based passengers in the second quarter of 2026, according to Nocella, and gained share in its other hub cities as well. It expects to largely complete United NEXT’s connectivity goals at its midcontinent hubs by summer 2027. More attention then shifts to coastal gateways and international expansion, including a planned return to New York JFK next year. Premium capacity will grow faster than main cabin capacity as United adds Airbus A321neo and A321XLR aircraft at scale. Comments by Andrew Nocella, shared by JonNYC United’s hubs in some of the best cities for card spend and long haul pre-existed Kirby (and those cities are more contested than other airlines face in their most important hubs). Kirby’s Starlink explanation in his Cheeky Pint interview describes how he plans to accelerate United’s gains. John Collison characterized the opportunity as a two-to-three-year window to win customers, and Kirby agreed. Other airlines will eventually have comparable low Earth orbit connectivity. American, Southwest, Alaska and even Frontier are all adding Starlink (and Southwest expects to complete its install around the time United does). they’re going to try us for Starlink, and they’re going to stay because all the other technology, and everything else is better. A temporary advantage can generate a customer relationship that outlasts it. And the biggest gap will be with Delta, which has committed to Amazon Leo that will maybe start becoming available in 2028, and where they’ve committed only to eventually outfit 500 aircraft. Delta’s current wifi is generally poor now that demands on the system by giving it away free have overwhelmed available bandwidth. Parker was right that competitors could copy a feature. Copying the feature doesn’t on its own win back the customer. American is finally reversing course. I first reported its explicit premium pivot in January 2025. In roughly 21 months they’ve changed an extraordinary amount, from better coffee and wine to improved lounges, new business class suites and more attention to the coach experience. They’ve committed to bringing back domestic seatback screens and adding more first class and extra legroom seats. They’ve announced Starlink installations beginning early next year. They’ve even instructed employees to stop involuntarily bumping passengers, giving airport leadership more authority to secure volunteers. American is changing what it asks employees to prioritize, and giving them tools to do it. And Flagship Dining at Los Angeles is finally reopening after more than six years, with access expanded to qualifying business class passengers. It’s a defensive move because Delta’s business class lounge is so much better, and United’s even had been better than American Flagship. I want this to work. I’ve spent years criticizing American because it had so much potential to be better. They’re making real changes and some customers will come back simply because the airline stops giving them reasons to avoid it. But matching what they already get elsewhere likely isn’t enough – American needs a value proposition for what they deliver to customers that no one else will. That’s Delta’s reliability argument (paired with service and screens that for years others eschewed). That’s United’s Starlink argument (paired with a stronger global network). American entered the pandemic with heavy debt after spending more than $12 billion on share buybacks under Parker. Borrowing while returning that much cash to shareholders left it weaker than competitors. It has too much debt service, less room to borrow, and less well-positioned to do acquisitions. The risk is that investors demand results before enough customers have experienced the improvements, or demand cuts to the spending that could produce real results. American’s domestic seatback screens won’t begin arriving on new aircraft until 2028, and the broader fleet project extends into the next decade. It needs the improvements it can deliver sooner to get customers back onboard and spending more before then. The interest and fuel bills are arriving now. Comments by Andrew Nocella, shared by JonNYC

United’s hubs in some of the best cities for card spend and long haul pre-existed Kirby (and those cities are more contested than other airlines face in their most important hubs). Kirby’s Starlink explanation in his Cheeky Pint interview describes how he plans to accelerate United’s gains.

John Collison characterized the opportunity as a two-to-three-year window to win customers, and Kirby agreed. Other airlines will eventually have comparable low Earth orbit connectivity. American, Southwest, Alaska and even Frontier are all adding Starlink (and Southwest expects to complete its install around the time United does).

they’re going to try us for Starlink, and they’re going to stay because all the other technology, and everything else is better.

A temporary advantage can generate a customer relationship that outlasts it. And the biggest gap will be with Delta, which has committed to Amazon Leo that will maybe start becoming available in 2028, and where they’ve committed only to eventually outfit 500 aircraft. Delta’s current wifi is generally poor now that demands on the system by giving it away free have overwhelmed available bandwidth. Parker was right that competitors could copy a feature. Copying the feature doesn’t on its own win back the customer.

American is finally reversing course. I first reported its explicit premium pivot in January 2025. In roughly 21 months they’ve changed an extraordinary amount, from better coffee and wine to improved lounges, new business class suites and more attention to the coach experience.

They’ve committed to bringing back domestic seatback screens and adding more first class and extra legroom seats. They’ve announced Starlink installations beginning early next year.

They’ve even instructed employees to stop involuntarily bumping passengers, giving airport leadership more authority to secure volunteers. American is changing what it asks employees to prioritize, and giving them tools to do it.

And Flagship Dining at Los Angeles is finally reopening after more than six years, with access expanded to qualifying business class passengers. It’s a defensive move because Delta’s business class lounge is so much better, and United’s even had been better than American Flagship.

I want this to work. I’ve spent years criticizing American because it had so much potential to be better. They’re making real changes and some customers will come back simply because the airline stops giving them reasons to avoid it. But matching what they already get elsewhere likely isn’t enough – American needs a value proposition for what they deliver to customers that no one else will. That’s Delta’s reliability argument (paired with service and screens that for years others eschewed). That’s United’s Starlink argument (paired with a stronger global network).

American entered the pandemic with heavy debt after spending more than $12 billion on share buybacks under Parker. Borrowing while returning that much cash to shareholders left it weaker than competitors. It has too much debt service, less room to borrow, and less well-positioned to do acquisitions.

The risk is that investors demand results before enough customers have experienced the improvements, or demand cuts to the spending that could produce real results. American’s domestic seatback screens won’t begin arriving on new aircraft until 2028, and the broader fleet project extends into the next decade. It needs the improvements it can deliver sooner to get customers back onboard and spending more before then. The interest and fuel bills are arriving now.
