#6193. How To Redeem Alaska Atmos Rewards Points: Rules, Fees, & Sweet Spots

Alaska Atmos Rewards (formerly Alaska Mileage Plan) has long been a favorite points currency among miles & points geeks, given the carrier’s unique array of airline partners, generous stopover policy, and attractive redemption rates.

In this post, I’d like to take an in-depth look at how to redeem Atmos Rewards points. How do you earn Atmos Rewards points, what are the rules around redeeming them, and what are the best uses?

There are several different ways to go about earning Alaska Atmos Rewards points, from credit cards, to outright buying points, to transferring them from other cards.

The Atmos Rewards program has three co-branded credit cards, issued by Bank of America, and they all have excellent welcome bonuses with limited eligibility restrictions:

What’s so great is that you can potentially qualify for all of these cards, so that’s an opportunity to earn lots of points. For example, I picked up both the Atmos Rewards Summit Card and Atmos Rewards Business Card on the same day.

The Atmos Rewards program is transfer partners with Bilt Rewards, so you can transfer Bilt Points to Atmos Rewards at a 1:1 ratio. This could be a great reason to pick up one of Bilt’s credit cards, with options including the Bilt Blue Card (learn more), Bilt Obsidian Card (learn more), and Bilt Palladium Card (learn more) (Rates & Fees). Personally, I think the Bilt Palladium Card is by far the most lucrative.

You can even pay rent with an Atmos Rewards card and earn 3x points while paying a 3% fee, which could be a useful deal, especially if you’re pursuing elite status.

The program also partners with Marriott Bonvoy®, so you can transfer over Marriott points. The ratio is that 60,000 Marriott Bonvoy® Points convert into 25,000 Atmos Rewards points (if you convert in different increments, it’s a 3:1 ratio).

This can be a solid value, and there are lots of credit cards that can earn you Bonvoy points, including the Marriott Bonvoy Business® American Express® Card (learn more), Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card (learn more), and Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more).

The Atmos Rewards program is pretty aggressive about selling points, and the program seems to offer promotions on purchased points every couple of months. When we see these offers, you can expect bonuses in the range of 90-110%. This is often an opportunity to acquire Atmos Rewards points for under two cents each.

It doesn’t cost anything to join the Atmos Rewards program, so I generally recommend signing up ahead of time — you have to be a member for at least 10 days in order to take advantage of one of these promotions.

Not only are there great ways to earn Atmos Rewards points either through credit cards or by buying them outright, but Atmos Rewards is also a good program to credit flights to.

For one, Atmos Rewards is the last major US frequent flyer program to give members the option to earn points based on distance flown rather than dollars spent. Atmos Rewards allows mileage earning on a variety of airline partners, ranging from Condor to Cathay Pacific. Atmos Rewards lets you earn points for travel on the following airline partners:

The one thing worth mentioning is that you can only earn Atmos Rewards points on Korean Air, Philippine Airlines, and Starlux Airlines, if you book through Alaska, rather than through one of the partners.

Alaska Atmos Rewards has some great redemption opportunities, though there are also quite a few rules to be aware of. Let’s cover some of those basics.

Alaska Airlines belongs to the oneworld alliance, though the airline has an array of partners beyond oneworld. It’s possible to redeem Atmos Rewards points for travel on the following airlines:

All Atmos Rewards award redemption partners can be booked online at alaskaair.com. If you have a complicated itinerary or are having issues with the website, you’ll want to call the Atmos Rewards partner award desk, which can be reached at 800-252-7522.

When it comes to redeeming points, Atmos Rewards has three simple award charts that are a combination of zone and distance based.

There’s the Americas award chart, which covers any travel from the United States to anywhere in the Americas, including North America and South America.

Then there’s the Europe, Middle East, and Africa award chart, which includes travel from the United States to Europe, the Middle East, and Africa, and travel within Europe, the Middle East, and Africa.

Lastly, there’s the Asia-Pacific award chart, which includes travel from the United States to Asia-Pacific, within Asia-Pacific, and between Asia-Pacific and Europe, the Middle East, and Africa.

The most significant thing to understand here is that the “starting at” prices are actually what you’re going to pay if there’s saver level award availability. All partners have the same award pricing assuming there’s saver award availability.

There are a few other important things to mention:

The Atmos Rewards program awards status points for award travel booked through the program. This applies for travel on Alaska, Hawaiian, and all other partner airlines.

Just book using Atmos Rewards points and have your Atmos Rewards number on the reservation, and you’ll earn one status point per mile flown, regardless of the class of service (this assumes you select to earn Atmos Rewards points based on distance flown).

This is a massive point of differentiation for the program, and if you ask me, it’s a contributing reason that many American loyalists might want to consider Atmos Rewards.

One of my favorite things about the Atmos Rewards program is that you are allowed a stopover on a one-way award ticket when traveling between regions. This is possible regardless of which partner you redeem with.

So if you book a roundtrip as two one-ways, this means you can potentially get two stopovers on a roundtrip ticket. To book a ticket online with a stopover, just use the multi-city function, and you can search each portion of the ticket individually.

Now, admittedly with the program being distance based, you are in some cases potentially paying more for itineraries with stopovers, but it’s still a useful feature.

On the surface, Atmos Rewards should have access to the same award availability as other partner airlines do, though in some cases Atmos Rewards inexplicably doesn’t have access to the same space. Most commonly:

This won’t be consistent, but it is something to be aware of, and it sure can be frustrating. There’s generally not any way to get around this.

When searching award availability on some partner airlines, you may see award pricing that’s way above what the chart suggests. This includes for some flights on Aer Lingus, Icelandair, Qatar Airways, and Starlux Airlines. In those situations, what’s happening is that there’s no saver level award availability, but Atmos Rewards has negotiated to have more award availability at a higher cost.

I know this kind of pricing frustrates some people and makes them think the program doesn’t offer good value. However, in these situations, other partner airlines simply wouldn’t have access to the award space. So I wouldn’t view it as a negative, but rather just as an opportunity you probably don’t want to take advantage of.

Atmos Rewards blocks many many partner awards within 72 hours of departure. I’ve been told that this policy won’t stick around, though I don’t have a timeline for when it will change, and it continues to be live. It’s certainly something to be aware of when it comes to last minute redemption opportunities.

Furthermore, Atmos Rewards doesn’t have access to any nonstop domestic American awards at the saver level within six days of departure. Don’t expect this to change, as it’s presumably a commercial decision on American’s part.

There are a couple of fees associated with redeeming Atmos Rewards points:

Atmos Rewards no longer has any change or cancelation fees for award tickets, which gives you lots of flexibility to speculatively lock in awards, or even change them if a better routing opens up. The only exception is that the $20 partner award booking fee can’t be refunded.

Atmos Rewards passes on carrier imposed surcharges (often referred to as fuel surcharges) for travel on some partner airlines. Specifically, these apply for travel on British Airways, Hainan Airlines, and Icelandair. Fortunately they don’t apply for travel on other partner airlines.

Atmos Rewards doesn’t allow award tickets to be placed on hold. To book an Atmos Rewards award ticket you need to have sufficient points in your account, though you can always cancel it for free.

Atmos Rewards points don’t expire. However, if you don’t have any account activity for over two years, your account may be locked for security reasons, and your points may be accessed by contacting Atmos Rewards and verifying personal details.

We all have different travel goals, so there’s never going to be a one size fits all answer as to what the best use of points is. Broadly speaking, my favorite way to redeem points is for aspirational redemptions in first and business class, since that’s where you’ll get the most outsized value.

However, nowadays I’d argue that the redemption sweet spot with Atmos Rewards is largely for shorter awards, given the distance based pricing. In some way, the Atmos Rewards award charts are almost a competitor to British Airways Club, in terms of the great value of short haul redemptions. Since you can redeem Atmos Rewards points for flights globally, I figured the best way to share some sweet spots would just be to take a look at each award chart individually.

Before I do, let me acknowledge a new reality of the miles & points hobby. The reality is that airlines are getting savvier when it comes to how they release award space, and in many cases, they open fewer award seats to members of partner frequent flyer programs. This is beyond any carrier’s control, but it does limit the arbitrage opportunities by using great frequent flyer programs.

Below is the Atmos Rewards award chart for the Americas, which applies exclusively if traveling within the Americas (including North and South America).

Here are some of the sweet spots, as I see it:

Honestly, I think this is the chart with the most consistently good pricing, whether traveling short haul or long haul. So if you can find award availability within the Americas, you should be pretty happy with the pricing. I redeem Atmos Rewards points constantly for travel on American, as it’s a way to get a good deal on domestic flights, especially in a premium cabin. It might not be the most aspirational thing on earth, but it sure is practical.

Below is the Atmos Rewards award chart for Europe, Middle East, and Africa, which applies if traveling within or between any of those regions, and also applies if traveling between the Americas and any of those regions.

Here are some of the sweet spots, as I see it:

Below is the Atmos Rewards award chart for Asia-Pacific, which applies if traveling within Asia-Pacific, and between Asia-Pacific and any other regions. Note that Asia includes the Indian subcontinent, since some other award charts put that in the same region as the Middle East.

Here are some of the sweet spots, as I see it:

Alaska Atmos Rewards is one of the most useful programs for redeeming points. Given the zone and distance based award chart, you’ll generally find the best value with the program for shorter distance itineraries, where pricing can be very attractive.

I’d say Atmos Rewards is a program that has become practical more than aspirational, and that’s something that I don’t mind, at least at this point in history. It’s not like there are many Cathay Pacific, Japan Airlines, or Qantas, ultra long haul first class awards to snag, so we’re not missing out on that much.

Atmos Rewards is my go-to program for most awards covering a distance of up to 1,500 miles, give or take.

What’s your favorite use of Alaska Atmos Rewards points?

#6192. Singapore Airlines’ New First & Business Class Cabins Will Be Unveiled This Week

In November 2024, Singapore Airlines announced a huge investment into its premium passenger experience, which will see the introduction of all-new cabin products, plus the expansion of first class. These cabins will be retrofitted on dozens of Airbus A350s, and will also be available on newly delivered Boeing 777-9s in the future.

The product was initially supposed to roll out as of the spring of 2026, though as is all too common nowadays, the project was delayed due to supply chain constraints, etc. The good news is that the wait is almost over — the new product will be unveiled on Friday, November 6, 2026, with an entry into service planned for the first quarter of 2027. Let’s recap all the details we know as of now.

Singapore Airlines will be investing 1.1 billion SGD (~835 million USD) to update the interiors of its entire long haul Airbus A350-900 fleet. This consists of a total of 41 jets, and includes the carrier’s seven A350-900ULRs, with the “ULR” standing for “ultra long range,” as these planes operate the world’s longest flights.

The only A350-900s that won’t be reconfigured are the ones that are specifically designed for regional flights, featuring the same cabin products you’ll find onboard Boeing 787-10s.

With this project, we can expect changes across cabins. We’ll see first class added to the carrier’s ultra long range A350s, an all-new business class product, refreshes to premium economy and economy, plus an updated inflight entertainment system and the installation of Starlink Wi-Fi.

How will the layouts of these jets change, once reconfigured? Singapore Airlines’ standard long haul A350-900s:

Singapore Airlines’ ultra long range A350-900s:

Singapore Airlines will be introducing new first and business class products. This isn’t just some new interim product, but rather this is intended to be the carrier’s new premium product in the long run. The same seats that are being installed on the Airbus A350-900s will also be installed on the carrier’s Boeing 777-9s, so these are very much “flagship” cabins.

Singapore Airlines initially intended to debut new premium cabins on its 777-9s, which were first supposed to be delivered in 2020. However, those have now been pushed back to late 2027 at the earliest. So clearly Singapore Airlines decided that it’s finally time to introduce new cabins, even if the 777-9 keeps getting delayed.

Singapore Airlines will introduce a new first class product on its subfleet of A350-900ULRs, which operate the world’s longest flights. This same product will be available on 777-9s in the future, but won’t be available on standard A350-900s. Furthermore, there are no plans to retrofit existing 777s with this product. A350s will have four of these seats, while 777s will have six of these seats.

Below is the first teaser picture of Singapore Airlines’ new first class.

Currently Singapore Airlines only has first class on its A380s and 777-300ERs, so it’s cool to see this product expand.

Official details about the new first class are limited, other than that it’s “designed with increasingly discerning travellers in mind,” and that the first class seats “promise to deliver an unparalleled in-flight experience.”

We have reason to believe that the new cabin will be in a 1-2-1 layout. Why? Well, Singapore Airlines filed a patent some time back, clearly for the carrier’s new first class product. The patent is for the 777-9, where the airline will have a first class cabin with six seats.

The plan seems to be to have individual suites along the windows, plus a double suite in the center. However, the center suite can be used by either one or two people, so if people are traveling separately, there’s a partition that can go up.

As you can see, there’s a bit of staggering with the cabin, to maximize the width of the suite, as the aisle curves a bit.

This looks like a very nice product, though to be perfectly honest, it doesn’t look like anything revolutionary. Nowadays some of the top first class products are in a 1-1-1 configuration, like what you’ll find on Japan Airlines and Emirates. Admittedly the flexibility of the double suite in the middle is great for those traveling with someone, since that’s not something that was really considered with the new Japan Airlines and Emirates products.

For that matter, we have reason to believe that Cathay Pacific may offer the world’s best first class on its 777-9s, as it could very well be in a 1-1 configuration.

This is super exciting. Singapore Airlines is one of the best airlines in the world, with incredible service, food, drinks, and more. However, at this point the carrier’s business class hard product isn’t really cutting edge anymore.

With details being so limited, all we can do is speculate as of now. So I have a few thoughts:

In late 2024, when this project was first announced, Singapore Airlines shared the following timeline for debuting the new first and business class seats:

Unfortunately that timeline didn’t stick. Several months ago we learned how the first retrofitted aircraft wouldn’t enter service until the first quarter of 2027, best case scenario, with the expectation being that some long range A350s would be reconfigured before the first ultra long range A350 gets a makeover.

The revised timeline reflects industry-wide supply chain constraints, as well as delays in the certification of one of the new seats (a common industry problem). The aircraft will be retrofitted by SIA Engineering Company in Singapore.

So, is that still the timeline we’re looking at? It would appear so. Singapore Airlines has confirmed on social media that it will unveiling its all new products on Friday, November 6, 2026.

From the first sketch to the final detail, discover how the new Singapore Airlines travel experience comes together across every cabin class and every part of the journey.Unveiling on 6 November 2026. pic.twitter.com/dTML7QmOXe

This announcement is actually being marketed as being about more than just seats, as it’s described as “the new Singapore Airlines travel experience,” and we’ll learn how it “comes together across every class and every part of the journey.” We’ve already seen the airline tease details of a new dining concept as well as new amenities across cabins, so presumably this will all come together to form the new experience.

Which routes are likely to get the new cabins first? While we’ll see how this plays out, based on historical precedent, it’s likely that Sydney (SYD) and London (LHR) will be the first two destinations, since those are the first destinations where the airline has sent all of its new long haul products.

Singapore Airlines plans to introduce all-new cabins on its Airbus A350-900s, which will also eventually be installed on Boeing 777-9s. Most exciting is an improved new business class product, which is long overdue. Singapore Airlines will also be adding first class to its subfleet of A350-900ULRs, with a boutique cabin having just four seats.

While this product was supposed to enter service as of the second quarter of 2026, the timeline has been pushed back to the first quarter of 2027, due to supply chain constraints and certification issues… a familiar story! The expectation is that the new cabins will be unveiled this week, on November 6, 2026. I’m mighty curious to learn the details, so I’m happy that the wait is finally (almost) over.

What do you make of Singapore Airlines’ plans to introduce new long haul cabins?

“Nowadays some of the top first class products are in a 1-1-1 configuration, like what you’ll find on Japan Airlines and Emirates.” Aren’t those the only 2 that have that? Ignoring the eff-up that is LH and LX’s new first class products…

This has the potential to be a massive improvement. I shifted all my SIN-US flying to United Polaris Studio as it is so much more comfortable, but having SQ soft product would be welcome for that long of a flight.

Tbh hard product is plateauing across the board. Beyond getting your own private bedroom like The Residence or something, there's only so much space someone can utilize on a flight. #6190. Hotel Guests Report Mold And Mice—It Still Passed Inspection The Next Day

A mother says mice crawled across her sleeping three-year-old at a Wyndham hotel near the Albany, New York airport. Other residents reported mold, cockroaches and soaked carpets. The hotel passed a county health inspection the next day even though the inspector recorded six violations. The rooms with violations weren’t occupied on the day the inspector arrived and were supposed to be repaired before being rented. We trust hotels to do some very basic things: Change the sheets Clean the bathroom Make sure the door locks And the brand on the hotel is supposed to give you confidence! Baymont by Wyndham Latham Albany Airport markets rooms to travelers. It also houses people placed by county social services. That’s often a good indication… One woman, staying with her nine month old daughter, described cockroaches, mice, mold and bedbugs in some rooms. Other residents described wet carpets and a strong smell. A guest said she’d filmed mice crawling over her sleeping child and had stopped letting the girl sleep in her own bed. There were complaints about mouse droppings and dead flies on a bed, and mold and dead flies in a refrigerator. The County moved some social service clients. Another county with one room there relocated their client as a precaution and suspended use of the hotel. What The Inspection Found Albany County inspected the hotel October 13, finding no public health hazards, but six violations: A removed smoke detector. Three exterior doors that didn’t self-latch. A stained bathroom ceiling tile. Evidence of pests in a room. The plan to fix the rooms before renting them helps explain how the hotel could continue operating, though a missing smoke detector matters even in an empty room. And it seems to me that pests in one room can easily spread. There were earlier maintenance concerns, too. A March 13, 2025 entry in New York’s inspection database notes water stains and possible active leaks at this property. You’re Supposed To Be Able To Rely On A Brand A big part of what a hotel brand sells is confidence that somebody has vetted the property. You know what you’re getting. The hotel may be franchised but it’s supposed to deliver to brand standards. Years ago I covered an Inside Edition investigation that found three of nine hotels tested hadn’t provided completely fresh sheets between guests. The beds were re-made with the previous guest’s used sheets. Then came pandemic promises of enhanced cleaning. Inside Edition went back in 2020, using washable marks visible under ultraviolet light. It reported unchanged bedding at a Hyatt Place and a Hampton Inn in Times Square. At Trump International, the sheets had been changed, but the report said a pillowcase hadn’t. More recently, I covered a Hyatt Place guest who went through three rooms and still wound up with filthy bedding. Hyatt refunded the stay and provided 15,000 points. You’re not supposed to have to even check recent reviews and traveler photos, and pull back the bedding immediately on arrival. I Wouldn’t Let An Airline Choose Where I Sleep, Either I’ve made the same argument about hotels airlines provide during overnight delays. I’ve reported on roaches, floors was so dirty they turned guests’ feet black, and worse. Airlines offering lowest-cost rooms aren’t necessarily delvering places you’d ever want to stay. A big part of what a hotel brand sells is confidence that somebody has vetted the property. You know what you’re getting. The hotel may be franchised but it’s supposed to deliver to brand standards.

Years ago I covered an Inside Edition investigation that found three of nine hotels tested hadn’t provided completely fresh sheets between guests. The beds were re-made with the previous guest’s used sheets.

Then came pandemic promises of enhanced cleaning. Inside Edition went back in 2020, using washable marks visible under ultraviolet light. It reported unchanged bedding at a Hyatt Place and a Hampton Inn in Times Square. At Trump International, the sheets had been changed, but the report said a pillowcase hadn’t.

More recently, I covered a Hyatt Place guest who went through three rooms and still wound up with filthy bedding. Hyatt refunded the stay and provided 15,000 points. You’re not supposed to have to even check recent reviews and traveler photos, and pull back the bedding immediately on arrival.

It’s gotten so bad that I bring a bright LED flashlight to check hotel rooms for bedbugs before we bring our luggage in. Too many friends of ours have encountered them.

Wyndham and you’re surprised. ? That’s the norm

I read the health department inspections each week. Most ” pass ” with the promise that correction will be made. Ugh. This is the world we live with

And people wonder why I only stat high end hotels. And sometimes THEY are not the best either.

Stayed, well checked in and checked out of the Baymont Abilene (Texas). It was the only Gov’t rate room available – $119 a night. Apparently a data center project books out every room in town.

Complete sh1thole, and I don’t know where they got the pics from their website. Homeless shelters would be an upgrade. #6188. Buy Finnair Plus Avios For 50% Off (1.06 Cents Each): Best-Ever Price Worth It?

The Finnair Plus program has just launched its newest promotion on purchased Avios, offering up to a 50% discount, which is an opportunity to acquire Avios for as little as 1.06 cents each. This is the best offer from the program of the year, and you can use this to acquire any “flavor” of Avios at an advantageous rate.

Strategically buying points for premium travel can be a great value, especially with a specific use in mind, so this is an offer I’d seriously consider.

Between 12:01AM EET on November 2 and 11:59PM EET on November 16, 2026, Finnair Plus is offering a limited time promotion on purchased Avios. If you purchase Finnair Plus Avios, you can receive the following deal:

Beyond the discount, you can also receive tier points toward status equivalent to 10% of the Avios purchased. This is of course useful if you’re going for elite status with Finnair, but otherwise, is of limited value.

Now, here’s where it gets interesting — Finnair lets you select the currency in which you want to buy Avios (you can find the option to switch currencies at the top of the screen), and the price differs:

So based on current exchange rates, you’re best off paying in JPY, followed by USD, followed by EUR. If you maxed out the promotion with a 50% bonus and paid in JPY, the best deal you could get would be to pay $2,110 for 200,000 Avios, which comes out to 1.06 cents per Avios (in USD), inclusive of all taxes and fees.

Note that this offer is only available to Finnair Plus members who joined the program before October 30, 2026, and have a minimum balance of 50 Avios in their account (though those Avios can be transferred from another “flavor” of the currency).

When Finnair Plus offers a promotion on purchased Avios, it’s common to see either a 50% bonus or a 40-50% discount. The 50% discount gives you the absolute best price, so this is definitely the time to buy Avios, if interested.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the program, before this one, with the highest bonus amounts offered.

Finnair Plus Avios purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach minimum spending, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending.

Since the purchase of Finnair Avios can potentially be billed in a foreign currency, there is one other great option. The Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card (learn more) offers 3x points on foreign purchases, so that’s a fantastic card for this kind of purchase.

What should you expect from Finnair Plus award pricing, and the best ways to redeem to Finnair Plus Avios?

Below you can find the one-way Finnair Plus award redemptions rates for travel on Finnair.

Awards also have surcharges, though they’re at least mild. If you have a connecting itinerary, you’ll only be charged the surcharge correlated to the most expensive segment flown.

When your award booking includes a connecting flight, Avios are charged separately for each flight, except for flights within Finland and Northern Europe. For example, a Frankfurt to Helsinki to New York business class award would cost you 82,500 Avios (20,000 Avios plus 62,500 Avios). One awesome thing is that Finnair Plus has an award seat guarantee, meaning there’s pretty consistently award availability when booking far in advance.

Finnair Plus also allows redemptions on partner airlines, though the pricing isn’t particularly attractive, for the most part. The more important thing to keep in mind is that it’s possible to transfer Avios between the various “flavors” of the currency.

Therefore this promotion is also an opportunity to earn Avios that you can transfer 1:1 to programs like Aer Lingus AerClub, British Airways Club, Iberia Club, Qatar Airways Privilege Club, etc. That opens up more redemption opportunities.

Finnair Plus has launched a promotion on purchased Avios. With this, you can receive up to a 50% discount when purchasing Avios, which is an opportunity to buy them for 1.06 cents each (in USD, when paying in JPY). This is the best price of the year from Finnair Plus on purchasing Avios (and the best price for purchasing any current of Avios this year, for that matter).

There’s absolutely value to be had here, especially since this is an opportunity to earn any “flavor” of Avios, thanks to the 1:1 transfer options.

Does anyone plan on taking advantage of this promo on Finnair Plus Avios?

When a program with a transferable currency offers a transfer bonus, it’s important to run the numbers to determine whether it is worthwhile.

Generally, you won’t want to transfer your points or miles unless you have a specific redemption in mind. After all, a large part of the value of transferable points and miles comes from their flexibility, which you’ll give up when you convert them to a partner’s currency. However, a transfer bonus can help you get more value from your points and miles if you frequently use a partner program or plan to redeem them soon.

#6185. Passenger Says Delta Flight Attendant Photographed Her Sleeping—‘You Might See It On Facebook’

Tasia Jewel had just arrived in Mexico City and checked into her hotel when she shared the story. She’d been at the Formula One race in Austin, stayed in Texas rather than going home, and was exhausted. She slept for about an hour and a half or so on the roughly three-hour flight.

Then she got to the aircraft door. She says three or four male flight attendants were standing there saying goodbye to passengers. One told her:

Hey, yo friend, I took a picture of you while you were sleeping.

She says the other crewmembers laughed with one adding, “Yeah, she was knocked out.” And the first flight attendant repeated, “You might see it on Facebook.”

Here’s her account, flagged by Paddle Your Own Kanoo:

The woman acknowledges he could have been joking. She also says she hadn’t spoken to him at all on the flight.

My first reaction was that, while Delta has built up its Austin flying, they don’t actually operated Austin – Mexico City. But in a follow-up video she says she flew from Dallas to Atlanta to Mexico City with the flight in question being Delta 602. She says she chose Delta’s Boeing 757 because she didn’t want the Aeromexico Boeing 737 MAX.

And she reports that Delta responded well to her complaint. Her original video caption said she’d filed a complaint. In later replies, she reports a phone call, an apology and an investigation. I guess what matters here was whether there was a fundamental breach or a bad joke. Either way, she says she felt unsafe.

I’ve written about a sleeping passenger who said a man photographed her, where the crew intervened and police met the flight. Here, the person allegedly taking the photos was an employee she was supposed to go to for help.

And last year I covered a flight attendant who caught a passenger secretly filming her and sending her image to someone else. It’s easy to understand why that bothered her. But a passenger can have the same objection when the roles are reversed.

I don’t want a ban on taking pictures inside an aircraft. Passengers need to be able to document how they’re treated. Delta’s customer photography guidance recognizes that people take photos and videos, while asking them to avoid interfering with safety and to be “respectful in your intent” when including employees. Employees ought to show customers that same consideration.

#6184. Save On Air France-KLM Flights With Amex Offers (Targeted)

The Amex Offers program has just rolled out a great new targeted offer for the purchase of Air France-KLM flights, which could be worth considering for anyone planning travel. We’ve seen this offer in the past, and I’m happy to see it return, as I always get significant value from it. However, this offer isn’t quite as lucrative as past ones.

With a new targeted Amex Offers deal, you can earn a $250 statement credit when you spend $2,500 or more with Air France-KLM by December 15, 2026. (Enrollment required)

It’s possible that there’s also a version of the offer for 25,000 bonus points rather than a $250 statement credit, and if so, I’d consider that to be more valuable. That’s because based on my latest miles & points valuations, Amex points are worth 1.7 cents each, so I’d value the 25,000 points at $425.

For what it’s worth, in the past when I’ve purchased sustainable aviation fuel with Air France in order to earn XP (the metric by which you qualify for status), that triggered an Amex Offers deal. So at least anecdotally, that seems to work. Furthermore, taxes and carrier imposed surcharges on award tickets also seem to qualify.

I’m always happy to see this offer available, though let me note that this isn’t as lucrative as in the past. In past situations we’ve seen a $200 statement credit or 20,000 bonus points after spending $1,000+, so as a percentage return, this definitely isn’t as good.

This Amex Offers deal is targeted, though it’s possible you’ll see it on multiple of your cards. If so, I’d highly recommend registering your American Express Platinum Card® for this offer. That’s because the Amex Platinum offers 5x points on airfare purchased directly with airlines on up to $500,000 per calendar year and then 1x.

Based on my valuation of 1.7 cents per Membership Rewards point, the 5x points offers an incremental 8.5% return on spending. On top of that, the Amex Platinum offers valuable travel protection, should you experience irregular operations.

In other words, if you took advantage of this offer with the Amex Platinum for a $2,500 ticket, you’d receive a $250 statement credit plus 12,500 points. By my valuation, that’s a return of $462.50 on $2,500 of spending, which comes out to an 18.5% return.

There’s a new targeted Amex Offers deal for a $250 statement credit when you spend $2,500+ on an Air France-KLM ticket. If you’re planning travel on Air France or KLM, this has the potential to be a solid deal. Ideally you’ll see this offer on the Amex Platinum, so that you can really maximize your points.

Were you targeted for this Amex Offers deal, and if so, do you plan on taking advantage of it?

#6179. Ouch: Flying Blue Makes Earning XPs Through SAF 50% More Expensive

The Air France-KLM Flying Blue program has just rolled out a quiet devaluation, and it’s one that many savvy Flying Blue members won’t be happy about. The airline group has increased the cost to contribute toward sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), and in turn, has reduced the ability to earn elite status through this method. And we’re not talking about a minor price increase either…

Personally I consider Air France-KLM Flying Blue elite status to be valuable, not just for the SkyTeam Elite Plus perks, but also for the more Air France- KLM specific benefits, like access to more award availability.

Earning Flying Blue elite status is based on the concept of XPs (“experience points”), and how many of those you rack up. One really innovative thing that Flying Blue has done is that it has been possible to earn XPs through environmental contributions:

As I see it, this is a win-win — this program can genuinely help you earn status, while doing something that’s good for the environment, and also contributing to Air France-KLM’s long term environmental goals.

Well, seemingly overnight, Flying Blue has increased the cost to purchase SAF, and in turn, earn XPs. With these changes, you earn one XP for every €15 contributed toward SAF, compared to the previous amount of €10.

A 50% overnight increase is rough. It gets even worse than that, though. There’s no longer any “rounding” with this, so for short haul economy flights you might find that you’re not offered any XPs if the contribution amount is €14, and you’re offered one XP if the amount is €28.

The past year or so has definitely been rough for the overall value of the Flying Blue program, including for elite members:

This is of course all frustrating, though I guess the other side of the equation is that Flying Blue Platinum status has become more valuable over time, but primarily through punitive measures:

How do we make sense of increasing the cost to contribute to SAF, and in turn, earn XPs? I wonder if Flying Blue management thinks that people will still buy SAF at the same rate as before? I know I certainly won’t, though maybe I’m in the minority (I’ll instead increasingly earn XPs through Flying Blue’s co-branded credit card in the US, since that opportunity was recently improved).

For that matter, I’m curious to what extent the number of people buying SAF matters to Air France-KLM? Does this materially contribute to any environmental initiatives, or is it not a priority?

I still get value from my Flying Blue Platinum status, and don’t have plans to change my strategy. Honestly, that partly comes down to how hard it has become to find award availability in business class on long haul flights through other programs.

But I’m definitely slowly becoming less enthused by the program. Then again, I guess that sums up the reality of miles & points more broadly — this isn’t what it once was, and it’s getting harder and harder to make the case for being loyal. It’s no different than World of Hyatt, where they’re clearly trying to cash in. I guess that is the goal of any for-profit business, eh?

Flying Blue has just devalued the rate at which you earn XPs for SAF contributions. You used to earn one XP for every €10 contributed, while you now earn one XP for every €15 contributed. A 50% increase in cost overnight is huge.

I always thought this was a unique aspect of the Flying Blue program, since it’s a win-win for consumers, the airline group, and the environment. Obviously they’ve decided on a different equation now, and for us members, this isn’t good news.

What do you make of this change to Flying Blue when it comes to earning XPs for SAF?

#6177. Airline Passengers Are Getting Scam Emails With Real Confirmation Numbers—Some Frontier Customers Are Entering Credit Card Details

Frontier Airlines passengers are reporting emails from scammers using their real flight details and confirmation numbers, promising refunds or claiming their bookings haven’t been paid for – and telling them to enter their credit card information to complete purchases or confirm return of funds. A reader sent me a refund email that claims a ticketing error caused duplicate taxes and fees and failed to apply a promotional credit. It promises a full refund after the customer confirms the original payment card. The message even supplies an explanation for why an airline that already charged you supposedly needs your card again: Because the settlement batch for this reservation has already closed, our payment system needs the original payment method confirmed so the refund can be routed back to your card. A closed settlement batch ordinarily means the merchant needs to process a refund rather than void the original transaction. In other words, it’s a made up reason meant to sound plausible. These Emails Are Using Real Reservation Details In a Frontier GoWild! Pass Holders discussion, numerous passengers say they received these emails. Several report that the confirmation numbers matched actual bookings. That includes trips already taken and travel still upcoming. One customer says the supposed refund was about five times what they’d paid. Another reports receiving both versions: a refund offer for a completed trip and a warning that payment hadn’t gone through for an upcoming reservation. A separate Reddit discussion reports the payment problem version, with an email that contained real flight information and confirmation number. Passengers report responding with their credit card numbers. One passenger says they tried several other cards before the site accepted the card originally used to book the flight. And of course a rejection message doesn’t mean the site didn’t collect the card number. Frontier Has Disclosed A Database Incident I wrote in July about a breach affecting 11,482 people. Separately, a security researcher reported that a confirmation number and last name could expose sensitive passenger information through Frontier’s systems. There’s also an October 2 notice from Frontier about a security incident involving its customer care database covering information submitted through its customer care form. They changed the database configuration and are ‘improving monitoring’. Security firm VenariX analyzed leaked samples associated with a group claiming Frontier among its victims. They found booking codes, flight numbers and dates, and evidence pointing to overly broad access permissions on Microsoft customer service portals. This Approach Has Been Used Against Hotel And Cruise Customers I’ve covered hotel scams where the sender knows the guest’s reservation details and uses them to demand payment or card verification. Knowing the hotel, dates and guest’s name makes the message much more persuasive. Norwegian Cruise Line customers reported a similar campaign in October, with messages containing real booking information and demanding payment verification. Norwegian issued its own warning. What To Do If You Received One Frontier won’t email asking you to reconfirm a reservation, re-enter card details, or supply payment information to receive a refund. Check the trip through Frontier directly. Open the app or type the airline’s website address yourself. Use contact information obtained there if something looks wrong. If you entered a card, contact its issuer. Lock it while you report the exposure and arrange a replacement. Include every card you tried, even ones the page said it rejected. Don’t assume leaving before clicking Submit protected the information. Web forms can collect what you type before submission. If you supplied a password, change it through the legitimate site. Change it elsewhere if you reused it. Check the reservation. Make sure the itinerary and contact information remain correct. Frontier’s published instructions say a confirmation code and last name can provide access to changes and cancellations, so changing your frequent flyer password may not close that separate route into a booking. Always check the sender information on an email. That can be spoofed but most scammers don’t go to that level of effort. #6176. Belavia Can Once Again Do Business With Boeing, As US Lifts Sanctions On Belarus

Belarusian national carrier Belavia has faced sanctions from the United States and European Union for quite some time, due to a combination of the “hijacking” of a Ryanair flight, along with the country’s support for Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Well, if Belarusian media is to be believed, these sanctions are now being lifted, so the country’s airline can once again buy planes from Boeing…

Belarusian state owned national news agency BelTA is reporting that the United States Department of Commerce has granted Boeing a license to resume full cooperation with Belavia. This was announced by Valentin Rybakov, the Belarusian representative to the United Nations. If true, this means that Belavia can once again purchase planes and parts directly from Boeing.

This all seems to be related to a visit to Belarus by an American delegation in September, where the country’s president, Alexander Lukashenko, met with US Special Envoy John Cole. This meeting included a larger lifting of sanctions. It also comes at a time when we’re seeing the Trump administration increasingly lifting sanctions on Russia in relation to the invasion of Ukraine.

In 2021, the United States imposed sanctions on Belarus, after the country engaged in what was referred to as a state sponsored hijacking. A Ryanair Boeing 737 was flying between Greece and Lithuania, and as the plane approached Belarusian airspace, an air traffic controller claimed there was a bomb onboard, and that the plane needed to divert to Belarus.

As it turned out, an opponent of the Belarusian government was onboard, so the real motive with this was to have him arrested. Obviously this violates all sorts of international laws and aviation treaties, which is why action was taken against the country. Then in 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, additional sanctions were imposed against Belarus, given its support for Russia.

Obviously having sanctions imposed on you by both the United States and European Union makes it challenging to buy new aircraft, given the aircraft manufacturing duopoly we have (unless you consider the aircraft manufacturers in China and Russia to be competitors).

So most of Belavia’s aircraft acquisitions in recent times have been smuggled into the country using shady middlemen. For example, in 2025, Belavia acquired Airbus A330s through an imaginary Gambian airline, as one does.

Belavia can reportedly once again buy aircraft and parts from Boeing, after the United States lifted sanctions that were imposed around five years ago, when the country hijacked a Ryanair plane. This easing of sanctions comes as part of a larger reversal by the Trump administration, as it takes less of a stance against Russia and Belarus.

It’ll be interesting to see what comes of this, and if Belarus places some big Boeing aircraft order in the near future…

What do you make of the US lifting sanctions on Belarus on the airline front?

#6173. Transfer Amex Points To Virgin Atlantic Flying Club With 30% Bonus: Worth It?

The Amex Membership Rewards program has just launched a new 30% transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. While Flying Club is in some ways a niche program, this is a deal that has the potential to offer outsized value, and I’m sure it will interest many people. I’d probably speculatively take advantage of this, except for the fact that I moved a bunch of points last year when there was a 40% transfer bonus.

Between November 2 and November 30, 2026, the American Express Membership Rewards program in the United States is offering a 30% bonus on points transfers to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club.

Ordinarily points transfer at a 1:1 ratio (in 1,000 point increments), while through this promotion you’d get 1,300 Flying Club points for every 1,000 Membership Rewards points transferred. Transfers are generally instant.

For context, Amex seems to offer a transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club once or twice per year. The last promotion we saw was over the summer, and this is the second offer so far in 2026. When we do see these offers, they’re typically in the range of 30-40%, so this is on the low side of that range, but could still represent a great deal.

Virgin Atlantic is definitely a frequent flyer program with more niche redemption opportunities. In addition to being able to redeem Flying Club points for travel on Virgin Atlantic, there’s also good value to be had for redemptions on Air New Zealand, All Nippon Airways, and Delta.

In late 2024 we saw Flying Club introduce dynamic award pricing for travel on Virgin Atlantic. While the changes are a mixed bag, what’s exciting is that on the low end, redemptions are cheaper than ever before. It’s now possible to fly one-way Virgin Atlantic Upper Class between the United States and the UK for under 30,000 points, and that’s before a transfer bonus.

Beyond that, Virgin Atlantic has several airline partners, some of which are more lucrative than others. Probably the best use of Flying Club points is for travel in ANA first & business class. You can find the redemption rates below.

Paying 45,000-47,500 Flying Club points for a one-way business class ticket between the United States and Japan is a phenomenal value to start with. Then when you consider the 30% transfer bonus, that means you could be paying significantly fewer Amex points. First class can also be a good deal.

All Nippon Airways’ new first & business class are amazing products as well. The major catch is that availability can be really tough to come by.

Through November 30, 2026, Amex is offering a 30% bonus when you transfer points to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. This is definitely more of a niche program, but with a specific use in mind, there’s a lot of value to be had.

With the 30% bonus, award travel on Virgin Atlantic will be an even better value. There’s also lots of value to booking on partners, ranging from SkyTeam airlines, to Air New Zealand, to All Nippon Airways.

Do you plan on taking advantage of this Amex transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club?

#6170. Are Authorized Users Eligible For Credit Card Bonuses?

Here’s a topic that seems to cause confusion among some people. If you’re an authorized user on someone else’s credit card, are you eligible for the bonus on that card if you apply outright? The answer is actually pretty straightforward, so let me explain…

Credit cards frequently offer huge upfront welcome offers, whereby you can earn a lot of bonus points for spending a certain amount within a limited timeframe. While there are different credit card application rules for each bank, there are generally restrictions whereby an existing cardmember can’t apply for a card they already have, while also receiving the bonus.

How does that work in the context of authorized users? If you’re the authorized user on someone else’s credit card, can you apply for the card as the primary cardmember and earn the bonus? The answer is universally yes — being an authorized user on someone else’s credit card doesn’t preclude you from applying for that card yourself, and earning the bonus.

When welcome bonus rules talk about existing cardmembers, they’re specifically talking about primary cardmembers, and not authorized users.

You don’t even need to cancel your authorized user card to be able to do this. For example, say you’re an authorized user on your spouse’s Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more), or Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more), or Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card (learn more). You could remain an authorized user, and still apply outright and earn the welcome bonus on the card.

For those in relationships, it can sometimes be difficult to decide under which circumstances it makes sense to apply for a card outright, rather than being an authorized user on a spouse’s card (and vice versa). There are pros and cons to each.

The advantage of adding someone as an authorized user is that it minimizes annual fees, since many cards have lower (or no) annual fees for authorized users, compared to the primary cardmembers. Meanwhile the advantages of having both people in a relationship apply for a card outright is that many cards have big welcome bonuses, and on top of that some cards pay for themselves on an ongoing basis.

For more on this topic, see my post on the best credit card strategy for families.

Many credit cards have amazing welcome bonuses, though you’re generally only eligible for them if you don’t already have that card. The good news is that across the board, being an authorized user on someone else’s card still makes you eligible to apply for that card outright and receive the bonus (assuming you’re otherwise eligible for the card).

Therefore this really comes down to deciding for each card whether the economics of applying outright make sense.

Have you ever applied for a credit card on which you’re already an authorized user?

If they get their own Platinum, we will cancel the AU card (because we don't want to pay an extra AF for that card). Is it possible for them to get all three? How would you go about this?

Delta Air Lines is adding another route from its fastest-growing “focus city.”

Over the weekend, the Atlanta-based carrier filed plans to launch nonstop service from Austin Bergstrom International Airport (AUS) to Northwest Arkansas National Airport (XNA) outside Bentonville.

Flights will begin in March 2027, with Delta offering service on board a Delta Connection regional jet.

The service will give the Texas capital a nonstop link to northwest Arkansas — not to mention parts of Oklahoma, Missouri and Kansas, which are all a relatively short drive from XNA.

SkyMiles news: Delta announces Medallion qualification requirements for 2027

The airport is also the closest option for travelers heading to the University of Arkansas.

For Delta, it’s the latest in a series of expansions in Austin.

The carrier has grown its flight offerings at AUS at a fast pace over the last couple of years, targeting the airport as one of its top non-hub “focus cities.”

That growth included the airline’s first nonstop service from Austin to Europe, which Delta revealed in August. Those flights to Paris will begin in April.

That’s on top of new routes to major tech hubs like San Jose in California's Silicon Valley and popular leisure destinations like Bozeman, Montana, and Cancun in Mexico.

All told, the airline plans to operate up to 70 daily departures by March, Delta chief commercial officer Joe Esposito told me this summer.

In 2019, it had 28 peak daily departures from AUS.

“The boom is incredible,” Esposito told me in August, noting that a growing number of Delta flyers will also start seeing itineraries with connections in the Lone Star State. That said, Delta has stopped short of saying it will ever make Austin a hub.

“We want to be the business carrier of Austin — we’re quickly moving in on the leading corporate carrier for Austin,” he said. “Then you wind up connecting people.”

It's likely no coincidence, then, that Delta would be interested in service to Bentonville: the region is home to Walmart's corporate headquarters.

As for this latest route, Delta’s service from AUS to Northwest Arkansas will launch on March 7.

It’ll be a late-night departure, with flights taking off just before 9 p.m. The return flight from XNA to AUS will launch the next morning, on March 8.

The service will be on board an Embraer 175 regional jet operated by regional partner SkyWest.

“This new direct route is another example of Delta’s continued investment in Austin and our commitment to making it easier for Austinites to get where they want to go as we continue growing alongside this important community,” Luis Guitart, Delta’s Austin-based regional sales manager, said in a statement to TPG Monday.

While Delta has grown its flight offerings in Austin rapidly over the past couple of years, Southwest Airlines remains the market leader at the airport.

Southwest, like Delta, plans to offer its biggest schedule ever from AUS in 2027.

The airport will also be home to one of its inaugural airport lounges.

Delta, for its part, is planning a second — larger — Sky Club at AUS for the coming years.

By the way, Delta's new route to Northwest Arkansas will add to a strong run of air service growth for that region, too.

This year, the airport will see 28% more total flights than it did just two years ago, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

Beyond its future route to Austin, Delta serves Bentonville from five other airports — all hubs: Atlanta, Detroit, Minneapolis, Salt Lake City and New York's LaGuardia Airport (LGA).

#6166. Capital One Adds New Airline Partner With 30% Bonus—Book Emirates Business Class Without Fuel Surcharges

All of a sudden Panamanian airline Copa is taking U.S. points transfer programs by storm. Did not have that on my 2026 bingo card! Capital One has added Copa Airlines ConnectMiles as a transfer partner, opening another way to book Emirates business class without fuel surcharges. They’re offering a 30% transfer bonus to launch the partnership, too. But even with that bonus, you’ll get fewer Copa miles than Citi and Rove offer at their regular rates. Beginning November 2, Capital One miles transfer to Copa at 2:1.5. That’s 750 ConnectMiles for every 1,000 Capital One miles. The 30% bonus runs through December 1, 2026, bringing the effective rate to 975 ConnectMiles per 1,000 miles transferred. I like seeing Capital One expand its partner list again. They haven’t done so in a year! I just wish they weren’t quite so tight with the transfer ratio. Citi Added Copa Last Week, Following Rove I covered Rove adding Copa on September 1. Their regular transfer rate is 1:1, and they launched with a 40% bonus through September 30. That meant 1,000 Rove miles became 1,400 Copa miles. Then Citi added ConnectMiles on October 25: Citi Strata Elite, Strata Premier, Prestige and AT&T Access More cardholders receive 1,000 Copa miles per 1,000 ThankYou points. Other eligible ThankYou cards, including the no annual fee Citi Strata, Double Cash and Custom Cash cards, transfer 1,000 points to 700 Copa miles. Here’s how the three programs compare today: Transfer From Copa Miles Per 1,000 Points Rove 1,000 Citi, with an eligible premium card 1,000 Citi, other eligible cards 700 Capital One, regular rate 750 Capital One, with 30% bonus through December 1 975 Capital One’s bonus nearly gets you to 1:1. Transfer 10,000 Capital One miles and receive 9,750 Copa miles during the promotion. Marriott Bonvoy also transfers to Copa at 3:1, with the usual 5,000-mile bonus for transferring 60,000 points. That’s 25,000 Copa miles for 60,000 Marriott points. When Rove added Copa, I liked having access to a program that the big U.S. bank currencies didn’t offer. Two months later, Citi and Capital One have followed. Rove’s 40% launch bonus is over, but their ordinary rate still beats Capital One’s promotional rate. The Value In Copa Miles Transfers Copa is a Star Alliance airline based in Panama. Its miles can book United Airlines and other alliance partners, but the redemption I flagged in September was Emirates. Emirates business class from the U.S. to Dubai for 80,000 miles one way, without carrier-imposed surcharges. Taxes and other applicable fees apply. United Airlines premium transcontinental business class for 25,000 miles one way when saver award space is available to Copa. Copa economy awards starting at 15,000 miles one way from its North America 1 region to Panama, Central America, parts of the Caribbean and northern South America. Capital One Now Has 23 Transfer Partners Capital One’s last additions were Japan Airlines Mileage Bank, Qatar Airways Privilege Club and I Prefer Hotel Rewards on September 23, 2025. It’s been more than a year, so it’s good to see them adding another option. Here’s the complete current list. These are the standard transfer ratios, before temporary bonuses, expressed as Capital One miles to partner miles or points. Transfer Partner Standard Ratio Aeromexico Rewards 1:1 Air Canada Aeroplan 1:1 Air France-KLM Flying Blue 1:1 Avianca LifeMiles 1:1 British Airways Club 1:1 Cathay Pacific Asia Miles 1:1 Copa Airlines ConnectMiles 2:1.5 Emirates Skywards 2:1.5 Etihad Guest 1:1 EVA Air Infinity MileageLands 2:1.5 Finnair Plus 1:1 Japan Airlines Mileage Bank 2:1.5 JetBlue TrueBlue 5:3 Qantas Frequent Flyer 1:1 Qatar Airways Privilege Club 1:1 Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer 1:1 TAP Air Portugal Miles&Go 1:1 Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles 1:1 Virgin Red 1:1 Accor Live Limitless 2:1 Choice Privileges 1:1 I Prefer Hotel Rewards 1:2 Wyndham Rewards 1:1 Capital One manages the economics of its rewards program tightly. They give you 750 Japan Airlines miles per 1,000 Capital One miles, and half as many I Prefer points as Citi offers with its premium cards. Copa is another useful partner, but with a less generous conversion rate. At the regular Copa ratio, earning 2 Capital One miles per dollar on Venture X spending means earning 1.5 Copa miles per dollar. Citi Double Cash earns 2 ThankYou points per dollar on purchases as you buy and pay, and pairing it with an eligible premium ThankYou card gets you 2 Copa miles per dollar. #6165. Buy Choice Privileges Points With 40% Bonus (0.74 Cents Each): Worth It?

Choice Privileges is currently offering a promotion on purchased points, offering up to a 40% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for as little as 0.74 cents each. While this isn’t among the best promotions we’ve seen from the program, it’s still better than no bonus, and there are many situations where you could come out ahead.

Let’s take a look at everything you need to know about this deal, and talk about under what circumstances it makes sense to buy Choice Privileges points. I generally recommend buying points only if you have a short term use in mind, and are sure the math checks out.

Link: Buy Choice Privileges points with a bonus

Between 12AM EDT on November 2 and 11:59PM EDT on November 26, 2026, Choice Privileges is offering a sale on purchased points. The accounts I manage show a bonus of up to 40%, which is structured as follows:

Different accounts may very well show different offers, so you’ll want to log into your Choice Privileges account to see what you’re eligible for.

Choice Privileges’ pricing when buying points isn’t linear, and you get a lower cost the more points you purchase, not even factoring in any promotional bonuses or discounts. Before factoring in any bonuses or discounts, the cost to purchase points ranges from 1.28 cents per point (if buying just 1,000 points) to 1.03 cents per point (if buying 180,000 points), and that’s inclusive of taxes and fees.

If you maxed out this promotion, you could purchase a total of 252,000 points (180,000 base points, plus 72,000 bonus points) for $1,854, which is a rate of 0.74 cents per Choice Privileges point.

Note that purchased points will post within 24 hours of completing the transaction, and the points earned don’t count toward Choice Privileges elite status.

Choice Privileges lets you purchase up to 180,000 points per account per calendar year, not factoring in any bonus points.

When Choice offers a promotion on purchased points, it’s typically either a 30-45% discount or a 35-50% bonus. So this 40% bonus is toward the bottom end of that range. Personally, I’d decide on whether to make a purchase more based on if I had an immediate use in mind, rather than the exact cost per point.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from Choice Privileges on buying points, before this one, with the highest bonus amounts offered.

Choice Privileges points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t generally count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. There is one exception — if you use a co-branded Choice Privileges credit card, then these purchases are rewarded in the same way as hotel spending.

Otherwise, I’d recommend using a card with which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. When in doubt, review which credit cards are best for buying points and miles.

While it doesn’t get much attention in the miles & points world, Choice is a huge hotel group, with over 7,000 properties in 40 countries, representing roughly 570,000 hotel rooms. Choice hotel brands include (among others) Ascend, Cambria, Comfort Inn, Sleep Inn, Quality Inn, Clarion, Rodeway Inn, and more.

The catch is that Choice doesn’t have that many aspirational properties. In general there’s the most value outright purchasing points if you have a premium redemption in mind, given that this is the best way to get outsized value compared to the cost of a stay if paying cash.

Choice Privileges doesn’t have a formal award chart, but award pricing usually ranges from 6,000 to 45,000 points per night. In Asia-Pacific, some properties cost up to 75,000 points per night.

There are definitely some properties where you’ll get outsized value acquiring Choice Privileges points at a discount. For example, Choice has an impressive footprint in Northern Europe, where hotels can otherwise be expensive when paying cash, especially in summer.

Let me just give some examples, and let’s just keep the math easy, to show redemptions where you’re getting well over one cent of value per point (which is way higher than the acquisition cost here). Generally the key is to travel during peak periods, since that’s when you’ll get the most outsized value from your points.

For example, if you wanted to travel to Tromso, Norway, in December (to see the Northern Lights), I see two properties charging $560-620 per night, when you could book them for 40,000-45,000 points per night, getting you very nicely outsized value.

If you wanted to travel to Stockholm, Sweden, in July (summer is popular!), I see two properties charging $420-580 per night, when you could book them for 25,000-30,000 points per night, getting you excellent value.

For an example closer to home, say you wanted to go to Dunedin, Florida, in March. I see a property charging $730 per night, when you could book it for 40,000 points per night, also getting you hugely outsized value.

Let me be clear — you won’t always find outsized value in this way. For example, say you need to spend a night near LAX, where you’ll see properties charging $102-149 per night, when a points redemption requires 20,000-30,000 points per night. Paying cash is the much better value there.

The key is to travel places during peak periods, where the cash rate would be significantly higher than usual, while the points rate isn’t as elevated.

Here’s a fun redemption option with Choice Privileges points. While Choice doesn’t manage these properties, Choice Privileges has a partnership with Preferred Hotels & Resorts, which is a group of over 500 luxury independent properties around the globe.

You can redeem Choice Privileges points for stays here, and the hotels cost anywhere from 25,000 to 118,000 points per night. You can find participating hotels and award costs here, and nowadays you can even book these awards online. There are some participating hotels where you can get significant value redeeming this way, though the recent devaluation sure doesn’t help.

Choice Privileges doesn’t have blackout dates, and points can be redeemed for stays up to 50 weeks in advance, as long as a standard room is available.

Choice Privileges points don’t expire as long as you have at least some account activity once every 18 months. Virtually any activity that involves earning or redeeming points would be considered qualifying for these purposes.

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Choice Privileges points to be worth ~0.6 cents each. That’s a conservative valuation, though if you’re strategic you should be able to get lots more value out of your points than that.

Several transferable points currencies have Choice Privileges as a partner:

As you can see, of those transfer partners, Wells Fargo is going to be the most lucrative, followed by Citi, followed by Amex and Capital One.

Through November 26, 2026, Choice Privileges is selling points with up to a 40% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for as little as 0.74 cents each. While I wouldn’t recommend speculatively picking up Choice Privileges points at that cost, with a specific and short term use in mind, there could be value with this offer.

Does anyone plan on buying Choice Privileges points?

#6163. American Airlines Philadelphia Flagship Lounge Expected To Double In Size, Taking Over The Admirals Club Next Door

American Airlines’ gorgeous Philadelphia Flagship Lounge may finally get the space it should have had from the start. Lounge staff are reportedly telling passengers it’ll take over the Admirals Club next door around March 2027, essentially doubling the size of the business class lounge before next summer’s transatlantic seasonal peak. That’s the change I called for when the lounge opened. But there’s a potential problem for Admirals Club members since there’s no announced replacement for the club they’d lose. A passenger reports being told by the employee managing Flagship lounge entry that it would expand into the adjoining A West Admirals Club “sometime around next March.” Another commenter says an agent separately told them about expanding to the whole floor (which is the same thing), after they gave up on finding a seat in Flagship and went next door. Officially, an American Airlines spokesperson tells me: Nothing set in stone right now, but we are always evaluating how we can best serve our customers during the summer peak next year. In my original review, I showed the connector behind the check-in desk. There’s already ‘swing space’ that can be opened to either lounge. During my visit it was part of Flagship. These are adjoining spaces with the same beautiful design, and they’re already connected. The dimensions of the spaces are: Flagship: 12,500 square feet, with 200 seats. Admirals Club: 11,000 square feet, with 181 seats. Additional flex space: 1,364 square feet. That’s nearly 25,000 square feet across the complex. Moving the Admirals Club space into Flagship would roughly double its footprint. I quite like this lounge. In the morning and early afternoon, it’s a lovely place to spend time. The trouble comes before the bank of transatlantic departures, when the passengers it’s supposed to serve all arrive at once. A business class lounge needs enough seats for people flying business class. And in the summer from Philadelphia that total grows quite a lot with American’s seasonal services. Things are even worse now that the A West terminal has lost the American Express Centurion Lounge for expansion into the British Airways lounge space, expecting to reopen by the end of 2027. I’ve covered the project taking over the British Airways lounge space below. The British Airways lounge is closed, too. I actually think Flagship was already better than both lounges. It’s just crowded (but not as cramped as Centurion was!). American has been investing more in lounge food. At Dallas recently, I found a better buffet, staffed charcuterie and food ordered by QR code that arrived at my table in four minutes. Philadelphia helped introduce that ordering system, coming after the Soho lounge at JFK which is shared with BA. Philadelphia wasn’t built with a separate Flagship Dining room. Those are operating in Dallas and Miami, and I broke the news that Los Angeles reopens this week. Chief Customer Officer Heather Garboden has talked about rethinking Flagship. Delta was the last of the big three to introduce a separate business class lounge, and I think Delta One lounges now offer the strongest overall product. American’s access rules are much more generous, including eligible elites flying coach on qualifying international trips and oneworld Sapphire and Emerald members from programs other than American and Alaska even on domestic itineraries. That makes having enough space especially important. American had an Admirals Club in A East. They closed it when these lounges opened in May 2025. I argued then that they should keep A East for Admirals Club members and dedicate A West entirely to Flagship. Under the reported plan, the nearest Admirals Club would instead be B/C. Someone paying for a membership, or carrying the Citi Executive card, would lose access to the beautiful A West club without gaining access to the larger Flagship Lounge. American should take back the A East space as well. Terrible idea. I just got the AA Executive card to use that lounge. I gave up the CSR. TheAA lounge between B and C is hospital ambiance circa 1965. It’s the old US Air lounge that hasn’t had 10 cents put into it since the merger.

Why can’t they keep the A AC open until say 3pm when the he FL rush hour begins?

#6162. Rosewood Beyond Sale: 30% Off Stays, Plus Rosewood Elite Perks

Luxury hotel group Rosewood has just kicked off its best sale of the year, offering savings of up to 30%, and it’s exclusively available through Rosewood Elite travel advisors. If you’ve been considering a stay at a Rosewood, this would be a great time to book.

With the Rosewood Beyond promotion, guests can save 30% off the best available rate when booking a Rosewood property through a Rosewood Elite travel advisor. To cover the basics:

In order to take advantage of the Rosewood Beyond sale, you need to book through a Rosewood Elite travel advisor. Ford’s team is happy to help with this, and can be reached at [email protected]. Other travel advisors are welcome to leave their contact details in the comments as well.

Let me emphasize that the 30% discount is off the best available rate, otherwise known as the flexible rate. So you couldn’t get this discount on an advance purchase rate, third or fourth night free rate, etc. So in some situations the savings here won’t be that significant, while in other cases they are huge.

While there are of course some restrictions and blackout dates, this is about as no strings attached as promotions get. The 30% off rate also offers the same flexibility as whatever the flexible rate would be, which of course varies by property.

Since the Rosewood Beyond sale is specifically being offered through Rosewood Elite travel advisors, the good news is that these reservations also unlock additional benefits, including the following:

Rosewood is a really high quality hotel brand, and you can find all the hotels here. If you’re looking for a getaway from the United States, it’s tough to beat the Rosewood Mayakoba, the Rosewood Little Dix Bay, the Rosewood Kona Village, Las Ventanas al Paraiso, etc. Rosewood also has lots of great city hotels, ranging from the Rosewood Hong Kong, to the Rosewood Sao Paulo, to The Carlyle New York.

Rosewood has brought back its biggest promotion of the year, offering 30% off the best available rate. This is valid for bookings confirmed November 3-10, 2026, and for stays through June 30, 2027.

Aside from a small list of excluded properties, this is a pretty straightforward offer that gives you the best deal you’ll find on Rosewood stays. You can even stack this with Rosewood Elite perks, to unlock breakfast, a property credit, a room upgrade, and more.

Just keep in mind that the discount is based on the flexible rate, and not based on any promotional rate you can find.
