#6119. Skift Aviation Forum 2026: Five Decisions in the Room

Jet fuel prices are still rising, and just about every variable affecting air travel is in flux — aircraft supply, air traffic volume, global partnerships, input costs. Decisions made today will determine who succeeds in aviation.

Passenger demand and airline revenues seem to be holding at a macro level. For now. Jet fuel prices continue to rise, aircraft remain scarce, and labor and airport costs keep rising. Meanwhile, global air traffic has been unpredictable throughout 2026, with wide regional differences.

Airlines at all levels of the market are shifting toward premium offerings to offset these headwinds and keep their revenues afloat. They’re redesigning cabins, loyalty programs, networks, ancillaries, and customer experiences. Skift Research describes the premium push as a normalizing trend: it’s now a baseline offering underpinning revenue expectations, rather than a stopgap strategy. [1]

The decisions industry leaders have to make today center on how to yield a competitive advantage within this industry-wide shift. The decisions underpinning every conversation at the 2026 Skift Aviation Forum will provide foundational evidence for these answers.

Fuel has become the industry’s biggest near-term margin test. Airlines entered the year with strong passenger revenue and high load factors, but the economics changed quickly as jet fuel prices climbed.

The impact is not uniform. Some airlines have more pricing power, stronger premium demand, better hedging positions, or networks that can absorb a shock more easily. Others compete in markets where travelers are more price-sensitive or where adding a fuel surcharge risks pushing demand to a rival.

The decision is how much of the fuel increase airlines can absorb before fares have to rise.

IATA expected the airline industry’s net profit to halve in 2026, a forecast made months before jet fuel prices peaked above $200 a barrel in October. [2] [3]

Airlines have spent the past several years reallocating space toward travelers who generate more revenue per seat. It’s not just major international carriers, either. Low-cost airlines have nearly doubled premium capacity since 2019.

Demand has kept up so far. More than 70% of travelers surveyed by Skift Research said they would consider paying for a premium cabin. [1]

The decision is how much further to push. Premium now affects cabin configuration, route planning, revenue management, airport strategy, and loyalty. Airlines need to know where demand still supports expansion and where the market is beginning to crowd.

U.S. domestic premium-seat capacity has grown 33% since 2020, roughly twice the 16% growth in economy seats. Premium revenues are significantly outpacing overall revenue growth and driving disproportionate value within airline revenue streams. [1]

The global traffic story has fractured by region. Middle East passenger traffic is expected to contract by 11.4% in 2026 amid airspace closures and reduced transfer demand, while Africa and Asia-Pacific will benefit from the shift. [4] Global load factors are reaching record levels because capacity remains constrained even as demand slows.

The decision is how to create the strongest return if capacity becomes more scarce. Slower global growth raises the cost of getting that call wrong.

Global air traffic growth is expected to slow to 2.1% in 2026 from 5.3% in 2025, while capacity increase is expected to be even lower at 1.6%. [4]

For many travelers, the ease of knowing they’ll get some miles and a few perks outweighs the headache of price comparison. AI changes this calculation, even for those who consider themselves somewhat loyal. Shopping tools can compare fares and products across airlines immediately. A traveler carrying points or status can still be presented with a better-priced or better-matched option somewhere else.

The decision for airlines is what loyalty has to deliver beyond points. Service, recognition, card economics, access, flexibility, and personalization can all strengthen the relationship. To avoid commoditization, airlines need to prove to travelers at every level of their programs that they can offer differentiated value.

The shift to premium is buoying revenue numbers, but AI platforms may not-so-quietly siphon off loyalty value from otherwise brand-agnostic travelers.

The industry has to make long-term commitments while near-term conditions remain volatile. Those investments have to make some assumptions about how the industry will operate years from now.

The decision is which bets deserve capital allocation. Growth alone is no longer enough justification. Airlines, airports, and manufacturers need a clear view of what each investment changes — capacity, economics, reliability, service, or competitive position.

Global airline passenger revenue is expected to approach $883 billion in 2027, but annual growth is projected to slow to about 3%. [5]

The airline industry’s next set of decisions centers on where to commit.

Airlines need to decide how much further to push premium, where capacity belongs, which rising costs customers can absorb, what keeps loyalty valuable, and which long-term investments deserve capital now.

Each decision comes back to the same constraint: airlines cannot pursue every opportunity at once. Skift Aviation Forum is focused on helping industry leaders identify where the economics still justify the strategy.

#6113. Voting rights groups, afraid of criminal penalties, cut back on help for Texas’ most vulnerable

This article was originally published by Votebeat, a nonprofit news organization covering local election administration and voting access.

Votebeat is a nonprofit news organization reporting on voting access and election administration across the U.S. Sign up for Votebeat Texasâ free newsletter here.

This story was produced with support from the Pulitzer Center.

ALAMO, Tex. â Eustorgia Santos de Torres has lived here for four decades. Last year, she turned to a trusted Rio Grande Valley nonprofit for help navigating the citizenship application process. The same nonprofit â La UniÃ³n del Pueblo Entero, or LUPE â then helped her register to vote, and she cast her first ballot as a citizen in the primary election last March.

Santos de Torres, 67, is retired after years cleaning houses and working as a healthcare aide. She speaks mainly Spanish and is the primary caretaker for her husband, Nemorio, who is blind. âYo soy sus ojos,â Santos de Torres said â I am his eyes.

But last month, Santos de Torres, a new voter, struggled to help Nemorio, an American-born citizen, understand and cast his mail ballot for the November election. All the information on the ballot is in English, she said, and the letters are small.

So Santos de Torres helped Nemorio to the car and made the familiar 7-minute drive to LUPEâs headquarters in the neighboring town of San Juan to ask for help with her husbandâs ballot.

This time, though, LUPE workers reluctantly turned the couple away.

In 2021, Texasâ GOP-dominated state Legislature passed a sweeping and controversial overhaul of election laws known as SB1. Among other changes, SB1 made it illegal for anyone to receive compensation for helping voters fill in their ballots.

That not only makes it illegal for paid nonprofit staff to help voters, but also criminalized common past practices, such as organizations giving volunteers gas money or stipends. Violations are a felony punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a fine of up to $10,000.

In the wake of the law, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican currently running in the stateâs nationally watched U.S. Senate race, investigated and prosecuted voting rights advocacy groups and organizers in heavily Latino communities across the state.

Groups such as LUPE say they have been forced to alter or stop some voter outreach as they worry about running afoul of the law. LUPE used to send workers out walking blocks to help voters. Now it has to instead ask volunteers to do more limited versions of that work.

Latinos and other non-English speaking voters will be key to the outcome of the stateâs high-profile U.S. Senate and House races this year. But the law means such voters, as well as those who are disabled and elderly, have fewer options for help.

LUPE is known for providing one-on-one assistance to people in the Latino community, so the restrictions on helping with voting are a real pain point for the organization, Executive Director Tania Chavez Camacho said. Texas has strict rules limiting who is eligible to use mail ballots, but people over 65 may do so. LUPE helps around 30,000 people a year, she said, including people with disabilities and many older people who, each year, âwant to vote by mail and they come in wanting help.â

Start your day with essential news from Salon. Sign up for our free morning newsletter, Crash Course.

Now, Chavez Camacho said, when the group holds public town halls for residents to instruct them on how to vote, if a voter pulls out their mail ballot to ask for help, organizers must ask the voter to leave so paid employees arenât near the ballot.

And if workers for LUPEâs advocacy arm are canvassing for candidates and a voter shows them a mail ballot and asks for help filling it out, workers have been trained to say they canât and walk away, Chavez Camacho said.

âWe literally have to turn them away,â Chavez Camacho said. âWeâve had to do a lot of training with our staff for the past three years because they were so accustomed to helping folks one-on-one and now they canât.â

Santos de Torres did what she could to help her husband, who mailed back his ballot about a month ago.

âBut I donât think itâs right that LUPE canât help us,â she told a reporter in Spanish. âThat law is not right. Itâs excluding people who need help.â

âWhat if,â she added, âmy husband didnât have me?â

The Rio Grande Valley, where LUPE is based, covers roughly 4,300-square-miles across Hidalgo, Cameron, Starr, and Willacy counties along the Mexico border at Texasâ southern tip. Itâs a diverse community with some residents who primarily speak Spanish. Younger generations of residents easily switch between English and Spanish in conversation.

Many households are made up of families whose members have mixed legal statuses, including some who have lived in the area for generations. The Valley also has a history of activism as the birthplace of the Texas farmworker movement of the 1960âs. Farmworkers â who harvested cotton, vegetables and fruits â organized and marched for roughly 400 miles from the Valley to Austin to demand fair wages and better working conditions. Mexican-American farmworker labor today remains key to the areaâs growth and agricultural economy.

But due to the lack of affordable housing, Mexican Americans for years purchased land they could afford in rural areas outside of city limits, often lacking basic infrastructure and public services. Those communities are known now as the colonias.

Alamo, where Santos de Torres lives, and San Juan, where LUPE is based, are neighboring cities. The landscape varies depending on the side of town. In the southern parts of the cities, closer to the border with Mexico, modest residential homes with green front lawns adorn along palm tree-lined streets. Shopping centers, chain restaurants, stadiums, and commercial developments lie to the north of the cities, along Interstate Highway 2, reflecting the transition from the once primarily agricultural community to a growing metropolitan hub. The Valley has for years relied on its trade of goods and services with Mexico. It has a population of more than 1.4 million people and 90% of them are Hispanic or Latino, according to Census data.

About 24% of people in the Valley live below the poverty line, which is more than double the national rate. And about 30% of Valley residents donât have health insurance â one of the highest uninsured rates in the country. The area also has one of the highest rates of diabetes in the country; Nemorio Torresâ blindness is a complication of the disease.

LUPE and other advocacy groups have long worked with residents in the colonias and all over the Valley, providing resources to find affordable housing and medical treatment, or helping with complex procedures such as filing taxes. Voter education and outreach was part of the mission.

Now, instead of providing one-on-one assistance, LUPE hosts group sessions with a screen projector showing what mail ballot applications and mail ballots look like. Facilitators point at the screen indicating what the instructions say and explaining how the forms should be filled out.

The limitations are frustrating, Chavez Camacho said, especially âsi una persona no sabe leerâ â if a person canât read. âIt doesnât matter that weâre doing those sessions because a person who doesnât know how to read has to do it on their own and we canât help them to know where to mark,â she said.

Instead, LUPEâs workers and volunteers now focus on letting people know key deadlines are coming up. They also have fewer volunteers willing to guide and interpret for voters at the polls, she said, because the law now requires such people to sign an oath affirming the voter is qualified to receive help because they are disabled or need an interpreter, and detail their relationship with the voter. They must also affirm they are not being paid by a candidate or political committee, which would be illegal. Volunteers fear any misstep while assisting voters could get them in trouble, Chavez-Camacho said.

âWe really feel that the people are not getting the support they need,â Chavez Camacho said.

Election and voting law experts say the courts have interpreted âcompensationâ prohibited from going to volunteers by SB1 as any type of benefit. That interpretation is so broad that it makes it difficult for voter outreach organizations to know whether they are violating the law, said Zachary Dolling, litigation director at Texas Civil Rights Project, which works with groups to design trainings in voter outreach that comply with the law.

Dolling said some organizations historically provided unpaid volunteers dinner, T-shirts, or pens, and others have given volunteers college credit for their work.

âAll of those things are items of valueâ and could be considered compensation, he said.

Texas Republicans passed SB1, the sweeping overhaul of election law, in part responding to false claims and conspiracy theories about the 2020 election.

Republicans claimed the law would increase public trust and confidence in the elections. Democrats argued the legislation would disproportionately burden voters of color and people with disabilities, and staged two walkouts and a 15-hour Senate filibuster in their failed attempt to defeat the bill.

Despite lawsuits from voting rights organizations including LUPE, the League of United Latin American Citizens and organizations representing Texans with disabilities, a federal appeals court ultimately upheld key provisions of SB1, including the restrictions on voter assistance.

Other attempts to expand voting help for people with disabilities were meanwhile unsuccessful.

In 2023, Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, vetoed a bipartisan bill that would have expanded vote-by-mail access for people with disabilities â specifically people who are blind or paralyzed and need assistance marking their ballot â by allowing such voters to request an electronic ballot and use a computer to mark their choices. Similar options in Texas are already available for military overseas voters and astronauts, but not for voters with disabilities.

The challenges Santos de Torres and her husband have faced are an example of what advocates worried about under SB1, said Lydia Nunez Landry, statewide coordinator for REV UP Texas, which works to get out the vote among people with disabilities.

âThat was our worst fear and now itâs happening,â she said. Nunez Landry has muscular dystrophy, uses a power wheelchair, and needs help doing basic tasks such as opening the refrigerator.

The state has made voting âjust so impossible and so arduous for people â and now people are also terrified of helping us,â she said.

Groups across the state have been changing their voter outreach work to comply with SB1.

Asian Texans for Justice conducts voter outreach in Asian communities, focusing on San Antonio, Houston, Austin, and North Texas.

The stricter rules associated with voting by mail under SB1 have created âa sense of anxietyâ in those communities, Executive Director Nabila Mansoor said. She said that the process is now much more complicated for elderly voters, who must provide one of two forms of ID on their application and pay close attention to pages of instructions that are written in font that is small and hard for them to read. In addition, an error could force them to restart the whole process of applying for a ballot.

âThat anxiety comes from this kind of fear that theyâre going to do something wrong,â Mansoor said. âWhenever you have that kind of fear, it is one more barrier for that person to actually go out and vote.â

Now that Asian Texans for Justice can no longer provide one-on-one help, theyâve turned to providing checklists for voters, she said, which she believes is less effective when some voters may need help reading and understanding the ballot and instructions

Mansoor said she believes that SB1âs goal was to make it harder for people to vote.

âIt means that we have to be more careful. It means that we have to dot our iâs and cross our tâs. It means that we have to take good records. It means that we have to be very thorough in terms of our training of our volunteers,â she said, adding that the organization assembled a legal team to defend against challenges to their work as well.

In the meantime, volunteers for LUPE and other groups say they are doing their best to fill the gap.

Maria Gomez, better known as DoÃ±a Mary, of Pharr, worked as a farmworker for years in Hidalgo County and has been a member of LUPE since the organization was founded. Gomez, 78, was involved in the farmworker movement years ago. She now ensures her elderly friends and neighbors are aware of election deadlines, know where to vote, and have a ride to the polls if they need one.

After she drops off her grandkids and great-grandkids at school, she makes her rounds around the Colonias in San Juan in her small red SUV. She chats up her neighbors, and asks them what they need help with or if they need resources or a ride. Sheâs always fielding calls.

âPeople donât vote because sometimes they canât leave their home and because they might not have access to that piece of paper that they need to sign to receive their ballot,â Gomez said in Spanish, referring to voter registration forms and ballot-by-mail applications.

One of her friends, 80-year-old Teresa Corona Garza of San Juan, has relied on Gomez for rides to the polls for some time now. Corona Garza struggles to stand for long periods of time and canât see very well out of her left eye. Even though she qualifies to vote by mail, she prefers to go to the polls in person.

âThereâs so much on there you have to fill out, and those letters are small,â Corona Garza said in Spanish. âNo, I prefer to go, quiero ver que mi voto cuenta,â she said â I want to see that my vote is counted.

The laws have gotten so complicated and strict that Gomez worries state leaders may even try to prevent volunteers like her from providing rides to the polls.

âI donât know whatâs going to happen, if theyâre going to keep making this harder for people,â she said, âbut I would like to see people who want to vote to be able to do it.â

Natalia Contreras covers election administration and voting access for Votebeat in partnership with the Texas Tribune. Natalia is based in Corpus Christi. Contact her at ncontreras@votebeat.org.

#6110. The global rise of listening bars

A version of this story first appeared in The Swell, Salon's culture newsletter. Sign up for early access to articles like this, for more culture that's made to last.

Nothing about Shibuya HiFi is loud. From its unmarked front door to its low-lit lounge, the Seattle vinyl bar is a subtle, pensive ballad of a place. So much so, in fact, that on the Wednesday night that we visited for a sold-out event, the sparsely populated lounge area was nearly silent.

That is intentional, said general manager Jerry Stotler. Wednesday nights are closed to everyone but ticket holders. “These are what we call deep listening sessions,” he explained, “so when you walk in, there isn’t any music playing. We want to ensure a pristine listening environment when we’re in the hi-fi room.”

Seattle has many vinyl bars, but Shibuya, open since 2023, sets the local standard for premium listening experiences. Every inch of its intimate sanctum contains the story of the venue’s principal owners, Quentin Ertel and Brian Rauschenbach. It’s named for the Tokyo district known for its jazz kissa, cafés dating back to post-war Japan where visitors listen to vinyl on premium sound equipment. Rauschenbach’s parents met in such a place nearly six decades ago, Stotler said.

Ertel, an interior designer, painstakingly curated the room. Cedar planks line the walls. Louis Poulsen chandeliers hang from the ceiling, along with several plush, crescent-shaped loveseats, acquired from Benaroya Hall when the concert hall underwent a redesign. A pair of deep seats covered in nubby upholstery sit close to this sacred space’s altar — a vinyl-stacked media console holding a vintage receiver and turntable, flanked by two ATC SCM50 loudspeakers. But one set of equipment reigns over everything: a pair of 1976 Klipschorns.

Shibuya’s schedule favors favorites such as D’Angelo’s “Voodoo,” Radiohead’s “Kid A,” or Charles Mingus’ self-titled opus. But on this Wednesday, the venue hosted a special listening session for Michael Kiwanuka’s fifth album, “Fudge,” a week before its Oct. 23 release.

Stotler humbly acknowledged the venue’s good fortune to be included on the very short list of people and organizations invited to preview the record, a relatively recent development. Previous pre-release sessions have debuted work by the Beastie Boys’ Mike D and Thundercat.

But I’m getting ahead of myself. While waiting for the magic to start, we listened to the hi-hat riff of ice cubes click-clacking as Stotler worked a cocktail shaker. Once the listening room doors open, all drinks, distractions and shoes must be left at the door. “So enjoy a cocktail in advance of the session to relax and reset,” he calmly says, sliding one of his potions across the bar to a fellow patron. “Then we’ll go back and drop the needle.”

I’ve been curious about the recent rise of listening bars. Life has gotten faster, noisier and increasingly disconnected. Low-friction digital convenience has sapped life and music of their organic weight.

Places like Shibuya, then, are a natural fit for what Ertel describes as a renaissance of meaning, driven by vinyl’s resurgence. “There’s a search for new ways to be together, but also, I think, just new ways to be,” he said when I caught up with him by phone a few days later.  “We live in sort of this two-dimensional world of scrolling. Everything’s flat and fragmented and fractured. When you have something that has kind of a wholeness to it, that is also linked to something that most of us love so much, which is music, it makes sense that people want vinyl records again.”

Younger audiophiles revived the medium from the dead starting in 2008 for many reasons, the simplest being that digital downloads don’t include eye-popping cover art. By 2020, vinyl record sales revenue hit $596.2 million, surpassing CDs ($531.1 million) for the first time since 1986, according to the Recording Industry Association of America. In 2025, vinyl purchases in the U.S. alone reached $1.04 billion, the RIAA reported in March.

Listening bars, meanwhile, have popped up worldwide. Tracks & Tales, a site founded by British writer Rafi Mercer, reports finding bars, hi-fi cafés and sound-first venues across 171 countries and 6,465 cities. That doesn’t count traveling experiences like The Listening Room, created by Seattle DJ Joshua Fields.

Fields was inspired by listening to “Voodoo” at Shibuya and wishing that he could talk about it with the other attendees. (He credits Rauschenbach as a mentor.) A little later, a back injury forced him to slow down and think about what he’d do differently — a “divine download,” he called it during a recent phone chat, that transformed into a monthly series of phone-free listening sessions that have so far taken place in Portland and Seattle venues.

The rules of engagement are consistent. Soft, comfortable seating is a must. No phones for the duration, or talking, singing or other interruptions once the needle hits vinyl until the very last track finishes. Afterward, he sets aside time for quiet journaling and discussion.

“The music is really the medium that gets us to this opening up,” Fields told me, “because what I’m solving for is the lack of human connection, with all our technology and our robots, all our things.”

As such, his model is a little more relaxed than Shibuya’s. Participants are served food and drinks, with each event inspiring a signature cocktail. For a recent sit with “Purple Rain,” he direct-messaged its co-star, Apollonia Kotero, to let her know he was naming a drink after her.  “She responded, which blew my mind,” Fields said. “She told me, ‘Make sure it’s spicy.’”

Listening events remind us that music can be a full-bodied, meditative journey, however you do it. There’s a ritual to setting the turntable stylus, or needle, into a vinyl LP’s groove for the first time, hearing the soft, crackling prelude to an opening melody and listening to a body of work front to back with silent focus. We can create that feeling at home, setting up a dedicated space to be comfortably still and take in your favorite records, or an unfamiliar one, from start to finish.

Still, there’s real value in leaving home and finding a place to listen — not simply hear, but listen —alongside strangers who love the art and spirit of music as much as you do. At events like Fields’, you may even meet someone you otherwise wouldn’t. He teased that a Dec. 4 Listening Room event in Seattle for India Arie’s “Acoustic Soul” will feature a special guest.

Want more from culture than just the latest trend? The Swell highlights art made to last. Sign up here

I look forward to inhaling “Fudge” many times on my stereo. But I’ll never be able to recreate the rush of hearing its blossoming piano and strings for the first time, sensing the soundwaves from those Klipschorn speakers penetrate my skin. It made me well up, which embarrassed me until I glanced around the room and noticed a few others dabbing their eyes, too.

“In a true kissa or a well-kept basement bar, the first thing you feel is not volume; it’s presence,” Mercer writes. “The room seems to steady itself around a note. The air thickens. You sit differently. Your breath slows without negotiation.

“Good sound doesn’t overwhelm you,” Mercer adds. “It invites you. That’s the quiet truth at the heart of every listening bar: the room listens back.”

#6107. It’s scary how watchable these stories are

A version of this story first appeared in The Swell, Salon's culture newsletter. Sign up for early access to articles like this, for more culture that's made to last.

Iâve never been great at the whole Halloween thing. By the time I remember itâs happening, all the good sweets are gone from grocery store shelves, so any visiting trick-or-treaters get butterscotch suckers, breath mints or candy corn. I donât do costume parties. I never got the point of carving pumpkins.

But movie and TV marathons? Sign me up â along with a lot of other homebodies. The horror genre is bigger than ever, according to a San Francisco Chronicle report that says this yearâs domestic box office reached nearly $1.3 billion as of the start of October.

Horrorâs surge has also yielded more films designed to play with our perception as opposed to the âSawâ-style torture porn dominating years past. Think âObsessionâ or âBackrooms,â both of which are among the 10 highest-earning movies of 2026 thus far. Thatâs good news for anyone who isnât partial to splatter flicks or slashers but still enjoys a creep show that makes you think, especially ones that are more thoughtful than scary. If thatâs your speed, the following options may be perfect for your reclusive Samhain.

I will bet good money the first bong-ripping undergrad to declare that all horror is metaphor cited George Romeroâs âNight of the Living Deadâ as a prime example. Thatâs not wrong; Romeroâs 1968 benchmark established the modern cinematic zombie as a stand-in for mindless capitalist consumption. But âBlack Zombieâ rewinds to the monsterâs Haitian roots to examine an even darker origin tied to that countryâs shared history with ours.

You may be wondering why Iâd recommend a documentary in a horror roundup, let alone one that explains how the modern movie flesh gobbler began as a manifestation of white fear. The answer is that Maya Annik Bedwardâs film doubles as an impressive cinematic syllabus.

By braiding Americaâs media history with its national history, Bedward and her assemblage of academics, creatives, authors and Vodou practitioners invite us to think differently about the prejudices driving movies like, say, Victor Halperinâs 1932 effort âWhite Zombie,â or 1943âs âI Walked with a Zombie.â

âBlack Zombieâ opens with a truth that has long escaped those fascinated by the shambling undead. To some, theyâre simply mindless hunters. But Haitians understand the horror of zombies to be one of dispossession, a curse enacted by enslavers that binds victims to mindless servitude, denying them liberation in the afterlife. But long after Romero transformed them from blank-eyed puppets to ravenous murder machines, Bedwardâs film demonstrates how Hollywoodâs version of the zombie impacts Americaâs perception of Vodou, Haitians and immigration.

âBlack Zombieâ not only asks us to think differently about an overexposed subgenre, but also thoughtfully examines Vodouâs central role in the revolution that drove out French colonizers, and Franceâs imposition of debt to punish Haitians for winning their freedom.

All of this informs the zombieâs continued proliferation across popular culture, in films like âWorld War Zâ and shows such as âThe Last of Usâ and âThe Walking Dead.â Theyâre terrific entertainment, certainly. But each is, in its own way, built upon decadesâ worth of misrepresenting Haitiâs syncretic faith to the detriment and demonization of a people. At the same time, âBlack Zombieâ recognizes this subgenreâs cultural resilience, arguing that recognizing the zombieâs true roots broadens its narrative possibilities.

Proving that point, one of Bedwardâs subjects, a Vodou priest, says he grew up loving Wes Cravenâs âThe Serpent and the Rainbow,â despite its message that visitors to his country risk having their nuts nailed to a chair. Â âItâs a fantastical world to scare children,â he says, before adding that his main problem is its inaccurate messaging about his faith. âWe say, âWow â Haitians are devils.â Thatâs what weâre taught.â

Iâd nearly forgotten about that movie. Now I might rewatch it for the first time in decades and expect to be horrified for entirely different reasons.

Stephen Kingâs classic may be more than half a century old and has undergone multiple adaptations, but it endures because its central moral that high school is hell never ages. Still, Mike Flanaganâs interpretation has divided the audience. Some, including King, appreciate Flanaganâs kinder portrait of Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) as an innocent unjustly sequestered from the world by fundamentalist parents who repudiate her extraordinary power. Others disagree with Flanaganâs alteration to the storyâs climactic scene, which shifts culpability for the prom massacre from Carrie to a character created expressly for the series.

Pretty much everyone questions the season finale, which hints at taking an âX-Menâ-style turn for its recently greenlit second season.

As someone who accepts nothing is sacrosanct now, not to mention a fan of the creatorâs other adaptations, including âThe Fall of the House of Usher,â I appreciated Flanagan using Carrieâs story to critique ignorance, knowledge suppression, and the dehumanizing effect of social media.

Besides, nearly all the key elements of âCarrieâ remain. The bullies are still awful, and the famous âplug it upâ shower scene in Brian DePalmaâs 1976 standard-setter is worsened by her tormentors posting Carrieâs frightened sobs on social media.

Some changes retain the spirit of past performances. Carrieâs mother Margaret (Samantha Sloyan) is still an abusive religious zealot fond of locking her daughter in a prayer closet, for instance. But after the law forces her homeschooled girl to join the festering sin den that is their local public school, Margaret throws herself into advocating for parentsâ rights, entirely disregarding her teenâs desire for a ânormalâ adolescence.

Part of the additional fun Flanagan has with this marquee property is strewing cultural Easter Eggs throughout. Some nod to whatâs happening in America, such as when Carrie discovers the school library and gravitates straight to books that have been banned from classrooms and community libraries across the country. Another winks at âArmy of Darknessâ fans; look for the logo on Margaretâs work uniform.

By the time we reach Carrieâs bloodbath, we may be left to question whether sheâs simply a bullied victim pushed beyond her limit or some version of a Final Girl empowered to vanquish tormentors who earn their reckoning. Even if you donât ultimately see Howellâs Carrie that way, itâs a fine dance with one of horrorâs oldest friends.

âCarrieâ is streaming on Prime Video.

For adults, Halloween is an excuse to mingle sensuality with morbid themes. Why cosplay as a grizzled cop when you can be a flirty detective? Why settle for pretending to be a humpbacked wiccan when you can troll for hookups as a sexy witch?

It refers to the mythical Slavic crone, Baba Yaga, who either gives heroes a boon or lures wayward children to a forest hut that moves around on bird legs. Playwright Kat Chandlerâs interpretation leaves open the question of whether our impressions of its witch are unwarranted or dead right, further muddling our judgment with the introduction of Carrie-Anne Mossâ university professor, Katherine Hargrove.

#6094. Are Mount Everest climbers dreamers, or just cultists?

In the title of his 1997 bestselling adventure tale, âInto Thin Air,â mountaineer and writer Jon Krakauer employs a double entendre so clever that its effect is extraordinary. Throughout the book, Krakauer recounts his attempt to summit Mount Everest the year earlier in what would become, at the time, the mountainâs deadliest season. Iâve been momentarily halted by that title each time Iâve picked up my tattered $5 thrift-store copy over the last few weeks. Itâs witty, but not grim; accurate but also imaginative. In three words, âInto Thin Airâ conveys not only the literal effect of Everestâs high altitude and how quickly the mountain can take a life, but also the ardent, almost fatuous confidence of those who choose to climb it.

The dissonance between reason and ambition is what makes âInto Thin Airâ such a compelling read. For someone like myself, who knows next to nothing about climbing, Krakauer powerfully elucidates the pull of a mountain like Everest and the trance-like state in which it ensnares its adversaries. Unlike some climbers, Krakauer can wax poetic while staying honest about the stakes. He writes about mountaineering as a spiritual practice, good for the mind and body alike, while questioning why some find that clarity only by staring death in the face. In that respect, extreme climbing is an incredibly selfish endeavor. Before he begins his push for the summit, Krakauer remembers his wife, Linda, telling him before he left for Nepal: âIf you get killed, itâs not just you who will pay the price. Iâll have to pay, too. For the rest of my life.â

That sentiment echoed in my mind throughout âEverest: The Other Side,â the remarkable new documentary from National Geographic, helmed by âFree Soloâ and âNyadâ co-directors Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin. The film is brutally honest in its depictions of cold human narcissism and the relentless pursuit of glory in the name of nebulous spiritual fulfillment. Yet itâs just as candid about humanityâs collective desire for all those things in one form or another.

Such a wanton, helpless display of pride makes for a character study as gripping as it is frustrating. From that disharmony, âEverest: The Other Sideâ forges a uniquely human story of actualization at all costs, revealing the true price of a life spent looking up and not around.â

We are an arrogant species, frustrated by our humble place in this ecosystem. And yet, we feel everything intensely. When we love, we want to take that love to the ends of the Earth. We want physical proof of emotions we cannot put into words. Maybe then all of this will mean something.

As âEverest: The Other Sideâ asserts, nothing in this already mystifying life is ever so simple. The filmâs subjects, mountaineer Jim Morrison and his partner Hilaree Nelson, found love at the edge of the world and made a life together, with Morrison becoming co-parent to Nelsonâs two young sons. But their shared lust for adventure created a prickly tension within their family unit, a strain between their passion and parentage that sits at the documentaryâs emotional center.

Like those pulled by devout religion or extreme acts of faith, Morrison and Nelson are powerless before their distinct higher calling â especially with the literal highest calling of all, Everest, in their sights. They donât just want to summit the mountain from its treacherous north face; they want to be the first people ever to ski down it. In their quest, personal glory and public vanity are forever at odds. Such a wanton, helpless display of pride makes for a character study as gripping as it is frustrating. From that disharmony, âEverest: The Other Sideâ forges a uniquely human story of actualization at all costs, revealing the true price of a life spent looking up and not around.

Because this is National Geographic, the film is only partially concerned with relaying that price. This documentary is made for IMAX-loving, secondhand adventure seekers. Those who want sweeping shots of impossible sights wonât be disappointed.Â

But while âEverest: The Other Sideâ includes countless breathtaking sequences of Earthâs tallest mountain and plenty of nail-biting anxiety in the eventual summit push and ski attempt, those moments are merely the filmâs selling points. The crux of this story is on Nelson and Morrisonâs shoulders, and their sincerity flies in the face of good judgment and self-editing, giving viewers a palpable sense of their egos. This isnât to say that either of them is a raging narcissist who cares only about themselves, but thereâs no doubt that their sportâs seismic, life-altering dangers are on full display, warts and all.

Early in the film, Nelson tries to communicate the draw of climbing, and how fundamentally at odds it is with her role as a mother. âPeople ask me, âHow do you find balance?ââ she says. âThere isnât. Itâs just chaos. Youâre just hanging on. You want to be with your family, but you have a passion, and you want to work, and you need to make money. Youâre all over the map.â

It would be easy to dismiss Nelson as selfish, or, at the worst and most damning, a bad parent. How can someone have young children and decide to part with them for two months for a climb that is about, at face value, little more than bragging rights? How can a parent let their children spend two months wondering if their mother is dead or alive?

These are easy questions to ask from the comfort of a living room or the cushion of a theater seat, but much harder to answer when youâre living the life. Itâs important to remember that, in life, most of us have desires that would yank us in severe directions. It reminds me that cult experts will tell you that any of us could fall into the clutches of a cult, and those of us who argue otherwise are likely among the most vulnerable. Anyone who insists they are too self-aware to be pulled into something that goes against their own interests is admitting that they donât know themselves or humanity very well. Thatâs one of lifeâs great mysteries: Why do we do things that we know are wrong, or bad for us? Death and taxes might be certain, but so are mistakes and regret, no matter how much weâd like to believe that weâre big enough to let go.

Conflict is ever-present in Morrison, who chooses to climb Everest despite its perils. For him, the adventure is about more than pride or titles; itâs about honor and love. The journey is intended both to strengthen his bond with Nelson and honor the memory of his late wife and their two children, who died in a horrific commuter plane crash in 2011, a decade before he and Nelson decide to attempt Everest. Recalling the aftermath, Morrison tells how climbing brought him clarity. Unable to move from the edge of his driveway, consumed by grief, he eventually found the strength to simply walk up the slight incline and into his home â a microscopic example of the human spiritâs extraordinary tenacity he hopes to commemorate in the Everest climb.Â

We are an arrogant species, frustrated by our humble place in this ecosystem. And yet, we feel everything intensely. When we love, we want to take that love to the ends of the Earth. We want physical proof of emotions we cannot put into words. Maybe then all of this will mean something.

But more tests lie ahead. The route to Everest proves demanding in heart and health. And while training together for the big summit push by climbing a lower peak in Nepal in 2022, Nelson loses her footing in an avalanche the size of a small snow drift. On a ski slope, the drift would be minor. But on a mountain, every movement is measured. Nelson is swept away and under the snow, toward a cliff. We see it happen in real time, captured on a helmet GoPro. The moment is almost unassuming in its speed, but it permanently shapes everything that follows. Nelson is lost amid a series of avalanches, and the clock starts ticking.

Counting the seconds seems futile. But climbing is futile, too. For Morrison, left to search for his partner amid the snow, hazardous ridges and cliffs, it all seems like a waste. More pain, more trauma, more memories that are left for only one person to hold onto. I was immediately reminded of what Krakauerâs wife told him by satellite phone before he began his push from Everestâs base camp. âSaying goodbye to you was one of the saddest things Iâve ever done,â he remembers her saying. âI guess I knew on some level that you might not be coming back, and it seemed like such a waste. It seemed so f**king stupid and pointless.â

Itâs hard not to dwell on that sentiment, already knowing what and who Nelson would leave behind if disaster struck. On some level, and to some people, it is all stupid and pointless. But that split second fortifies Morrison, confirming that his quest to Everest is for everyone that heâs lost, and every heartstopping moment along the way. Itâs a spiritual pursuit, the kind that we make when we travel to a family member or friendâs favorite place to scatter their ashes; the kind that we make when we give eulogies, or just sit in the grass, staring into space, thinking about everything and nothing, everyone and no one.Â

Some may be driven to climb Everest just to say that they did it, while others are looking for something else, something with no name. They want to pierce the heavens and reach through the atmosphere to grasp the indescribable truth that unites us all. And if they donât make it back down to share that peace with the rest of us, it might be enough to experience it just once.

#6092. Judge tosses DOJ lawsuit seeking to delay Alaska vote certification

A federal judge on Sunday tossed a lawsuit from the Trump administration that sought to delay the certification of the Alaska Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses.

Sullivan faces Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola and two other candidates in a contest that could help decide control of the Senate. One of those candidates is also named Dan Sullivan, which prompted the Trump administration to file its lawsuit, alleging that, under the state’s ranked choice system, voters may rank the challenger instead of the incumbent.

The complaint also asked the judge to allow a delay until an “investigation” into whether votes for the challenger, listed on the ballot as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., should have gone to the senator, who is listed as Dan S. Sullivan.

But in her ruling Sunday, Judge Sharon L. Gleason of the U.S. District Court for the District of Alaska said the relief requested by the administration was “infeasible.”

“[Many] voters have already cast their ballots in the November 2026 general election. Those cast ballots have been commingled and cannot now be segregated or the identity of the person who cast each ballot ascertained,” she wrote.

Should the Trump administration appeal the ruling, it would go to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit.

The case started on Oct. 22, when the Trump administration filed the lawsuit, arguing that the courts should delay the certification of the Alaska Senate race if the incumbent Sullivan were to lose and the margin was less than the number of votes the second Sullivan received.

The Justice Department argued that voters could be confused by the presence of a namesake challenger on the state’s ballot and not cast their intended vote for the incumbent. Initially, the lawsuit was filed against the state, but Peltola and Democrats have intervened to argue that the case should be tossed.

Then last week, The New York Times reported that aides for Peltola were involved in the effort to recruit the second Sullivan to enter the Senate race. The DOJ filed an amended complaint accusing Peltola and Democrats of misleading the courts.

“Apparently emboldened by the success of their reported plot to deceive Alaskan voters, Alaskans For Mary and the [Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee] appear to have turned to misleading this Court,” the DOJ filing said.

Trump himself has accused Peltola of executing a “FRAUD ON THE AMERICAN PUBLIC” and called for both her and the second Sullivan to be removed from the Senate ballot. Under federal law, the state finalized its ballot more than a month ago.

Peltola and Democrats pushed back in their own filing Friday, calling the DOJ’s claims “nonsense.” They also said that they “lack knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief about the truth or falsity of the allegation concerning the purposes of Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy and therefore deny any allegation about those purposes.”

And on Saturday, the Republican-led Alaska state government called on Gleason to dismiss the lawsuit, saying that “the relief demanded is inappropriate and not even possible given Alaskan voters’ vital right to ballot secrecy.”

Earlier this year Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired school teacher, successfully sued in state court to be included on the ballot after election officials had previously removed his name. The state Supreme Court ruled that the second Sullivan was a valid candidate and should be included.

Under Alaska rules, voters can rank up to four candidates on the Senate ballot. If no one takes a majority of first-place votes, the candidate in last position is eliminated, with those votes assigned to the voters’ next choice. The process repeats until one candidate has a majority of the remaining votes.

This story was originally published by The 19th.

This story was originally reported by Mel Leonor Barclay of The 19th. Meet Mel and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy.

RIO GRANDE CITY, Texas â When Cynthia Villareal voted for President Donald Trump in 2024, she did so trusting his campaign promises of lower gas prices, border security and âassistance for the people â for the middle class.â

The 43-year-old mother of four turned out for Trump alongside a sizable majority of voters in heavily Latino Starr County, which hugs the border with Mexico and had reliably turned out for Democratic candidates for five generations.

They havenât â they havenât at all,â said Villareal, who drives around the Rio Grande Valley for her job supervising home health aides and feels every little surge. Villareal manages workers in a shortstaffed, tough profession where wages have simply not kept up with the cost of living. Many of her best workers, she said, are immigrants without permanent legal status experiencing the brunt of Trumpâs immigration agenda.Â

âI mean, he didnât mention that these ICE agents were just going to be picking up all of these hardworking employees, you know, that have no backgrounds,â Villareal said, referring to immigrants without a criminal record. âTheyâre leaving people without their family, basically, and then some of the people are even dying in there,â she said of immigration detention. âLike, who knows what theyâre doing to these poor people?â

For Villareal, life is more expensive, and her job harder. âItâs just too much.âÂ

Latina votersâ rightward shift was a crucial part of Trumpâs reelection in 2024, and while more Latino men backed the president, Latinas actually made larger strides to the right in the last four presidential cycles.Â

Ahead of the midterms, Latinas are also registering higher levels of regret when thinking about their support for Trump, a dynamic that may decide the outcome of competitive races from Texas to Florida and beyond.Â

Voters like Villareal shed light on how Trump regret among this swingy and powerful group of voters âÂ Latinas vote at higher rates than Latino men â may be the swell that breaks into a blue wave for Democrats this November.Â

âI do think the narrative of this election could be that Latina women, in particular, help decide who is in control of the House of Representatives and the balance of government. And I say that because of the shifts weâve seen over time and the shifts back that we are seeing now among Latina women in particular,â said Stephanie Valencia, who studies Latino voters at Equis Research.

Latinosâ political power this cycle is spread across the midterms map. Latinos make up at least 15 percent of the population in six of the 17 most competitive congressional districts, as well as in 29 other districts considered broadly competitive, mostly in the Southwest, California and Florida. Latino voters could be the deciders in competitive races for the U.S. Senate in Texas and Florida. Some of the most dramatic shifts toward Trump and Republicans in 2024 were logged in Texasâ Rio Grande Valley, where Villareal lives. A string of counties in this part of Texas saw double-digit shifts in Trumpâs favor compared with the 2020 election, after significant shifts to the right from 2016 to 2020.Â

Latina voters in the Rio Grande Valley and around Texas will have a big impact on the Texas governorâs race, where Democrat Gina Hinojosa is locked in a dead heat with three-term Gov. Greg Abbott. #6084. Right-wing media and the mystery of Texas’ transgender mailers

On Thursday night, the smear at the heart of the mysterious transgender mailers that have rocked the final weeks of the midterm elections in Texas completed its journey. What began as baseless social media whispers quickly ascended the ladder of conservative influence, jumped into mailboxes across the Lone Star State and ultimately into the comforting prime-time embrace of Fox News.

At a town hall in Fort Worth, a Texas mother of six named Rebekah Smith told Vice President JD Vance that her 11-year-old daughter had received a letter explaining how to transition without her parents ever knowing, and asked how Republicans would keep the government out of her family. “I don’t know who sent that letter to your child,” the vice president said, “but I think the person who sends a letter to an 11-year-old about gender transition, what I call that in my family is a pervert, and that person ought to go to prison.” Host Jesse Watters, never one to let a grievance go to waste, promised that Fox would investigate “this perverted letter.” Vance asked Smith to talk to his staff because he would “like the Department of Justice to investigate that” as well.

Watters rushed to promote the spectacle. “WHOA! Texas MOM tells JD Vance her DAUGHTER received a letter telling her TO TRANSITION TO A BOY,” he posted on X, followed by Vance’s promise. Missing from that framing was the question that should have governed the segment: Who actually sent the material?

Nobody on that stage mentioned that the pamphlet was a fake. Nobody mentioned that the real transgender advocacy group named inside it had disavowed the mailer. Nobody mentioned that sworn testimony filed that same week had tied the text messages that accompanied it to a national Republican organization. The vice president was asking federal prosecutors to chase a forgery that may well have originated in his own party’s orbit — and he was doing it on a network whose viewers had been marinating in that forgery for weeks.

The race between Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic challenger James Talarico has become a crucible for dark-money maneuvers. As polls show the Republican grip on the Lone Star State slipping, conservative campaigns and their surrogates have resorted to increasingly desperate tactics. In early October, for example, Talarico took a brief hiatus from the campaign trail to recover from a severe case of the flu. Rather than accepting a routine human illness, the right-wing echo chamber treated a temporary absence as evidence of mental illness. Within days, the fabricated scandal has collapsed — yet the machinery of right-wing media simply pivoted to amplifying a more insidious operation designed to trigger visceral outrage.

This second October surprise involved millions of unsolicited text messages and a wave of physical mailers sent to Texas households with materials that directed readers to the website of the Transgender Education Network of

It does not need to survive scrutiny. It just needs to circulate upward.

Texas while inserting provocative advice on child emancipation that the real organization says it never authored or authorized. By flooding the electorate with extreme material disguised as progressive advocacy, right-wing operatives appear to have sought to create a fake controversy that could be weaponized in attack ads and campaign speeches. Vance, for instance, told the Fox News audience that Talarico has “a weird fascination with trans kids,” and that “he’ll probably defend the right of the person sending the letter, not the right of the parent who is rightfully creeped out by this.” Vance claimed that Talarico “has actually called it abusive when parents try to prevent their children from transitioning” and that Paxton “has fought hard to prosecute those people, whereas James Talarico has fought hard to protect those people.” Even the distortion had been laundered by then — Talarico called denying a child’s gender identity abusive, a different claim from saying parents must permit medical transition, but at the top of the ladder the difference no longer exists.

That is how a smear works in the closed ecosystem of the American right. It does not need to survive scrutiny. It just needs to circulate upward. An anonymous account posts it; an influencer adopts it; a donor-funded outlet reports the influencer’s outrage as news; an elected official demands an investigation, and the demand becomes proof the story matters; cable news books the controversy; a vice president promises federal action. Each rung launders the one below it. The correction, when it comes, travels in the opposite direction and arrives nowhere.

The paper trail looks like what you would expect from a covert operation. Texas Transgender Student Union LLC was formed in Wyoming on Sept. 2 through a commercial registered agent that helps owners stay anonymous. After CBS News Texas visited the agent’s address in Sheridan, Wyoming, the agent announced it was resigning. The mailers listed a Houston-area post office box. The Texas Observer reported that the barcode on the envelopes traced to a mail-tracking company that has taken federal campaign money from only one group this year, the National Republican Congressional Committee. The committee said it had nothing to do with the mailers, and the company would not say who paid. CBS News Texas reported that the bulk-mail permit belongs to an Illinois printer owned by the Zerrusen family, who have given heavily to Republican PACs and been photographed with Donald Trump.

When the real Transgender Education Network of Texas filed a petition in Travis County court to unmask the perpetrators behind the impersonation campaign, the partisan safety nets of the Texas judiciary eventually snapped into action. A deposition of Infobip, the messaging company that delivered the texts, which a Travis County judge ordered made public, indicated that the texts were sent on behalf of the Republican Women’s Caucus Fund and a man named John Braun. But on Friday, the Texas Supreme Court, composed entirely of judges appointed by Republican Governor Greg Abbott, issued an administrative stay that blocked its release. Chris Hilton, an attorney who previously served under Paxton, defended him during his impeachment trial and was later pushed out of office amid sexual harassment allegations, argued on behalf of the company that the mailers were not political speech because they named no candidate or party.

Dirty tricks are an old tradition of American politics. This cycle, Republican PACs in Nevada mailed a flyer calling a nonpartisan candidate, Danielle Ford, the “AOC of Nevada,” hoping voters would mistake her for the actual Democratic nominee, Aaron Ford. This week also brought word that the group that funded Cornel West’s 2024 ballot drives raised every dollar through a dark-money network bankrolled by Elon Musk.

The president’s party whines about decoy candidates in Alaska while running them at home. Ratf**king is a long and proud Republican tradition, and the Texas operation fits inside perfectly.

#6080. James O’Keefe election sting ends in his own felony voter fraud charges

Conservative activist James O’Keefe set out to expose alleged vulnerabilities in Minnesota’s election system. Now, he faces felony charges stemming from the undercover operation.

O’Keefe, formerly of Project Veritas and current CEO of the O’Keefe Media Group, and conservative influencer Cameron Higby were charged Wednesday with unlawful voting and identity theft after allegedly impersonating registered voters at Minneapolis polling places during the state’s Aug. 11 primary.

According to Hennepin County prosecutors, the men wore disguises, used fake accents and provided election workers with the names of registered voters without their knowledge or permission. They filmed the encounters and later posted videos claiming to expose weaknesses in Minnesota’s voter registration procedures.

The operation targeted the state’s *vouching* system, which allows registered voters to verify the residency of people seeking to register on Election Day. The process requires sworn statements and identifying information from prospective voters.

Neither O’Keefe nor Higby cast a ballot or signed the required vouching oath. Prosecutors contend that misrepresenting their identities while beginning the voting process was itself unlawful.

O’Keefe defended the operation as investigative journalism, calling the prosecution an attack on First Amendment rights. Higby also denied breaking the law, saying the pair intended to expose election vulnerabilities.

Start your day with essential news from Salon. Sign up for our free morning newsletter, Crash Course.

The charges are the latest controversy involving O’Keefe’s undercover tactics. In 2017, reporters at the Washington Post caught him trying to sell them a false story. In 2009, he collaborated on hidden-camera investigations targeting Planned Parenthood and gained national attention for videos involving the community organization ACORN. He later settled a lawsuit brought by a former ACORN employee for $100,000 without admitting wrongdoing.

But Minnesota officials say the latest operation demonstrated something different from what O’Keefe intended.

Election workers noticed suspicious behavior and reported it, prompting an investigation. Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said the state’s system for identifying and responding to potential misconduct functioned as intended. This vouching process itself accounted for fewer than 0.6% of votes cast in Minnesota’s 2024 general election, according to state election officials.

O’Keefe and Higby are scheduled to appear in court Nov. 16. Neither has been convicted.

#6078. This week: Campaigns make final frantic moves as Election Day arrives

A lot of the midterm vote has already happened in states where early voting and mail-in voting are common, but there’s still time to get supporters to the polls on Election Day.

President Donald Trump will use the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool as the location for his midterm closing argument, though he is expected to hold additional tele-rallies. Trump told reporters Sunday that he wants to show “how beautiful it is.”

Trump held in-person rallies Sunday in Iowa and Kansas. Those states have two of the four Senate Toss-up races, according to Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales.

In Iowa, Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson is trying to win the seat being vacated by retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernst. Hinson is facing Democratic State Rep. Josh Turek, a two-time Paralympic gold medalist.

In Kansas, Republican Sen. Roger Marshall finds himself in a Toss-up race against Democrat Adam Hamilton.

The other two Senate Toss-ups are in Alaska and Maine, which are both Republican-held seats — and in fact there are no Senate races rated a Toss-up or favoring the GOP where the current senator is a Democrat.

Iowa is also among the keys to the House, with several closely watched contests. Two Iowa GOP incumbents, Reps. Zach Nunn and Marinnette Miller-Meeks, made the 2026 cycle’s final list of CQ Roll Call’s most vulnerable House members.

Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who has continued to argue that the polling favorable to Democrats should not be believed, was traveling with Trump on Sunday.

“I work almost as hard as this guy. I try to keep up with him, he doesn’t sleep at all,” Johnson said of Trump, before briefly pulling out his impression of the president alongside him at a rally in Iowa.

Johnson is scheduled to join Rep. Jen Kiggans, R-Va., for an Election Eve rally in Virginia Beach before heading to Texas to kick off Election Day.

There, he’ll get things started with an early morning event with Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz, along with GOP candidates Eric Flores and Tano Tijerina.

Flores is running in the reconfigured 34th District to unseat Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez, while Tijerina is seeking to oust Democratic Rep. Henry Cuellar.

The big surprise of the final weekend came out of Michigan, where Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens abruptly announced her support for — and then appeared alongside of — Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, the GOP Senate candidate.

Stevens, who had competed in the Democratic primary for Senate and had been expected to appear with Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, made a last-minute pivot to embracing Rogers, a decision which left Democrats flummoxed.

“As you may have seen, our Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, Abdul, said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away. And he’s right. And that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers,” Stevens said Sunday in a video posted to social media.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., was among the national Democrats to criticize Stevens, calling her announcement a “despicable betrayal.”

Separately, Schumer convened a call with Senate Democrats on Sunday as part of the effort to prepare for potential efforts by Trump or his allies to undermine midterm results.

“If Trump and his allies attempt to interfere with the will of the voters, Senate Democrats are prepared to fight back immediately and aggressively, on Election Day and for as long as it takes to ensure the results are respected,” a Senate Democratic aide said in a statement.

Mary Ellen McIntire contributed to this report.

World Brief: The EU and Canada Struggle to Define Their Relationship

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at how deep Canada-EU ties will go, the resignation of European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde, and China’s latest political and military purge.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney hosted senior European Union officials in Montreal on Thursday to discuss bolstering trade and defense ties. Notably downplayed, though, was the EU’s previous offer to make Canada an “associate member” of the 27-nation bloc.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at how deep Canada-EU ties will go, the resignation of European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde, and China’s latest political and military purge.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney hosted senior European Union officials in Montreal on Thursday to discuss bolstering trade and defense ties. Notably downplayed, though, was the EU’s previous offer to make Canada an “associate member” of the 27-nation bloc.

Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen floated the idea during her annual State of the European Union address.

“We must urgently reimagine our partnerships,” von der Leyen said while standing beside Carney. “We share one ocean, one set of values, one way of seeing the world. And we will now build our shared future as well.” Canadian officials applauded the proposal, with Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada’s ambassador to the EU, saying at the time that Ottawa wants “to get as close as we possibly can” to the bloc.

Yet a statement prepared for this week’s annual Canada-EU summit included a watered-down version of such a future. Rather than explicitly noting the proposed associate member status, the draft text offered “an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself,” Politico reported on Wednesday. According to Reuters, a previous draft had included at least two direct mentions of Canada’s associate member status while adding that defining the term would take another year.

“Canada cannot become a full-fledged member of the EU because of geography, but we both want to bring our relationship to the highest level possible,” von der Leyen said on Thursday. She described this type of relationship as open “only to our closest partners outside of Europe who are ready to open a new frontier together,” and she stressed that associate member status is not fully off the table.

Von der Leyen’s decision to back off from her full-throated appeal for associate Canadian membership may have been made due to some member nations’ hesitance. Several EU countries, particularly Germany, had argued that they would not approve such a designation, as it had no legal precedent and had not been fully fleshed out. Others accused von der Leyen of not discussing the idea with European leaders first.

“Nobody was consulted about associate membership apart from [von der Leyen’s] closest staff, it would seem,” one diplomat told the Guardian. “This is all about fixing the plane while it is flying.”

The EU’s move to soften the language is likely to appease at least one foreign leader: U.S. President Donald Trump. Trump had called the EU’s initial proposal “laughable” and warned that such a designation could be considered a “hostile act” that could prompt the White House to cut off trade with Europe in certain areas. Already, U.S. trade relations with Canada and the European Union are greatly strained, with Trump repeatedly returning to his tariff war for economic leverage.

Still, Carney appeared to be unconcerned by Thursday’s language shift. “The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians.”

Who will run the ECB next? European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde announced on Thursday that she will step down from her role in February, officially triggering a race to determine who will take up the mantle of one of the European Union’s top posts. Her eight-year term was set to end in October 2027; her early departure allows the EU to choose her successor before one of its members, France, holds a consequential presidential election that could upset the bloc’s balance.

In April, France will hold a highly anticipated presidential vote that could see far-right National Rally candidate Marine Le Pen take power. Eurozone members had worried that a Le Pen victory could affect who is selected to be the new ECB president, as the populist lawmaker has previously criticized EU financial institutions and expressed disinterest in choosing another mainstream central banker to lead the body. Lagarde resigning early therefore allows outgoing French President Emmanuel Macron to have a say in her replacement instead.

Among the front-runners for Lagarde’s post are former Spanish Central Bank head Pablo Hernández de Cos and former Dutch Central Bank chief Klaas Knot. Whoever is chosen will have to contend with energy price shocks, bond market turmoil, and persistent high inflation.

Meanwhile, it is unclear what’s next for Lagarde, who was the first woman to serve as the ECB president. “I want to have the freedom of speech, the freedom of expression, and the freedom to engage on matters that are not monetary policy matters,” Lagarde said on Thursday. Some analysts believe that Lagarde, who is a French citizen, aims to become more vocal in the country’s politics, which have faced weeks of upheaval due to sweeping student-led protests.

Xi’s latest purge. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) confirmed the expulsion of 33 senior political and military officials on Thursday, in one of President Xi Jinping’s most sweeping purges since taking office in 2012. Those removed include Liu Jianchao, the former head of the CCP’s International Department; former Politburo member Ma Xingrui; Zhang Youxia, once the country’s most senior general; and Zhong Shaojun, a top military secretary to Xi.

It is unclear what charges these members faced beyond “serious disciplinary and legal violations.” But the expulsions are part of Xi’s extensive anti-corruption campaign targeting those considered disloyal to the party, and it comes as the longtime leader is preparing to clinch a fourth term in office. “While maintaining a tough stance against corruption, we should also strengthen checks on and oversight over the exercise of power,” read a communiqué released by the CCP’s Central Committee on Thursday.

The announcement concluded this year’s multiday Central Committee meeting in Beijing. Only 279 officials attended the annual conference, compared to 376 members when the current body was formed in 2022. This was the first time during Xi’s term that the plenary’s attendance dropped below 300 people. That suggests that nearly 100 officials were likely purged from the party over the course of just four years, China experts say.

National mourning. Spanish search-and-rescue operations stretched into Thursday following a deadly high-speed train crash the day before. At least 69 deaths have been confirmed thus far, with some 50 individuals still hospitalized, and local authorities fear that the death toll could rise. Madrid declared three days of national mourning starting Thursday.

Early Wednesday, a high-speed passenger train believed to be going around 120 miles per hour slammed into a stopped train near the central Spanish city of Toledo. An initial investigation found that an information technology failure involving railroad switching equipment was to blame. However, critics have accused the Spanish government of failing to provide adequate oversight and maintenance of the world’s second-largest high-speed rail network, particularly after another train crash on the same line killed 46 people in January.

“It is clear that we need to reinforce the safety of our train service to rebuild the trust in our high-speed rail,” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said on Wednesday. “It is not acceptable for a country like Spain to endure two high-speed train accidents in the same year.” With the country holding snap parliamentary elections next month, public transportation reform will likely be a top concern among voters.

The Vatican Museums opened a new exhibition on Thursday that celebrates more than 100 years of papal travel. Dubbed “A Century of the Popemobile,” the showing features eight Mercedes-Benz vehicles that popes have used since 1930 to travel among the faithful. Notable design alterations include Pope John XXIII’s 300 d Landaulet, which included removable rear side windows to allow the pontiff to reach out to those he passed on the road, and Pope John Paul II’s 230 G, which added the car’s transparent dome for greater viewing access.

Alexandra Sharp is the World Brief writer at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @alexandrassharp.bsky.social X: @AlexandraSSharp

#6069. Judge dismisses suit alleging FBI officials lied to Congress as ‘rush job’

A federal magistrate judge on Monday threw out a case accusing two former FBI officials of lying to Congress, criticizing it as rushed, flawed and politically motivated.

During an hourlong hearing, Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia found that there was no legal justification to continue the case against Nicole Floris and Bradley Benavides.

“What has transpired here cannot be described as anything other than weaponization” of government against the pair, the magistrate said, describing it as a “rush job” driven by a political push from President Donald Trump.

The government unveiled the charges last month, alleging that Floris and Benavides lied to the House Judiciary Committee during interviews in 2023 about their knowledge of a laptop that used to belong to Hunter Biden but was in possession of the FBI ahead of the 2020 election.

Faruqui, in ruling from the bench, said there was no evidence that Floris and Benavides knowingly said anything false to the committee. He also pointed to mistakes throughout the complaint against Floris and Benavides, as well as the probe that led to the charges.

“The rush to charge here led to critical mistakes,” Faruqui said.

Faruqui said he has signed off on some 400 criminal complaints in the last five years but had never held such a hearing or ruled against the government during one.

The ruling came after an unusual three-day hearing last week, which featured hours of testimony from FBI agent Bryan Witt. Witt testified that the investigation came from a direct assignment by FBI Director Kash Patel the morning after a primetime address by Trump in which he called for the prosecution of individuals involved in the agency’s shuttered Foreign Influence Task Force.

Floris and Benavides both served in supervisory positions at the task force, and Witt testified that the agency investigated the pair for months before focusing on their 2023 testimony to Congress.

Faruqui noted that the transcript showed that many of the supposedly false statements were not false and that officials did not do the work to show that Floris and Benavides knew at the time that some of their statements might have been false, a necessary element of the crime.

Statements by Judiciary Committee majority general counsel Steve Castor about the alleged lies were “inadequate, incorrect and not credible,” Faruqui said, adding that Castor talked about the impact of the supposed lies in the pair’s testimony without having attended the Benavides interview or reviewed the transcript of either interview.

According to Faruqui, the government offered an incomprehensible “word salad” justification as to why the pair might have lied to Congress by arguing they wanted to downplay the task force’s role in handling the laptop ahead of the 2020 election.

“It’s not close, it’s nothing,” Faruqui said.

The government could still appeal Faruqui’s ruling to Chief Judge James Boasberg or seek a grand jury indictment of the pair. However, Faruqui said it was “self-evident” that the government was avoiding presenting the case before a grand jury, noting he had to pause proceedings several times last week for the government to present grand jury indictments, including one failed one.

“It turns out ham sandwiches are harder to indict these days,” Faruqui said, referencing a famous aphorism that a prosecutor “could indict a ham sandwich.”

The government would have had to secure an indictment to proceed with the case regardless of his ruling. Faruqui said the decision to proceed with a complaint, coupled with the timing of the case, made him concerned about the political nature of the investigation.

“There is no other event on the calendar except for the midterm elections tomorrow,” Faruqui said. “I will not bury my head in the sand.”
