#6053. In DC on election night? Here’s where to watch results roll in

Some races may be too close to call, but one thing will be certain Tuesday no matter what — bar specials.

Residents of D.C. observe election night like some other cities observe major sporting events. And after the Nationals failed to advance to the postseason this year and with the first playoff game for the Washington Spirit still a few days away, the midterms will be the main ticket in town.

“It’s usually standing room only every time. I don’t think it matters whether it’s presidential or midterms,” said Matt Weiss, who owns Capitol Hill’s Union Pub.

The Halloween vibes aren’t over yet at Union Pub, thanks to a special “Midterm Massacre” menu. Inspired by competitive Senate races, it features $9 cocktails and shooters like the Haunted Horsefeather (Kansas), Maineiac Martini (Maine) and the Devil’s Duck Fart (Alaska).

While the pub will also be showing the Washington Capitals play the Dallas Stars at 7 p.m., Weiss said the sound will be on for election results rather than hockey. He expects around 50 percent more business than a regular Tuesday, which is already a busy night with weekly trivia.

Weiss said he can’t remember a time when his bar, which originally opened as Red River Grill in 1995, wasn’t showing election returns coming in.

“It’s just like being open for the Super Bowl or being open for the Washington Spirit being in the finals; we do benefit from having these types of events,” said Jesse Rauch, a partner at metrobar.

Rauch’s bar in Northeast D.C., known for its decommissioned railcar, isn’t usually open on Tuesdays, but election night is different.

With some races taking longer to call than others, Rauch said he’ll stay open as long as he can.

“We’re gonna play it by ear,” he said. “I do need to send my team home at some point to make sure that they’re well rested and all that. But we’ll stay open for as long as the energy is good.”

Given the District’s political leanings, most of the election night fans will be cheering on Democrats up and down the ballot. Kamala Harris carried more than 90 percent of the vote in D.C. in 2024, while President Donald Trump had 6 percent.

Rauch did point to one thing that might affect his sales, but he said he doesn’t mind.

“A lot of people in D.C. are in Maryland and in Virginia and in Pennsylvania door knocking, and they’ll be door knocking until the very end. Because of that, some people just aren’t in town, which I’m really proud of my neighbors who are able to do that,” he said.

If you’re looking for a place to be on election night, here are a few airing the results:

Teddy and the Bully Bar 1200 19th St. NW“We’ve got $8 oyster shooters, $8 NYC Mules, $4 New York style hot dogs, a $9.99 Angus beef smashburger, $5 soft pretzels with house-made beer cheese, $8 funnel cake with raspberry coulis and powdered sugar, and much, much more.”

Union Pub201 Massachusetts Ave. NE“Midterm Massacre Menu featuring $9 cocktails and shooters inspired by some of the country’s most competitive Senate races.”

Shaw’s Tavern520 Florida Ave. NW“Grab your crew, order a round of margaritas, and settle in as the results roll in … Taco and margarita specials all night.”

Barrel613 Pennsylvania Ave. SE“We’ll have the midterm election results on C-SPAN all night long, and we’re letting the cocktails have their own race: Blue Passion Fruit Margarita, Red Strawberry Daiquiri. Every drink counts as a vote.”

metrobar640 Rhode Island Ave. NE“Slices & Sips Happy Hour till 7pm … $10 pies from El Jefe and our rotating happy hour menu of craft cocktails, local beer, and wine.”

Boundary Stone116 Rhode Island Ave. NW“All parties, independents, political junkies, and the politically exhausted are welcome … All night happy hour. Burgers, wings, fish & chips & pub favorites.”

Red Derby3718 14th St. NW“Live Streaming RESULTS Watch Party: 1/2 price BURGERS, $4 Natty Boh’s, Blue Wave Shooters.”

Roofers Union2446 18th St. NW“Red or Blue? We’re voting for tacos! … Live election coverage, Taco Tuesday specials & margaritas.”

Highlands Tavern3421 Connecticut Ave. NW“To keep the energy going through the early morning hours, we are pouring $5 pints of local Senate Beer all night long.”

Pitchers 2317 18th St. NW“Join us at Pitchers for an election watch party and bingo as we watch the results unfold together.”

Busboys and PoetsAll locations“Enjoy live election coverage on TVs throughout the restaurant, games and activities, great food, community conversation, and all-night happy hour beginning at 3 p.m.”

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

The highlights this week: Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado returns home, Flávio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after losing the presidential runoff, and Latin American diplomats back their candidates in the race for United Nations secretary-general.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

The highlights this week: Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado returns home, Flávio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after losing the presidential runoff, and Latin American diplomats back their candidates in the race for United Nations secretary-general.

On Sunday, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado announced that she had returned to the country. Tens of thousands of supporters greeted her in the capital, Caracas. In a social media post, she pledged to work “for each family to be reunited, for freedom for every political prisoner, and for freedom for Venezuela.”

Machado was most recently staying in Panama after leaving Venezuela around a year ago to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. In the last few months, the Trump administration instructed neighboring governments to block her return to Venezuela, according to multiple media outlets.

Machado is an influential opponent of acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez. The United States is working with Rodríguez to revive the oil sector in Venezuela after forcibly removing President Nicolás Maduro in January. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio says the U.S. plans for Venezuela eventually include free elections, but no date has been set.

Though U.S. maneuvers have prompted some investments in the country’s oil sector, working-class Venezuelans are still grappling with poor economic conditions, including annual inflation exceeding 400 percent and daily, hourslong blackouts in some parts of the country.

The Trump administration says a no-bid deal it reached in August to take a partial stake in production at 17 Venezuelan oil fields will financially benefit Venezuelans. But a copy of the agreement viewed by ProPublica showed “the potential benefits to [Venezuelan] people are largely absent from the text,” whose terms “favor U.S. interests at every turn.”

Machado has called for presidential elections by mid-2027. Her team, as well as many Venezuelan analysts, argues that companies considering investing in the country will feel more secure about its regulatory environment after a vote. Elections would also allow Venezuela’s government more legitimacy to tackle macroeconomic problems.

In recent weeks, the United States acted to ease Machado’s reentry into Venezuela by telling the Rodríguez administration that it should permit the move, Rubio told journalists on Monday. The same day, the U.S. State Department announced its most detailed plans yet for when and how elections might occur.

Nominating committees chosen as part of a U.S.-backed dialogue between the Venezuelan government and opposition figures will select new judges for the top court and a separate electoral court by around the end of this year, an unnamed State Department official told reporters in a briefing.

At that point, Rodríguez is expected to declare the presidency formally vacant, triggering a six-month deadline for elections.

In a separate press briefing, Rubio responded to a question about whether Rodríguez might try to delay that timeline. He said: “I clearly intend to see this thing well in advance of the time I leave this position,” referring to the U.S. presidential transition in January 2029.

To many observers in Venezuela, the timing of Machado’s return and the State Department’s new statements on an electoral timeline was no coincidence. “María Corina’s arrival forced the United States to define a road map” toward a vote, economist Asdrúbal Oliveros said in a Wednesday radio appearance.

The U.S. plan to move toward elections is “the only game in town,” Rubio argued in his comments to the press, saying that Washington stands ready to use tools such as sanctions as leverage on the Rodríguez administration. “We have total control of Venezuela,” Trump said on Sunday.

Friday, Oct. 30, to Wednesday, Nov. 4: The United Kingdom’s King Charles III and Queen Camilla visit Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda.

Wednesday, Nov. 4, to Thursday, Nov. 5: Spain hosts Latin American leaders at the Ibero-American Summit.

Friday, Nov. 6, to Tuesday, Nov. 17: Pope Leo XIV visits Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru.

U.N. sec-gen race expands. Top diplomats from Latin American and Caribbean countries gathered at the United Nations this week to make public appeals that the next secretary-general come from the region. A group of former foreign ministers published an open letter defending the same position.

Informal U.N. tradition dictates that it’s Latin America’s turn for the role, but after weeks of candidates from Costa Rica and Guyana leading straw polls, a candidate from the United Arab Emirates entered the race last week—raising the possibility that the region could lose its chance to hold the top job.

In recent days, reports suggested that Turkey was considering nominating a former foreign minister and that the Trump administration was floating the idea of backing former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban.

Devex’s Colum Lynch wrote on social media last week that many in diplomatic circles thought the Emirati candidate would prevail, though China still appeared to support a candidate from Latin America or the Caribbean. Latin American countries have not announced a consensus about their own top candidate.

Supporters of former Ecuadorian presidential candidate Luisa González hold campaign banners and chant slogans demanding her release outside the Modelo Police Headquarters in Guayaquil, Ecuador, on Oct. 23.Marcos Pin/AFP via Getty Images

Opposition figure detained in Ecuador. Last week, Ecuadorian authorities arrested former presidential candidate Luisa González as she faces an investigation for violating campaign finance rules. González is now in pretrial detention; she denies wrongdoing. The arrest triggered fresh criticism that Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa is targeting political opponents.

This year, Ecuadorian authorities have blocked multiple opposition parties from competing in local elections scheduled for November. They include González’s left-wing Citizen Revolution Movement; the Amigo movement, which Citizen Revolution members hoped to use to run for office following that ban; the left-wing Unión Popular; and the centrist Construye.

In August, the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights issued a public statement of concern about the mounting legal challenges for opposition actors in Ecuador, calling on the government to “ensure pluralist political participation” ahead of the November vote.

González’s detention “deepens worries about the state of Ecuadorian democracy,” the editorial board of Ecuadorian newspaper El Mercurio wrote last week.

Tacos at the top. Restaurants that receive coveted Michelin ratings often suffer from pressure to maintain them. It was no different for a Mexico City taco stand. El Califa de León was Mexico City’s first taco stand to earn the distinction in 2024. But growing pains and a dispute over who most deserved the credit led the top grillmaster to leave within months, the Washington Post reported. The taco stand lost its star this year.

The affair triggered debates in Mexico City not only about what makes a good taco stand but also why Michelin took so long to honor one after awarding street food in other parts of the world. Those curious to try the Michelin star tacos can now sample them at El Califa de León as well as at its former chef’s new restaurant, Tacos Versalles.

Which of the following taco ingredients is least historically associated with Mexican tacos?

Hard-shell tacos are more associated with the Tex-Mex taco tradition than Mexican. Cotija cheese is from Michoacán, birria-style cooked meat is from Jalisco, and salsa fresca dates to the time of the Aztecs.

Brazilian Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro and his daughters arrive at Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport in Miami on Oct. 28. Joe Raedle/Getty Images

Enjoy our recent coverage of Brazil’s election: All FP links below are free to read.

A little over a day after Machado returned to Venezuela, another Latin American politician fled his country: Brazilian Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, who lost Sunday’s presidential election to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro is the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who also left Brazil after losing to Lula in 2022. He was later convicted of plotting a coup.

Brazil’s Supreme Court is investigating the younger Bolsonaro in multiple probes into alleged financial irregularities and money laundering. A Brazilian Supreme Court judge ordered Bolsonaro to hand over his passport on Monday after being briefed by police that he might try to run.

Though he said in a video posted that day that he would never flee Brazil, Bolsonaro and his family carried out a secret journey through Argentina and Ecuador to the United States between Tuesday and Wednesday. Trump advisor Jason Miller helped with the arrangements, the Wall Street Journal reported.

On Wednesday, Bolsonaro baffled observers with a public letter proclaiming himself the rightful president-elect of Brazil, then quickly editing it to simply call himself Brazil’s “leader.” Multiple Brazilian news organizations reported Thursday that the Trump administration communicated to Bolsonaro that it did not support him declaring himself president-elect.

The letter suggested that Bolsonaro was seeking to rally international backing for his claim of election fraud. But that support would have likely been limited: Leaders around the world—including right-wing Latin American presidents—overwhelmingly recognized Lula’s victory, and Bolsonaro’s campaign coordinator said he saw no evidence of fraud.

The United States had not yet recognized Lula’s win as of Thursday, when Trump said he did not want to comment on the election, calling it a “disgrace.” On Wednesday, he said he wouldn’t “get involved” in the controversy over Bolsonaro.

Meanwhile, one of Bolsonaro’s competitors for leadership of Brazil’s right, São Paulo Gov. Tarcísio de Freitas, posted a video on Tuesday saying the “election is over” and suggesting that Brazil move on. Though Flávio Bolsonaro’s trip to the United States may have allowed him to avoid prosecution, he may have also ceded leadership of the political field.

Catherine Osborn is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Latin America Brief. She is a print and radio journalist based in Rio de Janeiro. X: @cculbertosborn

#6050. The Chokepoint Trap

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

How the Search for Economic Security Will End in Geopolitical Calamity

Henry Farrell, Abraham Newman, and Yeling Tan

Policymakers used to ignore chokepoints. Now they have trouble seeing anything else. U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration warns allies against dependence on China while it hunts for ways to exploit those allies’ own dependence on the United States—on its market, technologies, financial system, and security umbrella. Beijing, meanwhile, accuses Washington of economic coercion while leveraging its dominance over critical supply chains to press the United States and Europe. Europe hopes to build the euro into an alternative global currency to evade the dollar’s iron grip. Smaller players, too, have gotten into the act, as Iran tries to leverage its control over the Strait of Hormuz to put a stranglehold on the global oil trade.

This obsession with wielding and countering chokepoint power may seem sudden, but it has evolved over the last quarter century as a byproduct of globalization itself. As economies integrated, chokepoints proliferated: manufacturers extended supply chains across borders, banks routed transactions through the U.S. dollar system to minimize costs and delays, digital services took advantage of economies of scale, leading the market to become dominated by a handful of platforms. After the September 11, 2001, attacks, the United States combined its advocacy for free markets with an increasingly ambitious effort to exploit its dominant position in these networks, surveilling global communications and using its influence over banks worldwide to cut off financial flows to its adversaries. But even as it did so, most politicians and business leaders continued to focus on globalization’s economic efficiencies.

Moves by Trump in his first term, however, caused world leaders to take more notice of chokepoints. The COVID-19 pandemic heightened countries’ fears of external dependence. Then, during Trump’s second administration, China learned that the best way to stop him is to squeeze a chokepoint. The United States’ hubristic erosion of basic norms of constraint led other countries, such as Iran, to explore options they had never previously dared to exploit.

Compared with an excessively rosy vision of globalization that emphasized the efficiencies of interdependence, it may now seem savvy to view the world economy as a system of chokepoints that countries can either turn to their advantage or see turned against them. But the chokepoint view has its own deadly blind spot. It is leading policymakers to focus on capabilities rather than strategy—to fixate on what leverage they have, and what leverage others have over them, rather than considering what happens when many countries build up their chokepoint power all at once.

The result is a familiar but dangerous dynamic: the security dilemma, in which one country’s efforts to secure itself make others feel threatened and respond in kind, leaving everyone less safe. The more that countries strengthen their control over chokepoints or protect themselves from coercion, the more they can make rivals feel that their own economic security has been undermined and provoke retaliation. As economic scholars such as David Bulman and Matt Ferchen have pointed out, each country’s individual actions contribute to the construction of a collective trap. The United States’ efforts to hamstring Chinese technology firms, for instance, led China to accelerate its technological development, which in turn spurred American fears of Chinese domination—a self-perpetuating spiral. Each side’s attempt to become safer makes others feel less secure, driving further escalation.

Escaping the chokepoint trap will be difficult precisely because it is collective. Any government that exercises restraint risks becoming a victim. And although the chokepoint trap may resemble the security dilemma, during the Cold War the measures that ultimately contained a runaway cycle of military provocations were implemented only after the deadly threat of the Cuban missile crisis focused leaders’ attention. An obsessive focus on chokepoints might lead to collective disaster, but it will be remarkably hard for states to jump off the escalator and balance making credible threats with offering credible assurances and seeking collective understandings. The most likely outcome is a fragmented world in which governments and private actors alike face increased volatility and the risk of escalation into something much worse: economic shocks, cascading disruptions, and even war.

In the traditional security dilemma, one country’s defensive move can appear offensive to another. A state may seek peaceful relations with a neighbor but worry that a belligerent leader could someday come to power next door. To hedge against that small but real risk, it might invest in a new weapons system or modestly increase the size of its army. Its neighbor could reasonably become alarmed. What if the buildup is preparation for an invasion? It may respond by ramping up its own defense spending, leading the first country to grow more suspicious and build up its military further, setting off an escalatory spiral.

Sometimes, of course, governments do have genuinely belligerent intentions. But even if all countries genuinely want peace, they can end up violently distrusting each other and seeking to field massive, expensive armies. In such a mistrustful atmosphere, innocent mistakes can easily be misinterpreted. In a classic 1978 essay about the security dilemma, the political scientist Robert Jervis argued that countries can mitigate the risk of misinterpretation by ensuring that the acts they undertake to enhance their security are obviously defensive rather than offensive—for example, by investing in fortifications deep inside their own territories instead of deploying troops to forward bases. But even passive defenses can heighten tensions: if a country feels better protected against retaliation, its rivals may fear that it will find aggression less risky.

In later writing, Jervis suggested that similar ambiguities might undermine economic and technological security, too. But economic warfare is even likelier to generate unintended escalation than the traditional security dilemma. Unlike military investments, economic policies can be difficult to classify as offensive or defensive. When China builds up its semiconductor sector, is it merely protecting its domestic economy or augmenting its capacity to coerce? Industrial policy can be enacted for a purely defensive reason—to establish resilience against geopolitical shocks. But if such a policy succeeds in building economies of scale, other states might reasonably fear that industrial dominance might be converted into coercive tools.

Economic security officials are usually more interested in building capacity than in restraint, whereas traditional economic policymakers are more accustomed to soothing their own markets than to assuaging the concerns of competitors, let alone adversaries. Defense bureaucracies have strong command-and-control structures for a reason: ill-disciplined communications and misaligned decisions can have disastrous consequences. The institutions that make economic policy, by contrast—including central banks and departments of commerce—are usually not set up to speak with one voice. Many are weakly coordinated, and significant authority is delegated to local-level investment and trade agencies. Sometimes, as with central banks, their autonomy is deliberately protected. Whereas military units deployed on discrete missions cannot act without explicit authorization, most economic agencies enjoy wide freedom to act without being accused of going rogue. As this year’s disagreements between the U.S. Department of the Treasury and the Federal Reserve over bond yields illustrate, standard bureaucratic infighting can shade into visible conflict.

When governments pursue chokepoint warfare, the problems these institutional ambiguities create get much worse. In September 2025, on the heels of a series of high-level economic negotiations between top U.S. and Chinese officials aimed at stabilizing the bilateral relationship, the U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security enacted the so-called affiliates rule, which expanded export controls to cover more subsidiaries owned by entities on two U.S. government watch lists. The bureau publicly described the measure as an attempt to close a loophole and lighten administrative burdens; it has since suspended the rule. But the timing made outsiders unsure how to discern its broader strategic meaning. Was Commerce merely tightening the enforcement of existing export controls as part of an ongoing bureaucratic process, or was the United States, as Chinese officials suggested, deliberately engaging in “maximum pressure” tactics in between rounds of bilateral talks?

It can be even harder to interpret what autocracies intend, since policymakers in such regimes are more insulated from public scrutiny. For example, even after China promised to relax its restrictions on the exports of rare-earth minerals and magnets in July 2025, companies that applied for export licenses experienced unexplained delays. It was unclear whether China was deliberately signaling its ability to control critical supply chains or simply struggling to channel requests efficiently through a newly created export-control bureaucracy.

Governments engaging in economic warfare often intentionally write or enforce regulations ambiguously to prompt private actors to overcomply. This behavior makes others much more likely to interpret even hapless bureaucratic mistakes, delays, and unintentional overreach as malign and deliberate plotting. Such mistakes deepen mistrust among great powers, which are already inherently inclined to overrate the possibility of deliberate threats.

Conversely, leaders are often excessively optimistic about their ability to surgically inflict economic pain on target countries. The flow of commerce cannot be steered as carefully as drones can be guided to bomb weapons factories. Even precision measures, such as putting specific firms on export-control lists, can be ineffective. Controlled goods may end up in the possession of subsidiaries or clandestine intermediaries. Broad attempts to close loopholes can go too far, putting thousands of firms with complex ownership ties in the cross hairs of the economic security state.

In October 2025, China again expanded the reach of its rare-earth export controls to retaliate against the affiliates rule and further efforts by Washington to restrict Chinese firms’ access to U.S. technologies. If these measures had not been suspended the following month, they would have affected production chains throughout Europe and Asia as well as in the United States. Officials who dream of an optimized form of chokepoint warfare in which they can fire an economic sniper rifle at judiciously selected targets regularly discover they are wielding a blunderbuss whose pellets fly in all directions—and the collateral damage only increases the risk of retaliatory spirals.

The more some countries move to control key chokepoints, the more others will worry about how those chokepoints may be weaponized and seek to leverage their own. The result is a world bristling with chokepoints and defenses in which every power still feels completely insecure. Even the most ordinary kinds of mutual dependence can begin to look like existential security risks. Put another way, in a world in which everything is connected, nearly everything could be considered a chokepoint. A piece of legislation introduced in the U.S. Senate in 2025 and the House in 2026, for instance, identifies even smart ovens and clothes dryers as potential security threats.

Historically effective ways of limiting trade disputes may fail in chokepoint warfare. In traditional tariff wars, governments often try to match like with like, responding to a butter tariff with a countertariff on eggs. Maintaining proportionality is much harder when economic security risks are diverse, when different chokepoints confer different kinds of leverage, and when countries that want to retaliate against the weaponization of one network have to turn to different networks to respond.

In April 2025, when the United States threatened China with sweeping tariffs and boosted its export controls on semiconductors, China could not retaliate by imposing an equivalent restriction on American semiconductors because it does not control the same chokepoint. Instead, it used its advantage over a different bottleneck, rare earths. But when countries weaponize entirely different chokepoints that sit at the center of complex and global supply chains, there is no easy way to judge whether a reaction will match the economic magnitude of the original act. Any notion of a simple escalation ladder that adversaries can climb up and down becomes a fantasy.

Rapid and unpredictable technological change makes this dynamic even more dangerous. As Jervis warned, countries persistently worry that technological innovation will create enduring advantages for their adversaries. Such anxieties can worsen the chokepoint trap, inspiring countries to try to impede their rivals’ progress and race to beef up their own autonomy. The Biden administration, anticipating that AI might swiftly accelerate advances in a variety of military and civilian domains, sought to impede Chinese AI development by restricting the country’s access to specialized semiconductors. Administration officials stressed that their goals were limited, describing their approach to China as “small yard, high fence.” Unsurprisingly, Beijing rejected this benign framing and saw the moves as a threat to its long-term future. China accelerated its own semiconductor development and is encouraging its companies to wean themselves from U.S. products, leaving the United States with less influence over Chinese technological development and more reason to worry about future Chinese aggression.

After the attacks of September 11, 2001, the United States began to make much more systematic use of economic and technological chokepoints: snooping on both adversaries and allies, and exploiting the dollar’s dominance to investigate and impose sanctions on foreign banks and companies. American officials came to see the global economy’s interconnectedness as something to manipulate—to deter U.S. opponents or strongarm allies into compliance. The George W. Bush and Obama administrations expanded sanctions to squeeze Iran’s economy, forcing Tehran to the negotiating table. The first Trump administration introduced new technological controls to limit Chinese companies’ access to advanced semiconductors, setting the precedent for the Biden administration’s efforts to impede Chinese AI more broadly.

But during this period, American officials usually paid little attention to the cumulative downside. Financial sanctions, for example, were attractive because most of the costs fell on the foreigners they targeted and foreigners who wanted to do deals with the targets. Exploiting chokepoints became a self-perpetuating enterprise with little purpose beyond sustaining itself. A 2024 Washington Post analysis found that the United States was sanctioning people, properties, or organizations in a third of all countries. Bill Reinsch, a former Commerce Department official, told the newspaper that such sanctions had become “the most important foreign policy tool in the U.S. arsenal,” but “nobody in government is sure this whole strategy is even working.”

Yet the more the United States exploited chokepoints in this way, the more it provoked countermeasures and imitation. And as other powers have begun to develop their own chokepoint capabilities, they are proving no more cautious. China has never hesitated to use economic pressure to get its way. But it used to threaten countries’ access to its domestic market rather than control global bottlenecks. Two key events altered this playbook. In 2013, leaks made by the former U.S. National Security Agency contractor Edward Snowden revealed the extraordinary reach the United States had in global information networks. Then, the first Trump administration’s punishing campaigns against the Chinese telecommunications companies ZTE and Huawei demonstrated Washington’s willingness to coerce.

After these shocks, China’s technological debates began to emphasize themes such as “information security” and “decoupling.” Chinese leader Xi Jinping, whose speeches once focused on straightforward industrialization, increasingly stressed how economic development could not be separated from national security. His “dual circulation” strategy both sought to reduce dependence on overseas markets and reduce China’s exposure to foreign economic pressure. As Beijing became more conscious of its vulnerability to U.S. technology and finance, it not only accelerated technological self-reliance but created new government structures that mimicked those that Washington used to target other countries, such as an export control regime and security screening for inbound and outbound investment.

China justifies these measures as self-defense. But it has rapidly moved from proportionate responses to dramatic counterescalation. When, in April 2025, Trump announced his “Liberation Day” tariffs, China not only imposed licensing restrictions on rare-earth exports but also suggested, a few months later, that its dominance over rare-earth processing gave it regulatory authority over the entire semiconductor supply chain. China also barred some exports of dual-use goods to U.S. defense contractors and civilian technology companies, sanctioned U.S. firms it claimed were engaging in arms sales or technology cooperation with Taiwan’s military, and launched antitrust investigations into Google, Nvidia, and DuPont. Although some of these measures were subsequently suspended or terminated as a result of negotiations with the United States, China has since repeatedly demonstrated its ability to hit back against what it perceives as foreign economic coercion.

In another counteroffensive, Beijing has begun creating a “blocking” regime to punish companies that comply with other countries’ economic security restrictions. Foreign banks that follow U.S. law and stop doing business with a sanctioned Chinese refinery could well be sued in Chinese courts in the future. Rules promulgated in August of this year make it illegal for Chinese firms to provide information or do business with six organizations that do due diligence and risk assessment on supply chains and promote labor rights, making it harder for them to generate the forensics that help companies worldwide comply with American laws.

By now, China has reshaped its economic policy around a narrow view of its national security concerns. And just like the United States’ chokepoint exploitation did, China’s moves to fence off ever larger parts of its economy will prompt destabilizing counterreactions and imitations. An examination of data from the Global Trade Alert, an independent monitor that tracks government policy changes affecting international trade flows, captures governments’ growing willingness to choke off trade. Since 2020, countries have, on average, enacted seven times as many export restrictions per year as they did between 2010 and 2019. The chokepoint trap is closing on governments as they find themselves entangled in an ever more complicated web of economic and technological conflicts.

In this dynamic, Europe—whose economy is nominally larger than China’s—finds itself perpetually forced to accommodate. Its ability to formulate coherent economic-security strategies and design policy tools is better developed than those of Beijing and Washington. Over the past few years, it has delivered what could be a powerful anti-coercion instrument that would allow it to retaliate extensively against economic pressure, an economic security strategy that identifies the risks of chokepoint warfare, and a Chips Act 2.0 that calls for maintaining Europe’s position as an “indispensable player” in supply chains. But it has struggled to turn words into leverage. It remains deeply dependent on U.S. technology and security guarantees; its dreams of controlling its own chokepoints dissipate in the face of the risk that Washington could tear up its NATO commitments. So far, Europe has not even attempted to deploy its anti-coercion instrument against the United States, despite the Trump administration’s repeated coercion.

Europe is increasingly constrained by dependence on China, too. When the EU imposed countervailing duties on Chinese electric vehicles it found were unfairly subsidized, China was quick to target vital sectors in EU member states, forcing European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to spend precious political capital keeping Berlin and Madrid behind a common EU policy. In September 2025, when the Dutch government attempted to assert its sovereign authority over Nexperia, a Dutch chip manufacturer that was purchased by a Chinese company, Beijing prevented the firm from finishing the chips in China, creating a supply chain crisis across the European car industry. According to a mid-2026 report by Tobias Gehrke, a senior policy analyst at the European Council on Foreign Relations, Chinese threats are preventing European member states from even contemplating the comprehensive actions they would need to reduce their dependence.

Every European wish to assert strategic autonomy is hemmed in by the expectation that the United States or China will split its solidarity. And national security decisions remain the domain of member states, preventing the EU from leveraging potential chokepoints. Europe has made huge strides in acting collectively to impose sanctions against Russia, but enforcement still largely depends on national governments. The result is a bloc that understands the dangers of escalation better than the United States or China but cannot do much to avoid them.

Japan, meanwhile, began to think about the threat posed by Chinese coercion early and has better tailored its approach, balancing strategic autonomy and resilience against potential external coercion with control over vital technological chokepoints. It has created a national stockpile of rare earths to mitigate Chinese efforts to pressure its economy while making itself indispensable to U.S. military supply chains. But even Japan has shown it can succumb to the seduction of chokepoint politics: in 2019, it limited South Korea’s access to key semiconductor chemicals in response to the country’s pursuit of reparations for World War II harms.

And now, even smaller, poorer countries have been caught up in the spiral. Some have benefited from the spread of chokepoint warfare in the short term: the Philippines, for instance, won millions in grants from the United States when Washington attempted to press allies to block Huawei from their telecommunications infrastructures. Others are simply getting squeezed. The Kachin Independence Army in Myanmar is selling dysprosium and terbium, which are used in industrial magnets, to fuel its civil war against the military junta—giving China, the main buyer, greater leverage over the conflict. Greenland, with its vast supply of natural resources, has faced repeated military threats from Trump. As time goes on, the costs are likely to heavily outweigh the benefits, even for countries receiving some side payments. Governments in smaller, poorer countries want the autonomy to chart a path toward greater prosperity for their citizens. The global obsession with economic security makes finding that path harder.

Right now, the United States and China are locked in a short-term stasis. Washington is moderating its use of chokepoints out of fear of ferocious blowback, and China sees little benefit in direct provocation. But this moment of stability is likely to be fleeting. Even after Trump leaves the White House, the United States will certainly keep pressing for global technological dominance, and it is likely to continue its efforts to dominate energy. China will keep pursuing policies aimed at quietly building dependencies and undermining the United States’ coercive power. Stalemates are fragile in a world in which the incentives inexorably point toward escalation.

The powers with the most latitude to shape the world now see chokepoints as capabilities. Their vision rarely stretches to the strategic implications of their actions. As they build their offensive capacities and shore up their defenses, they convince themselves that they are ensuring their own security. Instead, they are miring themselves in a chokepoint arms race that will render them, as well as everyone else, much less secure. The jealousies of the traditional national security dilemma are now spilling over into the global economy. A world in which economic chokepoints become forts, garrisons, and guns all at once will be characterized by perpetual low-level economic conflict and the ever-present risk of larger conflagrations.

To identify broader solutions, some scholars and policy thinkers look to the Cold War for inspiration, emphasizing the value of de-escalation and mutual restraint. During that era, the risk of nuclear war was mitigated with regular meetings to establish a shared understanding of redlines and systems that ensure effective communication in a crisis. Over time, these gave rise to more formal arrangements, such as treaties regulating arms and troop movements, enforced by satellites and other means of monitoring. An assurance-based security logic can, in some cases, insulate economic chokepoints from weaponization. Singapore, for instance, has signed agreements with Australia and New Zealand to keep essential supplies flowing between their countries. In 2022, the World Trade Organization’s members agreed not to place export restrictions on food purchased by the World Food Program for humanitarian purposes.

Yet it will be difficult to turn such commitments into a large-scale system of effective communication and mutual restraint. It took the Cuban missile crisis and the threat of nuclear annihilation to awaken the Cold War’s antagonists to how individually rational acts could lead to collectively awful outcomes. Today, as the cycle of mutual suspicion gathers speed, it becomes increasingly hard to reverse. The more governments create bureaucracies devoted to identifying and controlling economic chokepoints, the more a chokepoint logic becomes the default lens through which they make even routine economic policy. It is no coincidence that Europe, the great power that is the most hesitant to actually weaponize chokepoints, is also the power that is least capable of deploying them.

It is more likely that the chokepoint trap will tighten. Military competition has long driven states to build similar institutions—armed forces, defense bureaucracies, and domestic weapons industries. This kind of mirroring is already beginning to happen in economic security. China is becoming more like the United States, building bureaucratic tools to leverage chokepoints against its adversaries; meanwhile, the United States is imitating China, intervening in its domestic economy to reshape it around security concerns. The European Union will choose between managing its slide to irrelevance or radically reforming its internal balance of power in order to keep up. Smaller powers will do what they can to emulate bigger ones while relying on their protection.

This will be hard for governments, but much worse for international business. Firms will have to navigate a labyrinthine and unpredictable global economy in which payment and information systems are fragmented and clashing powers try alternately to press them into service or squeeze them out of existence. Multinational corporations may become unified entities in name only, as their subsidiaries face countervailing pressures from host governments. Economic efficiencies that seem natural today, such as the seamlessness of international financial transactions, may evaporate as governments equate global infrastructures with national insecurity.

Even this is not the worst-case scenario. The greatest risk posed by the chokepoint trap is not its predictable miseries but its unpredictable disasters. Suspicion, misunderstanding, and intense competition in the realm of economic security can create an ideal recipe for war. Take just one hypothetical. It is not difficult to imagine a scenario in which additional Chinese restrictions on rare-earth magnets degrade, among other things, the United States’ ability to rebuild the missile stockpiles that this year’s Iran war has depleted. Whether or not Beijing intended this effect, U.S. leaders could easily interpret such an act as evidence that China plans to launch a military offensive against Taiwan before the United States can achieve full independence from Chinese supply chains, prompting a sense of urgency in Washington to strike first.

There is plenty of historical precedent for what may seem to be a marginal and worst-case scenario. In The Economic Weapon, the historian Nicholas Mulder documents how, in the 1930s, Axis powers’ fears of League of Nations sanctions and potential economic isolation led them to aggressively seize territory and resources before it was too late. The chokepoint trap is bad enough. What it leads to can be worse.

HENRY FARRELL is Stavros Niarchos Foundation Agora Institute Professor of International Affairs at Johns Hopkins University and an External Professor at the Santa Fe Institute.

ABRAHAM NEWMAN is John Powers Chair in International Business Diplomacy at the School of Foreign Service and a Professor in the Department of Government at Georgetown University.

YELING TAN is Professor of Public Policy in the Blavatnik School of Government at Oxford University and a Nonresident Senior Fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics.

#6048. “The sitting president doesn’t win”: Ahead of midterms, Trump reflects on himself

On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as âThe most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.â

âWhen you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,â Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to âblow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.â

âIf the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,â Trump said midway in his speech. âNow that doesnât happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesnât win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.â

Start your day with essential news from Salon. Sign up for our free morning newsletter, Crash Course.

The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report âThe party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.â The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting âthat Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.â If a sweep happens in the toss up races, itâll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.Â

Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the New York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how big a role early votes will play in the outcome.

#6046. What Life Is Like by the Strait of Hormuz Right Now

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Dispatch: What Life Is Like by the Strait of Hormuz Right Now

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

BANDAR ABBAS, Iran—Along Iran’s main highway south, debris lies scattered across the road, while bridges and tunnels are damaged or destroyed. Half-buried in the dirt, a broken road sign points toward Bandar Abbas, Iran’s main port city and the gateway to the Strait of Hormuz.

“The war has never stopped here,” said Khaleh Zeynab, 51, a food vendor working alongside Bandar Abbas’s corniche. She gestures toward the beach and the strait. “My son Reza is out there fighting. He’s been working on a ship since the beginning of the war. I know he could be killed at any moment, and that scares me, but he’s a soldier. If he doesn’t do his job, somebody else has to. We have to defend our country.”

BANDAR ABBAS, Iran—Along Iran’s main highway south, debris lies scattered across the road, while bridges and tunnels are damaged or destroyed. Half-buried in the dirt, a broken road sign points toward Bandar Abbas, Iran’s main port city and the gateway to the Strait of Hormuz.

“The war has never stopped here,” said Khaleh Zeynab, 51, a food vendor working alongside Bandar Abbas’s corniche. She gestures toward the beach and the strait. “My son Reza is out there fighting. He’s been working on a ship since the beginning of the war. I know he could be killed at any moment, and that scares me, but he’s a soldier. If he doesn’t do his job, somebody else has to. We have to defend our country.”

When the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran began on Feb. 28, residents in Bandar Abbas watched ships burn, missiles streak across the sky, and fighter jets fly overhead. Months later, explosions from the strait can still be heard almost daily, though it is not always clear whether they are air defense interceptions or fresh attacks.

What is clear, however, is that the war has made life increasingly difficult for communities whose livelihoods depend on the Strait of Hormuz.

Khaleh Zeynab sells bread in Bandar Abbas on Sept. 19.

“It’s been tough to make ends meet,” Zeynab said. Before the war, Bandar Abbas drew tourists from across Iran as well as abroad. Since the fighting began, visitors have largely disappeared, while many residents—seeking safety after repeated attacks on the city—left for smaller villages elsewhere in Hormozgan province. At the same time, prices have surged across Iran, especially in urban centers. Food costs have risen sharply, often even doubling, adding to the pressure on families already struggling to get by.

Pouring dough onto a makeshift stove propped up on the sidewalk to make tomoshi, a thin flatbread popular in southern Iran, Zeynab said she is now helping her daughter-in-law care for her three children while Reza is away. He has returned home only once since the war began and has yet to meet his youngest daughter, born just two months ago.

“That’s what this war is doing to us,” Zeynab said with a shrug.

A road sign pointing toward Bandar Abbas, damaged in the U.S. attack on the Shur River bridge, on Sept. 19.

The war has left its mark on Bandar Abbas, too, home to roughly 700,000 people and the economic powerhouse of southern Iran. A critical gateway for imports and exports, the city handles up to 90 percent of Iran’s container shipping, and more than half of the country’s maritime trade passes through its ports.

Several ports, including the city’s fishing port, have been targeted in attacks. So has the Shur River bridge outside the city, which connects Hormozgan to neighboring Kerman province, as well as the provincial center of Iran’s state broadcaster, IRIB. The latter was “completely destroyed by 24 missiles,” said Ahmad Hosseini, a 64-year-old construction worker who witnessed the attack. “So what?” he added. “We will just rebuild it.”

Workers rebuild the Shur River bridge outside Bandar Abbas on Sept. 19.

The Shur River bridge, which was destroyed in a U.S. attack, on Sept. 19.

Ahmad Hosseini, a construction worker, shows us missile fragments he collected from around a damaged building, where they had been scattered by the impact, in Bandar Abbas on Sept. 20.

In recent weeks, attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz have intensified, pushing oil prices once again above $100 a barrel. U.S. President Donald Trump has threatened further strikes against Iran after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3. Tehran, meanwhile, has signaled that it is preparing for a possible resumption of hostilities and issued threats against Washington and its allies. At the same time, Iran continues to seek a diplomatic solution. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said recently that Tehran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days remained on the table—an offer that Iran submitted in mid-September, following the collapse of an interim cease-fire. Negotiations have stalled, however, with Iran’s security chief saying the United States had failed to address all seven conditions Tehran had set for reopening the waterway.

For coastal Iranians, however, the strait is more than a geopolitical chokepoint or negotiation tool; it is their lifeline. Fishermen, shipbuilders, tour guides, port workers, and smugglers all depend on the sea—which has now become the war’s front line—for their livelihoods.

Fishermen work by the roadside after a day’s catch in Bandar Abbas on Sept. 22.

Amir, 24, has spent the past five years smuggling alcohol across the strait from Oman and the United Arab Emirates. He declined to give his full name or be photographed, knowing that doing so could get him into trouble with the authorities. He grinned sheepishly as he explained how the operation worked.

Smugglers on either side of the strait use small speedboats to meet at sea, coordinating their movements over radios. Sometimes, Amir and his small crew travel deep into the strait, and on other trips, they cross all the way to the opposite shore.

It is dangerous work, even for someone who knows these waters as well as Amir does. The war has made the business even more precarious, but the income is good, he explained, especially amid soaring inflation and a battered economy.

Amir was still smuggling booze when the war broke out but was caught by the Omani coast guard and spent two months in prison in Khasab, Oman, he said. “After my release, I was deported to Afghanistan. The Taliban then sent me back to Iran,” he said, adding that he didn’t know why he was first sent to Iran’s eastern neighbor.

Twelve-year-old Mohammad works for Amir, who asked not to be photographed, selling shisha along the water in Bandar Abbas on Sept. 19.

Since returning, Amir has been serving shisha at a seaside park in the city. He still regularly hears explosions from the strait, which is why he has taken a break from smuggling. But despite the risks, he wants to return.

“My father is a smuggler, too,” he said. “This is where the money is.”

For Ahmad Mokhtari, a shopkeeper in a small village just outside Bandar Abbas, the conflict has brought an unexpected opportunity to make money.

Recent war games highlight how Washington can improve its air defenses so the next round of fighting isn’t worse.

Some dramatic long-term consequences are just beginning to come into view.

But the continued shortfall of refined products means little relief at the pump.

“Many people have moved out of the city to be safer, and this has given many villages a strange boost. I used to come to the city once a month to shop. Now I’m traveling here every single day. Demand in the village has grown so much.”

Bandar Abbas, meanwhile, has yet to return to full capacity. Fishermen cannot venture as far into the strait as they used to, and some ports are operating at reduced capacity. Still, a kind of normalcy has returned.

The beach in Bandar Abbas on Sept. 19, where crowds gather for picnics after sunset as the weather cools down.

Twenty-three-year-old Kiana (foreground) poses for a portrait at the seaside on Sept. 19. She traveled to Bandar Abbas from Kerman with her family for a holiday.

In the evenings, when the heat and humidity become more bearable, people venture out along the corniche to meet friends, catch the sea breeze, grab a snack, or pose for photographs. It’s a laid-back atmosphere as the streets fill up. There’s music in the air, and occasionally, some people even dance.

But farther out, tankers remain stranded in the strait, some of them visible from the shoreline. The occasional sounds of explosions are carried across the water.

A beached boat near the shore of Bandar Abbas on Sept. 20. Locals offer conflicting accounts of its provenance; some say it was not there before the war and others that something happened to it during the conflict with the United States and Israel.

“We’ve gotten used to it,” Zeynab said. “The explosions and fighter jets are normal to us now.”

A woman wades offshore in Bandar Abbas on Sept. 23.

Stefanie Glinski is a journalist who covers conflicts and crises with a focus on the wider Middle East. X: @stephglinski

Mohammad Mohsenifar is a journalist based in Tehran.

#6045. Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

Showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses. “Who Is America?” The answer, on its face, will not surprise you: we are a nation of easy marks. Not merely easy, but willing.

Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.

Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom. But today, being on camera is so natural and desirable to most of us that we are willing to say or do just about anything for a few of the 15 minutes we believe to be our birthright.

“Ali G” and the characters the show introduced, including Borat Sagdiyev and Brüno Gehard, also were born years before Project Veritas and InfoWars and other right-wing vehicles of disinformation made hidden camera hoaxing into something sinister.

All of which is to say, “Who Is America?” is not, as Showtime would like you to believe, “the most dangerous show in history.” At best, it is an occasionally funny one.

But to anyone who mourns the collective deterioration of our population’s capacity to engage in critical thought, but has no idea of how urgent of a crisis that happens to be, Baron Cohen’s new endeavor is less of a comedy than a fright show. “Who Is America?” A nation of pliable dullards ripe for the hacking.

“Who Is America?” was produced in secret, and its pre-show marketing largely consisted of publicized declarations of outrage by such right-wing figures as Joe Walsh, Sarah Palin and Roy Moore. Each attempted to transform their extreme embarrassment at having been duped by a British clown hiding behind layers of latex and spirit gum into some approximation of righteous anger at said comedian’s dishonesty.

Showtime, meanwhile, maintained the aura of mystery surrounding the series almost to the brink of its debut, revealing the title only a little more than a week prior. The network released the briefest of clips featuring one famous interview subject, Dick Cheney.

This in itself was a bit of flimflam Showtime’s part: “Hope you’ll tune in next week for an interview with me,” Cheney says in the video, only to be a no-show in the premiere.

You can’t blame “Who Is America?” for saving its biggest fish for later, because the famous politicians in the opener prove the problem of our collective gullibility just fine by themselves. In fact, although liberals may have gotten a hearty guffaw out of hearing Palin’s wailing about having been faked out by Baron Cohen, the very same character — Dr. Billy Wayne Ruddick Jr. PhD of Truthbrary.org — sat down for a conversation with none other than the honorable junior senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders.

Prior to the premiere Billy Wayne tweeted a response to Palin’s accusation that he made fun disabled veterans. “I did NOT say I was a War Vet,” Ruddick’s “official” response reads, going on to explain that the service was in was “not military, but United Parcel”.

Nor does he make such assertions to Sanders, with whom he debates the merits of a universal healthcare plan. And when I say debate, what I mean is that Sanders very calmly shares statistics with Billy Wayne long after the interviewer’s line of questioning stops making sense. And when Sanders asks Billy Wayne to confirm that he is disabled, given that he is conducting the interview while seated on a motorized scooter, Baron Cohen’s character replies that no, he is not. “This here scooter is to preserve my body’s finite energy,” Billy Wayne says.

READ MORE: That viral “strangers on a plane” Twitter story: Not a rom-com but a horror show

One may be tempted to qualify Sanders’ appearance by pointing out that he acquitted himself well in the face of a person best be described as a few coconuts short of a beach vacation in Binomo.

But this fails to answer the question of why Sanders signed a release, allowing this interview to be broadcast. Did anyone on Sanders’ team vet Truthbrary.org the moment Billy Wayne mentioned it? Even if they thought he was genuine, what is to be gained from being seen in a televised debate with a guy whose site includes a page titled  “Obamanoids — For Real!”?

(To be fair, reportedly Baron Cohen almost fooled veteran news anchor Ted Koppel as part of his project. Koppel told The Hollywood Reporter that he was contacted to appear in a Showtime project titled “Age of Reason,” said to feature “conversations with distinguished experts in science and public policy, highlighting the brightest and most reputable minds on today’s most important topics.” Koppel, perhaps receiving brainwaves from his colleague Sam Donaldson, wised up before Baron Cohen could pull him too deeply into his game.)

A second character introduced in the premiere, an NPR shirt-wearing hyper-liberal named  Nira Cain-N’Degeocello, visits the opulent South Carolina home of wealthy Trump supporters he says are  “afflicted with white privilege.” But it soon becomes clear that his marks’ problem isn’t close-mindedness but over-correcting in the acceptance department. When Baron Cohen’s interviewer waxes on about encouraging his daughter Malala to “free bleed” on the American flag as a lesson, they simply nod and listen; when he chats about his wife’s ongoing affair with a dolphin, they don’t have any questions like, say, whether what they’re hearing is real.

This brings us to another answer to “Who Is America?”: we’re so aware of cameras, and desperate to have its focus upon us, that we will do and say anything without thinking of its possible permanence.

Demonstrating this is Baron Cohen’s third character Rick Sherman, an ex-con turned TV host who visits a Laguna Beach, California gallery to show his work, which is a series of capable but otherwise unextraordinary portraits rendered in feces and ejaculate.

Now, it’s entirely possible that the woman who runs the gallery might have been thinking she could have the next Andres Serrano on her hands. On the other hand, please.

This is a subject entirely aware of being on view, so obsessed with appearing erudite that while Rick is off camera, having excused himself to the facilities to commit another brown-and-white vision to paper, she addresses the camera like the host she was born to be.

“Who knew the world was capable of such oxymoronic paradoxical juxtapositions?” she muses. And this is before the homemade pubic hair paintbrush comes out.

Baron Cohen has pushed the limits of tolerant everyday people many times in the past, mostly in a way that makes them look reasonable or, at the very least, more intelligent than the put-ons he inflicts upon them. And this is perhaps one of the most depressing aspects about “Who Is America?”, its demonstration of how endemic our lack of analysis truly is. I’m not saying that gallery owner is a stupid woman, understand.

But her interview is an example of prizing exposure over lasting consequence. By that I’m not merely referring to the fact that she placated a man who not only handed her pieces of cardboard purportedly smeared with his own dried excrement, or waited to receive a fresh sample of his work, but that she decided she needed to share her expert observation as to why she needed to do so by uttering a sentence full of five dollar words that add up to absolute nonsense.

(Either that or she’s a friend of Baron Cohen’s and in on the gag. I hope it’s option two, as opposed to her actually legitimizing the artistic relevance of number two.)

A number of reviews of “Who Is America?” have pointed out that Baron Cohen’s sneaky deceit is no longer funny because the formerly insane viewpoints Baron Cohen’s tactics expose have been normalized.

This has always been the danger, but it’s one every sort of parody or satire contends with in the current climate. It’s difficult to lampoon leaders seeking to legislate ludicrous patches to crises like gun violence instead of adopting common sense solutions like stricter regulation.

Which brings us to the portion of “Who Is America?” guaranteed to dominate Monday’s gallery of crazy clips, fronted by Baron Cohen’s Col. Erran Morad, a self-styled Israeli anti-terrorism expert who calls himself “the terrorist terminator.”

The fake Mossad officer is there to promote his “Kinderguardians” program, a proposal that aims to train and arm toddlers in the classroom because, Moran says, arming teachers is crazy.

And this is the portion that has Walsh’s boxers in a bunch, because he joins House representatives Dana Rohrabacher and Joe Wilson in lending on-camera endorsements. Walsh’s comments are interwoven with a series of fake testimonials from the likes of Larry Pratt, executive director emeritus of the lobbying group Gun Owners of America and rape joke enthusiast.

Nobody forced Walsh to say, with gusto, “The way to stop a bad guy with is a good child with a gun. Happy shooting, kids!” If he didn’t want to say it, he wouldn’t have.

What Walsh might be upset about is being upstaged by Pratt, who earns some of the episode’s biggest laughs by reading the “science” behind the effectiveness of the fake program, revealing he doesn’t know the difference between human anatomy and hitmakers who grace Billboard’s pop charts.

Yes, “Who Is America?” gets mileage out of highlighting the callousness, sexism and extraordinary gullibility of conservatives, as Baron Cohen always has. But the things they say to him in disguise aren’t all that different than what they’d say on CNN, Fox, MSNBC or talk radio. Whatever power his comedy used to reveal is diminished by the fact that the charlatans no longer operate in secret.

Next week’s episode introduces one or two new characters, although I don’t imagine they do anything more “dangerous” than the four we met on Sunday. For a number of viewers who love Baron Cohen’s schtick, that won’t matter.

To them “Who Is America?” is precisely on brand, showing Americans famous and everyday reacting to bizarre situations with varying degrees of what we consider to be normalcy in a time where the baseline version of normal is constantly morphing and shifting.

To other viewers, however, “Who Is America?” is a confirmation that Baron Cohen has run some tests and can confirm there is limited and ever decreasing brain activity in this worsening patient we know as America. It is something to behold, that’s for sure. But I’m not sure it’s the stuff of groundbreaking comedy. It’s not even really news.
